outcomes.note: The structure is real and the headline numbers reproduce. The 24-module SCC has exactly the named membership and 95,192 raw lines in the top-level files. The 3-module SCC {compute_targets, selector_vocabulary_v2, topology_selectors} also exists. All 13 sites exist in production code before each file's cfg(test) line. The predicate use counts match (8/7/4/4/3) and the file sizes are right (engine_eval is 15,306 lines by wc, one off). Three parts of the characterization do not hold. (1) dirty.rs:282 -> engine_fixpoint::run_unified_pass_seeded is not an upward edge. engine_fixpoint imports only cache and deps. Removing this edge leaves the SCC unchanged, and with it kept, dirty falls out of the SCC once the other sites are cut. (2) 'Nearly all pure predicates' is overstated. expand_solver_position_expr mutates an expr and pushes diagnostics. realize_sub_override_handles takes &mut kernels. run_unified_pass_seeded is the Kahn core. Only the geometry_ops predicates, is_optimized_userfn_cell and sub_refs_in_op are clean predicates. (3) Moving the proposed 9 helpers does not dissolve the SCC. With the 6 module-pair edges those moves remove cut, a 5-module SCC remains: engine_admin, engine_build, engine_edit, engine_eval and geometry_ops. It remains because geometry_ops -> engine_build::realize_sub_override_handles, which the next_change does not move. Cutting all 13 still leaves a cache<->deps 2-cycle (cache.rs:13 uses deps::DependencyTrace, deps.rs:12 uses cache::NodeId) and an engine_admin/engine_edit/engine_eval 3-cycle. The statement does not mention either. The refactor would shrink the SCC from 24 to about 5 modules, not remove the layering problem.

outcomes.note: All claims hold at a030ee75. snapshot.rs::value_for and loop_closure.rs::resolve_joint_value implement the same order: direct binding, coupling follows parent, fixed sentinel, range midpoint. wrap_jointvalue_for_joint has the same 7-arm match as the pub(crate) loop_closure::value_for_joint, with the same coupling-parent sub-match. snapshot.rs already imports joint_range_midpoint from loop_closure, so the shared helper is reachable. The copies diverge on multi-DOF. snapshot's value_for keeps only JointValue::Scalar from the midpoint and returns None otherwise, so an unbound planar joint, or a spherical one (whose midpoint is the identity quaternion), makes the snapshot Undef. loop_closure resolves the same joint to Planar/Sphere/Cyl. One small difference: value_for returns a direct binding as a raw Value, while loop_closure converts it through jointvalue_from_bound_value. That does not weaken the claim. The test doc for snapshot_with_unbound_planar_returns_undef says joint_range_midpoint returns None for planar and defers the fix to #2670. That is false: joint_range_midpoint has a Planar arm returning Some(Planar([mx,my,mθ])), and a loop_closure test asserts [0.5,0.5,π/2]. Task 2670 has status done, and its deliverables include the planar finite-difference fallback. The comment in wrap_midpoint_for_joint (line ~1493) repeats the same stale claim. The cited deferral is therefore dead, and the test pins the divergence.

outcomes.note: The structure is real and the next_change scenario holds. Trampolines get `cancellation` from the per-dispatch handle. The GUI only sets `Engine::active_solve_cancel`, which reaches code via a thread-local installed in engine_compute.rs. elastic_static ignores its `_cancellation` parameter and polls the ambient handle. modal_ops polls only the parameter and never reads the ambient context. The per-dispatch handle is never cancelled in production. Three measurements are off. The first `#[cfg(test)]` is at line 271, and the counts come from the real tests-mod boundary at 5801, so the figures agree in spirit. (2) The `.running` cancel sites number 2, not 1: engine_eval.rs 10613 and 11667. Only the second carries the 'branch is dead' comment, though both use a fresh `next_index`/`c_id` and are equally unreachable. (3) modal_ops.rs also has a sixth function at line 3183 with an unused `_cancellation` param, so modal_ops is not uniformly polling. The source also documents the elastic_static choice. At lines ~3790 the comment says cancellation rides the ambient context rather than the 'deliberately unused' `_cancellation` parameter, to avoid threading it through the AdaptiveProblem trait. That weakens 'advertises a parameter it does not honour' as an accidental disagreement, but the two-channel split still exists.

outcomes.note:
The structure is real. Four top-level branches each carry their own spawn and PASS/FAIL recording. The helpers do reach branch state through globals: _ra_skip_engine rewrites _h2_discovered_list, _ra_skip_state_write reads `failures`, and _ra_partial_failed_names reads _H2_WORKDIR. The 6 spawn sites, 5 RESULT: FAIL sites and the per-branch coverage counts for sanitize, fail-detail, H3 and retry all reproduce. One caveat on the coverage count: the final backstop `_ra_interrupt_if_worktree_gone` at line 2057 runs after every branch, subset included, so the 2/4 for worktree-gone only holds for the per-iteration check. The code comment calling the backstop 'common to both pool and legacy' understates this.

The 'follow-up commits porting a feature to another branch' measurement does not hold, though. Only 3ef7845834 (collect FAIL-detail on the subset retry path) and 7439d071b2 (sanitize the subset re-emit) are ports into the subset branch. 746b4474ea introduced the git-env scrub as a new concern and wrapped all six spawns in that one commit, so it is a uniform rollout and the opposite of a branch-by-branch gap. 889910ef1d extends the _ra_collect_fail_detail sed chain to match _ra_emit_sanitized, so its 'second site' is a second function, not a second branch. The count is therefore about 2 of 44, not 4 of 44.

The omissions also look largely deliberate rather than accidental. The subset branch's header says it never consults _h3_exclude and runs a single attempt. The H9 branch says it deliberately ignores _h3_exclude. This weakens the 'nothing structural ensures a new concern reaches every branch' framing, because test_infra_git_env_isolation's end-to-end probe covers scrub propagation.

The next_change scenario is plausible, but its weight is overstated by the miscounted evidence.

findings.statement: Cooperative cancellation reaches trampolines through two unrelated channels, and the trampolines in this slice disagree on which one they read. solve_elastic_static_trampoline takes `_cancellation: &CancellationHandle` and ignores it. It reads the thread-local `solver_progress::current_solve_dispatch_context()` instead, which `engine_compute.rs` fills from `Engine::active_solve_cancel`; that is the handle the GUI sets via `set_active_solve_cancel` (gui/src-tauri/src/engine.rs). modal_ops (run_modal_analysis, run_mechanism_modal, run_transient_response) polls only the `cancellation` parameter. In production that parameter is a fresh `CancellationHandle::new()` created per dispatch in engine_eval.rs and stored on `ComputeNodeData.running`. The only code that calls `.cancel()` on it is a branch the source itself labels dead ('Until then the branch is dead', engine_eval.rs). So the modal checkpoints poll a handle that production never cancels, and the elastic-static trampoline's signature advertises a parameter it does not honour.
findings.proposal: Pick one channel. Either have the engine pass the active solve cancel handle (or a handle linked to it) as the ComputeFn `cancellation` argument and delete the ambient read in elastic_static, or remove the parameter. Then add one e2e test that cancels through Engine::set_active_solve_cancel and asserts Cancelled from every registered long-running target.
findings.next_change: Plausible change: 'make modal_analysis / transient_response cancellable from the GUI', or add a cancellable poll to a new trampoline. The agent would naturally use the `cancellation` parameter, because that is what the ComputeFn signature hands it and what modal_ops already does. To get it right they must find out, outside this slice, that only engine.active_solve_cancel is ever triggered and that it reaches trampolines through a thread-local. Nothing catches the wrong version: modal's cancel unit tests call `run_modal_analysis` with a hand-cancelled handle and pass, while the GUI cancel button stays inert for modal solves.

findings.statement: Every compute target decodes the same stdlib structures from `Value` with its own hand-rolled readers, and the failure policy changes from file to file. ElasticMaterial's youngs_modulus/poisson_ratio are read by elastic_static::isotropic_from_data (Result, with Failed naming the argument, but dimension-blind `scalar_si_field`), buckling::extract_material (panic!), modal_ops::extract_isotropic_material (a missing field silently becomes 0.0) and as_printed_material::read_base_elastic (Option). modal_ops::read_scalar_si takes `si_value` from a Scalar of any dimension and maps every non-numeric value to 0.0. It feeds the beam geometry, E and ν, the forcing magnitudes, the time grid, the Rayleigh α/β and the reference direction. The canonical dimension-checked reader, reify_ir::arg_acceptance::accept_arg/accept_field (PRD dimension-checked-readers.md), is used in this slice only at elastic_static's Point3/Vector3 component positions. extract_loss_factor is the one modal reader that fences read_scalar_si off by hand. Fix history shows the closure being done one position at a time: task 7019's dimension gates touched only elastic_static, and d10bad1deb gated only loss_factor in modal.
findings.proposal: Give the shared stdlib input structs (ElasticMaterial, ModalOptions, BucklingOptions, ElasticOptions, load kinds) one typed decoder each, built on arg_acceptance::accept_field and returning a single error type. Have every trampoline map that error to ComputeOutcome::Failed in one place, then delete the per-file readers.
findings.next_change: Plausible change: add a material or option field to a modal or buckling solve (e.g. honour `density` units, or add `ModalOptions.mass_lumping`), or harden modal against malformed input the way task 5087 (D9) hardened elastic_static. The agent has to learn three reader dialects and pick one. Nothing tells them that a wrong-dimension or bare value in modal will be read as SI metres or pascals, or as 0.0. A wrong version passes every modal test because the type checker normally fills the fields; it fails only for hand-built or mistyped Values, which none of the e2e tests construct.

findings.statement: solve_elastic_static_trampoline is one function spanning lines 409-1578 that branches inline on five independent axes. (a) Calling overload (dims / body / field): it is inferred by sniffing positional Value variants ('[1] is GeometryHandle OR Undef AND [2] is a List'), and the body call is then normalised to placeholder 1 m dims, so every dims reader needs its own `!body_path` guard. (b) Shell vs tet route. (c) Material model (iso / aniso / heterogeneous). (d) Adaptive lane (none / uniform / gmsh-localized, with runtime fallback). (e) Realized mesh present or absent. It returns at 11 points and builds the ElasticResult field list twice, once for the shell arm and once for the tet arm. More than half of its lines are comments, including several PERF NOTE blocks addressed to reviewers.
findings.proposal: Make the overload explicit: register the body overload with its own entry point, or pass an overload tag, instead of sniffing Values. Split the trampoline into a decode stage that produces a typed request, a route selection that returns an enum over (shell / tet × adaptive lane), and per-route solvers, each returning a typed result that one ElasticResult builder turns into a Value.
findings.next_change: Plausible change: enable the shell route on the body overload, add a fourth material model, or make the adaptive loop reuse the seed solve. The agent must load all 1,170 lines (more than half of a default Read) to find every place an axis is checked, including which dims readers need a `!body_path` guard. A wrong version, such as a new dims-derived advisory without the guard, fires spuriously on body solves. Nothing catches that unless a body-path e2e happens to assert the absence of warnings, and the body e2e tests mostly assert 'no Error diagnostics'.

findings.statement: modal_ops.rs is 12,835 lines: four compute targets (modal::free_vibration, modal::mechanism_modal, modal::transient_response, modal::displacement_at), a face-name Dirichlet realization subsystem (build_dirichlet_bcs, FaceCompany, FaceRealization, DeclaredSupport, face_bound, 'x_min'…'z_max' strings), damping classification, and options readers. The in-file test module imports 47 names via `use super::{…}`, 30 of them fully private: policy units such as face_company, face_realization, classify_damping, plan_modal_damping and solve_generalized_eigen are tested by private path, not through a seam. A clean partition exists (see h14_measurements); its one cycle hazard is where the ModalResult builders go.
findings.proposal: Split along the partition in h14_measurements. Give the BC realization a narrow seam (`realize_supports(options, nodes, dims) -> DirichletRealization`) and the damping planner a seam (`plan_modal_damping`), and move their tests onto those seams.
findings.next_change: Plausible change: change how PinnedSupport is realized (e.g. the #7097 Part path brings real faces), or add a fifth modal target. The agent must load a 12.8k-line file whose module doc points them at the wrong scope. A refactor of the BC subsystem breaks dozens of private-path tests even when behaviour is preserved, which pushes the agent to preserve internal factoring rather than behaviour.

findings.statement: Diagnostic identity in modal_ops is mostly a message-string prefix. 24 distinct mnemonics (E_ModalNoMassMatrix, W_ModalRigidBodyMode, E_MechanismModalNoMass, …) are emitted as the leading text of the message, and only 3 carry a DiagnosticCode. Comments call the prefixes 'consumer grouping keys', and tests match on substrings. In one case the mnemonic contradicts the severity: run_mechanism_modal emits 'I_MechanismModalNModesTruncated' through Diagnostic::warning, so an Info-named diagnostic arrives as a Warning, while I_ModalPinnedFaceRealization correctly uses Diagnostic::info.
findings.proposal: Mint DiagnosticCode variants for the modal family, as was done for ShiftAtEigenvalue/ShiftSkippedModes/ModalOptionUnsupported, and assert on codes. As an immediate mechanical fix, emit I_MechanismModalNModesTruncated via Diagnostic::info, or rename it W_.
findings.next_change: Plausible change: reword a diagnostic message, or let the GUI group modal warnings. A reword that touches the prefix breaks consumers silently; only the substring tests that happen to cover that message catch it. An agent filtering by severity for Info notes misses the truncation note.

findings.proposal: Move promote_tets_to_p2 to a production module of reify-solver-elastic (e.g. p2_tet or mesher), re-export it, and leave test_support with only fixtures.

Modal and buckling P2 then break or silently renumber. The P2 accuracy benchmarks would catch numbering drift only if they run, and a cfg gate fails only at build time in the eval crate.

findings.statement: The force-density form-finding input contract has no single home. Each entry point re-implements it inline: form_find_anchored, form_find_anchored_surfaces and form_find_anchored_surfaces_aniso in form_find.rs, plus form_find_free/form_find_free_surfaces in form_find_free.rs. The cable q>0 / strut q<0 sign rule is spelled out as a `match kind { MemberKind::Cable => qi > 0.0, .. }` loop in 6 production places, and MemberKind has no impl. The anchor partition is copied 3 times, the member-force loop 3 times, the cotangent fixed-point loop 2 times (isotropic and aniso, line-identical except the assembler), the surface-stencil scatter 3 times and the line rank-1 scatter 2 times (scatter_line_members vs form_find_free::assemble_force_density_matrix). Three error enums (FormFindError, AnisoFormFindError, FreeFormError) share 5 variant names, and map_ff_error translates between them. Enforcement is not uniform. The anchored kernels range-check surface corners but not member endpoints or anchors, so `is_anchor[a] = true` and `d[(j, j)]` panic on a bad index. Only the reify-eval trampoline's crack_anchors/check_index protects them, while form_find_free::validate_explicit does check member indices. form_find_anchored and the aniso entry have no production caller.
findings.proposal: Validate once into a typed problem value (members, kinds, q, anchors, surfaces, each range-checked at construction) with `MemberKind::admits(q)` as the sign rule's only home. Use one shared input-error enum nested in the per-solver errors. Drive the isotropic and anisotropic loops from one fixed-point driver parameterised by a per-triangle stencil. form_find_anchored becomes the empty-surfaces case.
findings.next_change: The plausible next change is a new input guard (anchor index range, a NaN q), a new surface-stress model, or a change to the stop criterion. The agent has to find all four or five entry points across two files, and know that form_find_free has a separate validate_explicit and that the reify-eval trampoline does part of the validation. Nothing catches a missed copy except a per-entry negative test, and fix 6563 shows each entry needed its own commit and test.

findings.statement: Element-level shell primitives (ShellFrame, build_shell_frame, plane_stress_d, KAPPA, membrane_node_pair_block, rotate_blockdiag) live in the assembly-level module shell_assembly.rs. Lower and sibling layers import upward into it, and shell_assembly imports them back, which closes module cycles. elements/degenerate_shell.rs:81 does `use crate::shell_assembly::build_shell_frame` while shell_assembly::degenerate_stiffness_core does a fn-local `use crate::elements::degenerate_shell::{..}`. shell_kinematics.rs:11 does `use crate::shell_assembly::ShellFrame` while shell_assembly calls `crate::shell_kinematics::shell_kinematics`. elements/membrane_cst.rs:22 and geometric_stiffness/membrane.rs:27 also reach into shell_assembly for frame and rotation helpers. The #[cfg(test)] fixture tilted_q_for_shell_tests is likewise hosted in shell_assembly and reached from 6 other modules' tests.
findings.proposal: Move ShellFrame, build_shell_frame, plane_stress_d, KAPPA, mat3_mul, membrane_node_pair_block and rotate_blockdiag into a lower module (e.g. elements/shell_frame.rs) that shell_assembly, elements/* and shell_kinematics all import downward. Move tilted_q_for_shell_tests into a test_support module.
findings.next_change: The likely change is a new shell element (a curved MITC6, say) or a change to the frame convention. The agent must know that the frame and plane-stress law it needs live in the assembly module, not in elements/, and that changing build_shell_frame ripples through 7 modules. Adding the new element under elements/ makes it import from shell_assembly, which deepens the inversion. No check catches the layering, because Rust permits intra-crate cycles.

findings.statement: The bubble-condensation numerics are copied between shell_element_stiffness_mitc3_plus and degenerate_stiffness_core, and the copies have diverged. The 2x2 K_BB inverse plus Schur correction block appears twice. Only the degenerate copy has the release-time near-singular guard (`det_bb > 1e-14 * k00*k11`, else zero correction). The MITC3+ copy divides by det_bb unguarded, behind a debug_assert. The flat-kinematics bubble-bending K_BB loop is duplicated verbatim, and the t*D / t^3/12*D scaling block is written 5 times. kappa_g = KAPPA*G and ElementStiffness packing are each written 3 times. The shear-correction factor KAPPA = 5/6 is defined independently in shell_result.rs (stress recovery), and G = E/(2(1+nu)) is inlined 16 times across solver-elastic. degenerate_stiffness_core selects its formulation with two bool flags (use_ans_membrane, use_rotation_bubble) behind three public wrappers.
findings.proposal: Extract the condensation (with its guard), the bubble K_BB integral, and a `scaled(d, s)` helper into shared functions. Put KAPPA and the shear modulus on the constitutive/section type. Replace the two bools with an enum or struct for the membrane and bubble variants.
findings.next_change: Task 4068/4065-style work that activates K_NB on the MITC3+ path, or changes the shear-correction factor (a section property, say), must find every copy. A fix to the condensation guard lands in one copy only, and a changed kappa in shell_assembly silently desynchronises stiffness from shell_result's stress recovery. The flat benchmarks would not catch the MITC3+ singular-K_BB divide, because K_NB is bit-zero there.

findings.statement: A compute target is identified by a bare &'static str, and every per-target capability is a separate string-keyed table in a different module. Persistence: PERSISTABLE_TARGETS plus two `match target` codec blocks in compute_persist.rs. Significance: is_opted_in plus a `target == "solver::buckling"` branch in significance_filter.rs. Post-dispatch fold: `target == "shell-extract::extract"` written twice in run_compute_dispatch, once in the persistent-HIT arm and once in the Completed arm. Upstream insertion: `target == "solver::elastic_static"` twice in engine_eval.rs. engine_admin.rs adds a `match node.target.as_str()` classifier. The HIT arm must mirror the Completed arm's per-target hooks by convention only, and a prose NOTE in run_compute_dispatch says so. Commit a148207c93 was exactly that mirror missing: the HIT arm did not replay solver diagnostics.
findings.proposal: Register a per-target descriptor (codec, significance comparator, completion hook, demands) alongside the ComputeFn in ComputeDispatchRegistry. Then run_compute_dispatch and compute_persist consult one typed record, and both completion arms call the same hook.
findings.next_change: Registering a new heavy target that should be persisted or significance-filtered, or that needs a post-dispatch fold, means editing four to six string tables. The agent must find them by grep and keep the HIT and Completed arms symmetric. A misspelled literal or a missed arm compiles cleanly and fails silently (no persistence, a stale topology table). Only a per-target e2e test would catch it.

findings.statement: The reify-solver-elastic integration tests carry the FEA harness as private copies in each file instead of a shared module. kuhn_split_hex_to_six_tets, box_p1_mesh, dirichlet_fix_face, end_face_nodes, distributed_tip_load and dedup_bcs each have 5 copies (analytical_validation, aposteriori_validation, determinism, dwr_boundary_tests, solver_gate_smoke), and gather_u_p1 has 4. aposteriori_validation.rs labels its block 'ported FEA harness helpers (tests/analytical_validation.rs, task 2928)'. findings.statement: The per-element DOF-layout invariant has no single home and is not enforced uniformly. ElementStiffness exposes `pub n_dofs` and `pub data`, so `data.len() == n_dofs^2` is never checked. Its doc still says 'the DOF index is 3 * node_idx + axis', while shells emit 6 DOFs/node and the global assembly derives the stride per element. AssemblyElement's stride `d_e = k_e.n_dofs / connectivity.len()` is recomputed inline at 3 code sites in global.rs. Only assemble_global_stiffness asserts non-empty connectivity, divisibility and node range. detect_orphan_dofs checks only empty connectivity and node range, behind debug_assert, and has no divisibility check, so a non-divisible element silently truncates d_e there. The validated path panics on the same element.
findings.proposal: Give AssemblyElement a validating constructor and a `dofs_per_node()` accessor that both entry points call. Make ElementStiffness's fields private behind zeros/get/add/from_row_major, and fix its doc to state the stride as n_dofs / n_nodes.
findings.next_change: Adding an element kind with a new DOF stride (a 7-DOF warping beam, say), or calling detect_orphan_dofs as a pre-check, requires knowing an invariant stated only in rustdoc and enforced in only one of the two entry points. A malformed ElementStiffness can be built freely. detect_orphan_dofs returns a wrong summary on it rather than failing, and no test exercises that path.

findings.statement: The spatial hash is correct only under the completeness keystone r_a + r_b >= threshold(a,b). That keystone is restated as a literal 0.75 at two code sites (max_r and r_i in compute_adjacency_with_stats) and is not derived from the thresholds' own coefficients (0.5 touching + 0.25 slack in adjacency_threshold and inter_layer_threshold). Raising the slack in either threshold silently breaks completeness, so the hash drops true adjacencies. The differential test shares the threshold functions and has no pair near the boundary, so it would not catch this. The same function carries a stale comment ('degenerate ... beads floor cell_size to 1e-9' against a 1e-3 floor two paragraphs up) and a same_layer branch in the inter-layer loop that cannot fire by construction. parse_prusaslicer_gcode also carries a stale comment (';LAYER_CHANGE / ;Z: are handled in step-8', though both are handled just above it).
findings.proposal: Define one SLACK (or inflation) constant and derive both the thresholds and r_i from it, with a debug_assert of r_a + r_b >= threshold at probe time. Delete the dead branch and the stale comments.
findings.next_change: Tuning adjacency slack for a new slicer's overlap, the next plausible FDM change, means editing adjacency_threshold alone, and the hash under-enumerates. Only a fixture with a pair between 0.75(w_a+w_b) and the new threshold would show it.

findings.statement: closed_chain_inverse_dynamics repeats snapshot_inverse_dynamics's mechanism/snapshot marshalling instead of sharing it. The repeated steps are: the per-body at/id extraction, parent_idx from joint_parents, topo_order plus its inverse permutation, the motion subspaces, slicing q̇/q̈, the snapshot world_transform index, and the RneaLink build loop. The copies have already diverged. The open chain computes `compliance` through joint_compliance (spring and damping), while the closed chain hard-codes `compliance: None`. The closed chain's comment justifies this as 'mirrors the open-chain snapshot literal above (`snapshot_inverse_dynamics`), which also passes `None`', which is false. As a result, a flexure joint inside a loop-closed mechanism silently loses its spring and damping torque, and no diagnostic reports it. Both functions are around 225 lines with deep Option-early-return chains.
findings.proposal: Extract one `MechanismTree` parse: from (mechanism, snapshot, n_tree, q̇, q̈, positions) to a typed struct holding links, ordering, dof_counts, at_joints and ids. Both paths build from it. The closed chain then gets compliance either through that parse or through an explicit, named refusal. Delete the false parity comment.
findings.next_change: Plausible next changes are wiring compliance into the closed-chain path, adding a body field to the mechanism map, or changing how world transforms are keyed. The agent has to know that a second copy of the marshalling exists 400 lines further down and keep both in step. The mechanism is a stringly-keyed Value::Map, so the compiler catches nothing. The comment that claims parity would actively mislead them. Only a closed-chain test that uses a damped or sprung joint would catch the drift, and none exists.

findings.statement: stdlib builtins return a bare Value::Undef with no reason attached. Diagnostics are produced afterwards by classifier hooks that re-run the builtin's validation to infer why it failed. fea::diagnose says its 'Check ordering faithfully mirrors linear_combine's own per-entry Undef order'. It re-implements the arity, cases-map, weights-map, empty, String-key, numeric/finite-weight, known-case, container, displacement/stress resolution and metadata_matches checks in the same order, citing linear_combine by stale line numbers (fea.rs:140-173, 180-196, 209-250). dynamics::eval::diagnose openly documents 'Best-effort attribution… the diagnostic will attribute the failure to mass' even when Undef came from something else. reify-expr's emit_undef_builtin_diagnostics runs six such hooks in a row. This is the doc's 're-derives state in order to check it' smell: the invariant that says why a builtin returns Undef has two homes per builtin.
findings.proposal: Have each builtin's validator return a typed failure (for example Result<Value, BuiltinFailure> with an optional DiagnosticCode). eval_builtin then maps a failure to Undef plus a diagnostic at a single point, and the six re-deriving classifiers go away. This is a cross-area contract change in reify-expr's builtin dispatch.
findings.next_change: Plausible next changes are relaxing a weight rule (for example, accepting a dimensionless Scalar), reordering linear_combine's checks, or adding a new failure mode. The agent must find diagnose and make the same edit in the same order. Otherwise the diagnostic names the wrong cause, or none at all. Only the roughly 10 diagnose-specific tests catch a mismatch, and only for the modes they enumerate.

findings.statement: The MassProperties Value shape (mass Scalar{MASS}, com Point of lengths, inertia Matrix of MOMENT_OF_INERTIA scalars, origin Frame3) is built by two producers and read by two inertia parsers in two crates. The producers are reify-stdlib's dynamics::eval::make_mass_properties and reify-eval's dynamics_ops::assemble_mass_properties plus inertia_value. The parsers are stdlib's inertia_3x3_from_value and reify-eval's dynamics_psd::inertia_3x3_from_value. Only `origin` was consolidated, through the shared default_frame3. The stated reason for the copy is 'Re-spelled locally from reify_eval::dynamics_psd::inertia_3x3_from_value (that one lives in another crate)'. That reasoning points the wrong way: reify-eval already depends on reify-stdlib as a normal dependency (reify-eval/Cargo.toml `reify-stdlib.workspace = true`) and already imports resolve_body_mass and mass_properties_from_value from it.
findings.proposal: Make reify-stdlib's dynamics module the single owner: a typed `MassProps { mass, com, inertia }` with `to_value`/`from_value`. reify-eval's assemble_mass_properties and dynamics_psd call it, and the reify-eval copies are deleted.
findings.next_change: Plausible next changes are adding a field such as a principal-axes frame, changing the inertia dimension, or accepting a new encoding. The agent must find both producers and both parsers across two crates. A single-sided edit leaves the PSD hook (reify-eval) and RNEA (stdlib) reading different shapes, and only an end-to-end dynamics test would notice.

findings.statement: No type or accessor in reify-ir encodes the axis order of Regular3D SampledField data. reify-ir's doc says only 'Flat row-major data'. Readers each spell out the index themselves: shell-extract medial::sample_at_index uses `data[i*nj*nk + j*nk + k]`, and reify-expr interp::index_3d and sampled_fd do the same. Producers flatten with hand-written loops. One production producer, reify-eval compute_targets/shell_solve.rs::build_slab_sdf (wired by engine_eval to feed shell-extract's extract node), flattens z-outermost over axis_grids [x(16), y(16), z(7)]. That transposes it relative to the reader, so shell-extract sees a scrambled field rather than a slab. Only a non-empty-mask check guards it. Inside shell-extract, the grid-sampling primitives live in medial.rs. walk_direction imports medial::{normalize3, sample_at_index} while medial imports walk_direction::medial_walk_direction, which forms a 2-cycle. Six private slab_sdf_3d fixture copies re-spell the layout, and tests/common/mod.rs has to warn 'do not copy' the transposed eval fixtures.
findings.proposal: Give SampledField in reify-ir a `flat_index_3d([i,j,k])` / `at_3d` accessor and a `from_fn_3d` constructor that state the axis-0-outermost order. Move shell-extract's sampling primitives into a `grid` module beside grid_validation, which breaks the medial↔walk_direction cycle. Rebuild build_slab_sdf and the fixtures on the constructor.
findings.next_change: The plausible change is a new SDF producer, either a real OpenVDB lowering or another placeholder, or a new reader such as a gradient cache. The agent must infer the axis order from one consumer's private helper. Nothing in the type system or tests checks producer/reader agreement, as the existing transposed producer shows.

findings.statement: The ShellExtractionResult <-> Value::StructureInstance projection has one hand-written string-keyed encoder (shell_extraction_result_to_value) and three independent decoders with different strictness: value_to_shell_extraction_result (persistent-cache rehydration; returns None on any mismatch, does not check inner type_name), fold_mid_surface_attributes_into_table in the same file (re-decodes naming.face_records/edges with a warn-and-skip policy), and reify_eval::engine_admin::parse_shell_extraction_result (GUI populator; checks inner type_name "MidSurfaceMesh"/"SegmentationResult" and accepts vertex rows of any length, where decode_real3_list demands exactly 3). The encoder is lossy (regions -> voxel_count only, diagnostics -> Debug strings, region_pair dropped) and the decoder defaults regions/diagnostics to vec![], so a persistent-cache warm serve returns a Value whose segmentation.regions is [] where the cold dispatch had N>0 entries. The only guard that no consumer reads those fields is a prose census in value_to_shell_extraction_result's doc ("Verified: the only two consumers..."), and tests/harness_topology_selector/shell_extract_persistent_cache_round_trip.rs pins the divergence (cold regions > 0, warm regions == []) rather than preventing it.
findings.proposal: One typed codec for the projection (named field constants, encode(&ShellExtractionResult) -> Value and decode(&Value) -> Result<view, DecodeError>) used by the persistence bridge, the fold hook and the GUI populator; make the round trip lossless by construction, either by projecting only what decode rebuilds (so cold == warm) or by persisting the projected Value itself.
findings.next_change: An agent adding a field to the projection (region classification for a GUI overlay, real producer diagnostics, region_pair for edge selectors) must find and edit the encoder plus up to three decoders in two files, and must know that the persistent cache silently drops anything the rehydration decoder does not rebuild. A new consumer that reads segmentation.regions passes every cold-path test and gets [] on a cross-session warm hit; nothing catches that except a test written specifically for warm hits on that field.

findings.statement: The persistable-target set is a string allowlist (PERSISTABLE_TARGETS). Each target's typed cache container and Value bridge are chosen by `match target { "solver::elastic_static" => .., "solver::buckling" => .., "shell-extract::extract" => .., _ => None }` in both persistent_lookup and persistent_write; all six arms share one ~35-line read_entry/write_entry + tracing::warn shape and differ only in the cache type, the bridge fn and the message text. The same strings sit in engine_hash_tests.rs (PERSISTED_TARGET_SOURCES) and in the test-only persistable_target_fixtures, and significance_filter::is_opted_in holds an overlapping matches! list. Drift between the lists is caught today, but only by test cross-checks (persisted_target_sources_cover_exactly_the_persistable_targets; the assert_eq in persistable_target_fixtures plus per-target round trips). In release builds the `_ => None` / `_ => {}` arms mean an allowlisted target with no arm is silently never cached. Cross-cutting envelope changes (diagnostics replay 2026-09-09, structured_detail 2026-10-05) each had to be threaded through and pinned per arm.
findings.proposal: A trait per persistable target (cache type, to_cache(&Value) -> Option<Cache>, from_cache(&Cache) -> Value) with one registry keyed by a typed target id, so lookup and write are each one generic body and the allowlist, the fixtures and the engine-hash table derive from the registry.
findings.next_change: Persisting a fourth target (modal, membrane_load) means editing five places and copying a 35-line arm twice. A cross-cutting change to the envelope (a new replayed channel, a new error policy) must be applied to every arm, and an arm missed in release silently disables caching for that target.

findings.statement: MpcRow's invariant (dofs.len() == coeffs.len(), non-empty, coeffs[0] finite and non-zero, rhs finite) is enforced only in MpcRow::new, but all three fields are pub and neither consumer checks it again. apply_mpc_row_elimination divides by coeffs[0] and zips dofs[1..] with coeffs[1..], so a length mismatch silently truncates the constraint and a zero pivot writes +/-inf into K and f. buckling_kernel's MPC reduction reads row.dofs[0] and row.coeffs[0] in the same unchecked way. The unvalidated path is actively pinned: tests::mpc_row_type_compiles_with_documented_field_shape and the lib.rs crate-root doctest both build MpcRow from a struct literal. The struct doc still says "Constructors that enforce this invariant are deferred to T10 (Task 3020); for now consumers build via struct-literal initialization", and the module doc calls T10 "pending", although new, shell_tet_tying and apply_mpc_row_elimination all ship in the file.
findings.proposal: Make the fields private with read accessors so new / shell_tet_tying are the only constructors; delete the struct-literal smoke test and doctest line; rewrite the module and struct docs to describe the shipped surface.
findings.next_change: An agent writing MPCs for a new junction type (beam-solid or shell-shell tying) follows the struct doc and builds a literal; a sign or length slip gives a silently wrong or non-finite stiffness instead of a panic naming the row, because apply only asserts DOF range and sparsity.

findings.statement: The stress builtins (von_mises, principal_stresses, max_shear, safety_factor, stress_invariants, dispatched from registry_dispatch) accept any 3x3 matrix Value from user .ri code. The kernels read only the upper triangle and check symmetry with debug_assert!, so an asymmetric user matrix panics the evaluator in debug builds (the profile the test suite and agents run) and returns the upper-triangle answer in release. compute_stress_invariants_3x3's own doc states this: "A user passing a genuinely asymmetric 3x3 .ri matrix will panic in debug builds". The symmetry predicate is a closure copied verbatim into compute_von_mises_3x3, compute_eigenvalues_3x3 and compute_stress_invariants_3x3. Nothing checks symmetry at the Value seam, and no test uses an asymmetric input.
findings.proposal: Validate (or symmetrize) once at the Value boundary, in one helper every builtin uses, returning Undef or a diagnostic for an asymmetric 3x3. The f64 kernels keep the documented precondition and share one is_symmetric_3x3 for their debug asserts.
findings.next_change: Adding another tensor builtin (tresca, octahedral shear) copies the debug_assert a fourth time. Making asymmetric input a user-facing Undef or diagnostic means touching three kernels. Until then a debug test run and a release GUI disagree on the same .ri.

findings.statement: "Registry-free StructureInstance" has two incompatible type_id conventions. analysis.rs defines REGISTRY_FREE_TYPE_ID = StructureTypeId(u32::MAX) as a private const; its doc admits it is one of several copies and that the dedup is "deferred beyond task 2884's scope". There are now five production const copies. Meanwhile shell_extract_compute.rs (8 sites) and reify-stdlib tensegrity.rs (10 sites) mint registry-free instances with StructureTypeId(0), and 0 is not a sentinel: StructureRegistry::intern assigns ids from by_id.len(), so 0 is the first real interned structure. reify_eval::value_type_kind_matches resolves a TraitObject cell type through registry.meta(data.type_id). A 0-tagged instance is therefore checked against the trait bounds of whichever structure was interned first, while a u32::MAX instance resolves to None.
findings.proposal: One pub constructor in reify-ir (e.g. StructureInstanceData::registry_free(type_name, fields), or a single pub const) used at every minting site, with the StructureTypeId(0) placeholders migrated to it.
findings.next_change: A new compute target or builtin that mints a result instance has to pick a type_id. The slice's own examples teach both conventions, and the wrong one misbehaves only when the value reaches a trait-object-typed cell. Nothing catches it.

findings.statement: The fact that libgmsh is absent from this build travels as a substring of GeometryError::OperationFailed(String). The two kernel-gmsh stubs format STUB_UNAVAILABLE_MARKER into their message, and two consumer-side copies of map_geometry_error (volume_refine.rs and mesher.rs) recover the fact with msg.contains(STUB_UNAVAILABLE_MARKER) to produce RefineError::GmshUnavailable / Mesh2dError::GmshUnavailable. Sharing the constant protects against a reworded message, but not against a new stub entry point that formats its own text: that stub would be classified as a runtime gmsh failure.
findings.proposal: Return a typed variant (GeometryError::BackendUnavailable { backend }, or a kernel-gmsh error enum) from every stub, and match it structurally.
findings.next_change: A new kernel-gmsh entry point (a sweep or remesh variant) adds a stub that returns OperationFailed with its own text, plus a third map_geometry_error copy. Stub-build callers then get Gmsh(..) instead of GmshUnavailable, and the "not available in this build" diagnostic in elastic_static's refinement path never fires.

findings.statement: TetSpatialIndex::build(nodes, elems, tol) pads its AABBs by tol but keeps neither the mesh nor tol, so locate/locate_counted make the caller pass the same nodes, elems and tol again. The same-mesh contract is checked only by two debug_assert_eq! on lengths, and the same-tol contract is not checked at all. A query tol larger than the build tol under-pads the boxes and breaks the documented guarantee of results bit-identical to locate_element_p1; the doc calls under-padding "not possible here". volume_refine::TetShape has the same shape: its doc concedes the proof token "does not pin which mesh", so refine_with_size_field_validated and project_per_element_sizes_to_vertices carry a prose same-mesh caller contract.
findings.proposal: TetSpatialIndex<'a> borrows nodes/elems and owns tol, and locate takes only the point; likewise TetShape<'a> carries its &VolumeMesh.
findings.next_change: qoi.rs's doc names TetSpatialIndex as the upgrade path for many queries against one mesh. An agent wiring it in builds with one slack and queries with LOCATE_BARYCENTRIC_SLACK (1e-9), or the reverse, and results diverge from the linear scan only for points near faces, where no current test looks.

findings.statement: A Diagnostic carries no structured link to its constraint. Retracting a stale `constraint {subject} indeterminate` claim after a verdict upgrade therefore parses message text, and three consumers do it with three different matchers. replace_superseded_constraint_diagnostics uses `d.message.starts_with(claim)`. Engine::build's 4229 merge loop (engine_build.rs, the two `d.message.contains(&needle)` sites) uses a bare substring match. reify-cli main.rs uses an exact-subject parse (indeterminacy_subject_in / is_falsified_indeterminacy). The CLI leg was moved to the exact parse by task 5748 precisely because a substring match let a verdict for `Foo#constraint[1]` delete the still-true warning for `Foo#constraint[10]`. The engine_build leg still has that defect today. The grammar is produced at two independent format! sites: reify-constraints/src/lib.rs (SimpleConstraintChecker) and engine_constraints.rs::Engine::dispatch_constraints. It is then rewritten by Engine::labeled_diagnostics through `message.replace(id_str, label)`. Task #7991 tracks the convergence and is pending at low priority.
findings.proposal: Do what #7991 describes, at higher priority. Attach the ConstraintNodeId to verdict diagnostics structurally at push_constraint_result / the checker boundary, then replace all three matchers with one structural comparison so the engine_build over-match disappears.
findings.next_change: Plausible next changes: a new surface such as the GUI session or a purpose re-check needs to retract an upgraded verdict's stale warning, or someone edits the checker's message wording. The agent must know about the grammar, the three existing matchers, the label substitution, and the CLI tests that pin collision safety (in another crate). A wrong version, such as a fourth substring matcher or a reworded message, compiles and passes every test except the CLI's own, because no test pins the engine_build or engine_constraints matchers against id-prefix or short-label collisions.

The claim string is 'constraint {subject} indeterminate' and the match is starts_with on that, so it is already anchored and cannot collide. Its test at engine_constraints.rs ~4060-4160 builds eleven constraints so that [1] and [10] share a prefix, and calls replace_superseded_constraint_diagnostics. The statement that no test pins the engine_constraints matcher against id-prefix collisions is wrong. Second, only one of the three matchers (engine_build) carries the defect, not several. The real finding is narrower: one unanchored substring matcher plus duplicated grammar across 2 producers and 2 matcher styles.

findings.statement: solver.rs is 11788 lines: 4686 production lines and 7103 embedded test lines, with a field-set pin test module sitting in the middle of production code. The production code holds nine separable concerns: trial-value folding, residuals, the alpha robustness floor, gamma interval derivation, centrality/cost function, the Nelder-Mead core, the tradeoff blend, uniqueness verification and the ConstraintSolver API. They are not layered. The floor concern calls back into the core (constraints_witness -> solve_core_with_sd_tolerance under FeasibilityWitness), while the core calls the floor (synthesise_floor_constraints, floor_infeasible_diagnostic, objective_is_money), so the two form a call cycle. derive_param_intervals needs effective_bounds from the cost/bounds region while that region needs derived_seed_box from derive. The 143 embedded tests reach 34 of the file's 70 private items directly (e.g. solve_core, verify_uniqueness, classify_uniqueness, resolve_bounds, derive_from_expr, ConstraintCostFunction), so they pin internals rather than ConstraintSolver behaviour. The file carries 105 commits since 2026-07-06; the core function alone is ~450 lines. Its name, solve_core_with_sd_tolerance, describes a parameter every caller now passes as NM_SD_TOLERANCE, and it returns `unique: true` as a documented placeholder for callers to overwrite.
findings.proposal: Partition into a solver/ module tree layered trial < residual < derive(+extract_initial_point) < bounds/cost(+effective_bounds, default_bounds_for) < floor < core(+constraints_witness, which closes the cycle by living with the core or taking the re-solve as a closure) < tradeoff < uniqueness < api. Move tests to the ConstraintSolver seam or the layer's own interface, and rename the core once the tolerance parameter is gone.
findings.next_change: Plausible next change: a gamma/derivation or uniqueness fix, which is where the recent fix history clusters (#7883 strict bounds, #6465 determinedness, #5711 uniqueness). The agent must load the core, the floor ordering invariant, the derivation's 'one policy for four consumers' contract and the uniqueness re-solve, all in one 4686-line production body. A wrong change is caught only by whichever of the 143 internal-pinning tests happens to cover the touched helper. A behaviour-preserving restructure turns those tests red even when behaviour is right.

findings.statement: Every gmsh mesher must follow a library-session protocol, and each entry point restates it by hand. The order is: init::lock, init::ensure_initialized, MeshSizeScope::entered, ffi::clear, General.Terminal=0, LogCapture::armed (which must come right after the Terminal write), then mesh_generate_with_recovery (which no caller LogCapture seam may also cover), then read_tet_connectivity and a trailing best-effort clear. mesh_to_volume, refine_volume_with_size_field, mesh_surface_to_volume_with_attribution and mesh_plane_2d each repeat it. The invariant is enforced by prose that enumerates the callers by name (mesh_generate_with_recovery's doc: 'None of this function's four callers ... Each ... arms one LogCapture right after its own General.Terminal write'). The copies have already diverged: mesh_plane_2d has no trailing clear, and refine_volume sets ElementOrder before Algorithm3D where the others do the reverse. The P1->1.0/P2->2.0 ElementOrder mapping is copied 3 times. The P1->4/P2->10 tet stride is copied 3 times in-crate (init, fill_metrics, through_thickness) beside reify_ir::VolumeMesh::nodes_per_element, and init.rs's own doc acknowledges that with no task cited.
findings.proposal: Introduce one session constructor in init.rs that performs lock + init + size scope + clear + terminal + capture, returns a session type the meshers take, and owns the trailing clear on drop. Move the element-order tables to the reify_ir type that owns the fact.
findings.next_change: Plausible next change: adding a fifth mesher (e.g. a 2D->3D extrusion or quad mesh) or adding a session-wide option. The agent must reconstruct the order, and the double-annotation rule, from prose in init.rs and from copying a sibling. Nothing structural catches a missed MeshSizeScope (option leak across calls) or a LogCapture covering the recovery call (duplicated diagnostics). The GmshGuard witness proves only that the lock is held.

findings.statement: Engine names its kernels by String, and the production constructor files its picked adapter under the sentinel string Engine::DEFAULT_KERNEL_NAME ("__reify_eval_default_kernel"). Engine::with_registered_kernel is that constructor, used by reify-cli cmd_check/cmd_build and the GUI. The sentinel encodes a construction mode, not a kernel. Production code branches on it in engine_build.rs (`default_kernel_name == Engine::DEFAULT_KERNEL_NAME` selects backward-compat fallback vs NoKernelChain) and in realization_content.rs::resolve_realization_kernel, where a canonical-name miss falls back to the sentinel. Because the sentinel resolves to nothing in the static registry, the engine cannot ask its own kernel's CapabilityDescriptor. Task 6169 therefore added Engine::repr_capable_kernel: Option<bool>, recorded by two constructors, plus a registry fallback with a benefit-of-the-doubt rule. Explaining why the lookup cannot work takes 64 doc lines on has_repr_capable_kernel and unmeasured_reason.
findings.proposal: Key geometry_kernels by KernelId (or keep the KernelRegistration alongside each adapter), and make the backward-compat mode an explicit enum on Engine rather than a reserved string, so capability is read from the held kernel's descriptor.
findings.next_change: Plausible next change: any capability-dependent decision about the engine's own kernel, such as Indeterminate attribution for a new measured constraint or routing a query only to kernels that answer it. The agent must know that the String key is a sentinel on every production surface, that a registry lookup by key silently yields benefit-of-the-doubt true, and which constructors record a substitute. A wrong version (`registry.get(name)`) compiles, passes unit tests built with Engine::new(checker, Some(mock)), and is dead on every shipped binary, as the task-6169 review round found.

findings.statement: Engine::check runs eval() and then three check-time passes: dispatch_constraints' RepresentationWithin interception, measure_gdt_conformance and measure_dfm_rules. Their verdicts are read from Engine fields that eval() never writes or clears. achieved_repr_tol is written only by tessellate_realizations and cleared only on the Tessellate* surfaces. realization_handles is written by build and cleared only on the Build/BuildSnapshot surfaces (engine_build.rs reset match: the 'build<->tessellate asymmetry'). capture_repr_tol is set by a separate setter. check()'s own doc states the ordering contract: callers must call set_capture_repr_tol(true) then tessellate_realizations before check(). measure_dfm_rules is a no-op unless a prior build() stamped realization_handles. A check() after an edit without a fresh build injects handles from the previous build, keyed by RealizationNodeId, into the GD&T and DFM measurements.
findings.proposal: Pass the realized geometry view (handles + achieved deviations) into the check passes as an explicit argument produced by build/tessellate, instead of reading retained Engine fields.
findings.next_change: Plausible next changes: adding a check-time geometric pass (a new DFM rule, another Conforms-like measured predicate) or calling check() from a new surface such as an LSP or a GUI re-check after edit_param. The agent must know the build/tessellate/setter call order and which surface clears which map, and none of this appears in check()'s signature. A wrong ordering yields silent Indeterminate (no handles) or verdicts measured on the previous build's geometry. Only end-to-end tests that happen to use the right order would catch it.

findings.statement: The guard-activation policy (Bool(true) activates the then-branch, Bool(false) the else-branch, anything else neither) is implemented three times over two different data shapes. Engine::collect_active_constraints walks TopologyTemplate.guarded_groups via guard_value_cell and serves check(), check_snapshot, check_constraints_post_geometry and measure_gdt_conformance. EvaluationGraph::active_constraint_ids (graph.rs) walks graph.guarded_groups via guard_cell and serves recheck_active_constraints, i.e. check_constraints_with_values (edit_check) and upgrade_indeterminate_verdicts. invariants.rs::guard_inactive_members restates it over members/else_members with a doc comment saying it 'Mirrors'. No shared predicate exists, so the check() path and the edit/upgrade path pick active constraints by independent code.
findings.proposal: Give the guard decision one home (a function from guard Value to an active-branch enum), and have all three walks call it. Better still, derive the edit/upgrade path's active set from the same template walk check() uses.
findings.next_change: Plausible next change: a change to guard semantics, e.g. an Undef guard should keep both branches Indeterminate rather than drop them, or a new else-if group shape. The agent must find all three copies across engine_constraints.rs, graph.rs and invariants.rs, and know that two different structures (template vs graph groups) hold the same groups. Editing one copy makes check() and edit_check disagree on which constraints exist, and no test asserts the two paths select the same set.

findings.statement: measure_dfm_rules already knows each measurement's kind statically (DfmRuleKind::Overhang/Draft, thickness pair). It still reports through reify_stdlib::dfm_diagnose with a builtin-name string ('unsupported_overhang_faces', 'min_draft_angle', 'min_wall_thickness', 'min_feature_size_measure') and an untyped Value verdict whose meaning varies by arm. For overhang, wall and feature, Bool(true) means violation, the opposite of fits_build_volume's polarity. For draft the verdict is List[Bool draft, Bool undercut] by position. dfm_diagnose's `_ => Vec::new()` arm means a misspelled name emits nothing. Under the C1 rule ('never a false Violated') emitting nothing is also what a conforming or unmeasurable verdict does, so a typo is indistinguishable from a pass. Rule recognition is likewise duck-typed by field-name strings ('severity' as Enum 'DFMSeverity', 'applies_to', 'max_overhang_angle', 'draft_angle', 'min_feature_size'), and the severity/applies_to prelude is repeated in dfm_rule_spec and dfm_thickness_spec.
findings.proposal: Have the engine call typed violation constructors (overhang_violation(severity), draft_violation, ...) or a typed DfmVerdict enum, and keep the string entry point only for the language-level builtin hook in reify-expr.
findings.next_change: Plausible next change: adding a DFM measurement such as min hole diameter or an overhang direction from the rule. The agent must add a matching string arm in reify-stdlib dfm.rs, pick a verdict encoding and polarity, and extend the field-name duck-typing. A misspelled name or inverted polarity compiles and emits no diagnostic. That reads as 'conforms', so only a test that asserts a violation fires would catch it.

findings.statement: dispatch_constraints implements one algorithm: peel RepresentationWithin, bucket the rest by registered target, run each bucket, and weave results back by index. Around that sit three performance short-circuits (no-registry/no-RW fast path, all-RW, no-RW-after-peel) plus the no-registry pass-through. Each short-circuit rebuilds a ConstraintInput and calls self.constraint_checker.check itself. The function has 6 exits, 5 checker invocations and 5 ConstraintInput constructions in 205 code lines, plus 220 comment lines, most of them defending the fast-path guards' allocation cost.
findings.proposal: Keep the single peel-bucket-weave path, with the fallback bucket as one checker call, and drop the special-case exits or reduce them to one guard. Move the cost argument to the commit history.
findings.next_change: Plausible next change: a cross-cutting post-processing step on checker results, e.g. attaching structured subjects (cg-ck.1) or a new interception like RepresentationWithin. The agent must apply it on every exit. A missed exit is caught only if a test drives that specific registry/RW combination.

findings.next_change: Plausible next change: the planned kappa DRF seam pass, or another GD&T pass named in run_gdt_check_passes' doc. A divergence, such as a prelude/module precedence change applied to one copy, would make the enumerator and the conformance pass disagree on which instances are callouts, and nothing pins them together.

findings.statement: geometry_ops.rs's child test module (34,226 lines, 542 tests, `use super::*`) drives geometry_ops through its internals rather than its entry points. It calls 41 private and 25 pub(crate) functions directly, at 609 call sites. This pins the current factoring of a 13,242-line file that is already an h14 alarm and is the area's top fix-churn file (fix-history lead: geometry_ops/tests.rs 69 commits, geometry_ops.rs 60). Any move of a helper into a submodule or change of its signature breaks tests that do not test behaviour at the seam the engine uses (compile_geometry_op, try_eval_*).
findings.proposal: Re-home helper-level tests next to the helper's new module during the split. Convert the rest to drive compile_geometry_op / try_eval_* (or an Engine fixture), and treat a new direct call into a private helper as review-blocking.
findings.next_change: An agent executes the h14 split of geometry_ops.rs, such as moving selector resolution or pose composition into its own module. It must also rewrite every test that names a moved private helper, without a way to tell which tests assert behaviour and which assert factoring. A behaviour regression hidden among hundreds of mechanical test edits is caught by nothing but the reviewer.

findings.statement: Within the first `impl OcctKernel` block, the same logic is copied several times instead of shared. (a) The sweep-history decode (6 buffers, cap indices, 3 counters, take-last) is copied verbatim into extrude_with_history, revolve_with_history and sweep_with_history, about 45 lines each, plus a loft variant. decode_six_buffer_history already factors exactly this pattern for the boolean and local-feature histories. (b) Revolve's five validation checks and their messages are duplicated verbatim between the execute Revolve arm and revolve_with_history; Extrude and Loft have the same pairing. (c) The curated handle-to-canonical-index mapping is copied into 5 methods (fillet_edges, chamfer_edges, chamfer_asymmetric_edges, draft_faces, shell_solid_faces) using two different algorithms (linear position vs HashMap). (d) extract_edges, extract_faces and extract_vertices are three near-identical bodies differing only in cache field, FFI getter and BRepKind. (e) The finite-positive check is open-coded 17 times beside 15 calls to validate_positive_finite, sometimes with the same message text.
findings.proposal: Add decode_sweep_history(history) mirroring decode_six_buffer_history; one validate_revolve_params / validate_extrude_distance shared by both paths; one map_selection_to_indices(parent_ids, selection, label); one extract_subshapes(kind) behind the three extract_* methods.
findings.next_change: An agent tightens a threshold (e.g. ANGLE_ABS_MIN) or a message for revolve, or adds a counter to SweepOpHistory. It must find and edit 2-4 copies. Missing one makes execute() and the *_with_history path disagree; the integration tests exercise one path per op, so nothing catches it.

findings.statement: stdlib geometry builtins report failure in two separate string dispatches over the same names. eval_geometry(name, args) returns a bare Value::Undef with no reason, from 84 return sites over 47 names. diagnose(name, args) re-dispatches on the name and re-classifies the args to reconstruct why, for only 19 of those names. The other 28 names (e.g. frame3, transform3 with a wrong-kind arg) are silently Undef. Where both arms share a classify_* Result (affine_map) the reasons agree by construction; elsewhere the eval arm's early `return Some(Value::Undef)` guards and the diagnose arm's checks are independent code. diagnose itself is 229 lines, 112 of them prose (49%), largely rulings, escalation ids and task histories (A7, esc-5791-3, RULING #6126) answering reviewers. The same eval_X/diagnose twin pattern recurs in at least 7 stdlib modules with three different signatures.
findings.proposal: Have each builtin arm return Result<Value, Rejection>, and derive both the Undef and the Diagnostic from the Rejection at the single call site in reify-expr. Move the rulings prose to the PRD/docs, with a pointer.
findings.next_change: An agent adds a geometry builtin or a new rejection reason to an existing one. It must add the eval arm, remember to add a matching diagnose arm, and keep the two guard orders aligned. Forgetting yields an Undef with no reason, which no test fails, because tests assert result.is_undef() and diagnose separately.

findings.statement: OcctKernel::execute picks each result's BRepKind by exit path, not by a stated policy. 27 of the 53 constructive arms fall through to the shared tail `Ok(self.store(shape))`, which stamps BRepKind::Solid whatever the input or result kind; the other 26 return early with a fixed, classified or delegated repr. Affected fall-through arms: the transform arms Translate, Rotate, Mirror, Scale, RotateAround, AffineApply and ScaleNonUniform; the pattern arms; and Extrude, Revolve, Sweep and Pipe. The sibling ApplyTransform arm instead inherits the source repr via apply_transform_to_handle. The DSL translate() lowers to GeometryOp::Translate (geometry_ops.rs::transform_translate), so translate(rectangle_profile(..)) is stamped Solid; repr_of then misroutes Centroid away from the face-centroid branch. The same stamp lets translate(union(disjoint a, b)) pass run_local_feature_with_history's Solid-input guard. That guard's own comment claims the opposite: "apply_transform_to_handle propagates the repr, so fillet(translate(union(a, b)), ...) is rejected too". That route is not taken, and no test pins it. Separately, the all-edges Fillet/Chamfer arm (empty `edges`) calls ffi::fillet_all_edges/chamfer_all_edges directly and bypasses that guard. The curated-edge path enforces it, so the same op has two different preconditions.
findings.proposal: Remove the default tail. Have each arm return (shape, ReprPolicy) with ReprPolicy = Classify | Inherit(source) | Fixed(kind), and store once after the match, so a new arm cannot compile without choosing. Default transforms to Inherit and patterns/sweeps to Classify. Route the all-edges Fillet/Chamfer through the same Solid-input check, and correct the run_local_feature_with_history comment.
findings.next_change: An agent adds a new GeometryOp arm, or fixes a reported wrong repr on one arm such as Mirror of a face. To get it right it must know three things the arm does not show: the shared tail silently stamps Solid; run_local_feature_with_history and the Centroid query trust repr_of; MockGeometryKernel in reify-test-support mirrors the policy (task 7331 did so for booleans). A wrong choice compiles and passes; it is caught only if someone writes an integration test asserting repr_of for that specific arm, which exists for booleans and the guided sweeps only.

findings.statement: Point-, vector- and bbox-valued GeometryQuery answers cross the kernel/eval boundary as JSON-shaped strings and are parsed back by hand-rolled parsers. This includes Centroid, CenterOfMass, BoundingBox, EdgeTangent, FaceNormal, ClosestPointOnShape and FaceNormalAt, all encoded as `Value::String("{\"x\":..}")`. Typed variants already exist: Value::Point, Value::Direction, Value::BoundingBox and Value::Matrix. The same query() already uses Value::Point/Direction/Plane/Axis for FaceAnalyticDatum/EdgeAnalyticDatum. centroid_json's doc says other arms keep inline format! because "no cross-arm equality contract applies". Yet the four inline arms emit the identical shape precisely because one eval parser (topology_selectors::parse_xyz_value) consumes them all, so the contract exists and is held by convention. FaceSurfaceKind/EdgeCurveKind also return enum names as strings, decoded downstream by try_from_str.
findings.proposal: Return Value::Point / Value::Vector / Value::BoundingBox / Value::Matrix from query(), with one typed accessor in reify-ir per shape. Delete the 11 parsers, and return the surface/curve kind as Value::Enum or a typed enum.
findings.next_change: An agent adds a point-valued query, such as a vertex position or a principal axis, or teaches a new kernel (gmsh, manifold) to answer Centroid/BoundingBox. It must find and reproduce the exact string grammar, which is defined nowhere but in the parsers. A field-order or whitespace difference compiles and passes the kernel's own tests; it shows up only as QueryFailed("malformed JSON") or Undef in whichever eval consumer exercises that parser.

findings.statement: get_shape is documented as the single chokepoint that refuses null/IsNull topology "loudly" (fix 5211): it returns OperationFailed("shape handle .. wraps null/empty topology (IsNull)"). Every query-side caller discards that through `.get_shape(id).map_err(|_| QueryError::InvalidHandle(id))`, so a corrupted but present handle is reported to the user as an invalid handle. export/tessellate do the same into ExportError::InvalidHandle/TessError::InvalidHandle. The guard's test (get_shape_rejects_null_topology_and_queries_return_err) asserts only `is_err()` on the query paths, so the message loss is unpinned.
findings.proposal: Add one `fn shape_for_query(&self, id) -> Result<&OcctShape, QueryError>` mapping InvalidReference(id) to InvalidHandle(id) and OperationFailed(msg) to QueryFailed(msg), with sibling helpers for ExportError and TessError. Replace the 54 sites and assert the message in the existing null-topology test.
findings.next_change: An agent diagnosing a user report of "invalid handle for query" on a handle that plainly exists (after a reload or with a fixture compound) cannot tell null topology from an unknown id, and may 'fix' the handle bookkeeping instead. An agent adding a new query copies the erasing idiom, because it is the local convention 51 times over.

findings.statement: The OCCT geometry warm-start machinery (impl WarmStartable for OcctKernel, about 250 lines) has no production consumer. Its own comment states that nothing outside the crate's tests sends OcctRequest::WarmState/WithWarmState; no `kernel.warm_state()` or `with_warm_state()` call on a geometry kernel exists in crates/*/src. It nevertheless shapes the kernel's state design: every OcctKernel field must be classified in three exhaustive destructures (reset, warm_state, with_warm_state). It also carries a debug completeness cross-check and a documented latent next_id-lowering aliasing hazard, and it absorbed 22 of the 110 lib.rs commits since 2026-07-06. Most of its prose is reviewer-answering (a 50-line justification of the bounded-payload filter, including "Verified at the time this filter was added (task #5162): no in-tree production caller").
findings.proposal: Either wire OCCT warm start into a real consumer, or reduce the impl to the trait's no-op (return None) behind the existing inventory registration and drop the persistence logic until a consumer exists.
findings.next_change: An agent adds a field to OcctKernel, such as a per-handle attribute cache. It must decide PERSIST/CLEAR/RUNTIME semantics for a restore path no product uses, and write tests for it. A wrong classification is caught only by warm-state unit tests of an unused path.

findings.statement: Geometry kernel query replies for points, directions and bounding boxes (GeometryQuery::Centroid, BoundingBox, FaceNormal, EdgeTangent and others) cross the GeometryKernel seam as Value::String JSON text, and reify-eval decodes that text with four independent hand-rolled tokenizers: topology_selectors::parse_flat_number_object (wrapped by six pub(crate) parse_* functions and reached from geometry_ops, selector_vocabulary_v2 and engine_constraints), engine_build::parse_bbox_all_extents, primitive_attribute_seed::parse_normal_z and primitive_attribute_seed::parse_bbox_xyz_min. engine_build's own doc says parse_bbox_xyz_min 'parses the same format' and was left out of scope. Structured carriers already exist: Value::Point and Value::BoundingBox{min,max}. geometry_ops::dispatch_bounding_box turns the JSON string back into Value::BoundingBox. The parsers disagree on edge cases (parse_flat_number_object rejects unknown keys; the bbox_z variant tolerates the other four extents by an inline whitelist), and test mocks already carry a different shape ({"min":{..},"max":{..}} in harness_stress_scenarios/stress_query_consistency.rs) that the production parsers would reject.
findings.proposal: Make the GeometryKernel reply typed for these queries: kernels return Value::Point/Value::Vector/Value::BoundingBox (or a GeometryQueryReply enum), and the four tokenizers and six wrappers are deleted. dispatch_bounding_box becomes a pass-through.
findings.next_change: An agent adding a consumer of a point or bbox query (a new extremal or DFM selector, a mass-property check) or changing how a kernel formats one (Manifold emitting nested min/max like the stress mock, or a new kernel) must find all four tokenizers and both emitters, none of which share a type. The compiler does not catch a mismatch. Mock-based unit tests feed hand-written strings, so a format drift is caught only by OCCT-linked integration tests, and only for the parser those tests happen to reach.

findings.statement: Production realization goes through GeometryKernel::execute_with_history. engine_build.rs calls it at lines 836, 1125 and 8712, all before its #[cfg(test)] blocks. For OCCT, the decision of which ops have a history-aware primitive is made inside the kernel-thread match loop of OcctKernelHandle::spawn, not in OcctKernel, and that loop lowers the ops itself. It reads Extrude.distance, Fillet.radius and Chamfer.distance with Value::as_f64. OcctKernel::execute reads the same three fields through extract_length_f64, which runs reify_ir::check_length_field (the units-length tripwire) and emits the canonical non_numeric_kernel_field_message. So the production path is blind to the detector for these fields, and its error text ('fillet radius must be numeric') differs from the canonical one. The doc on OcctKernelHandle::execute_with_history says it is 'Channel-routed to the kernel thread's inherent OcctKernel::execute_with_history dispatcher', but no such method exists: git grep finds execute_with_history only in handle.rs, stubs.rs, reify-ir and test mocks.
findings.proposal: Move the op-to-history dispatch into lib.rs as OcctKernel::execute_with_history and share per-op field extraction (extract_length_f64 plus validation) with execute. The actor arm becomes a one-line forward like every other request.
findings.next_change: Adding history capture for another op (Draft, Shell, offset) means adding an arm to the spawn() match. An agent copies the neighbouring as_f64 arm and skips the tripwire again. To get it right it must know that lib.rs execute owns per-field extraction and that the units-length detector exists. Nothing catches the skip: the detector is warn-only, and no test asserts it fires on the history path.

findings.statement: Each kernel capability routed across the OCCT actor channel is written out by hand four or five times in handle.rs: an OcctRequest variant, an inherent sync method that builds it, an optional _async twin, a match arm in spawn() that unpacks it and calls OcctKernel, and a GeometryKernel trait method that forwards to the inherent method. The no-OCCT stubs.rs is a sixth copy, and it already lags: it defines neither measure_mesh_deviation nor make_compound, so those silently fall back to trait defaults in non-OCCT builds. This boilerplate is what makes handle.rs 1999 production lines.
findings.proposal: Replace the per-method enum with one closure request, Run(Box<dyn FnOnce(&mut OcctKernel) + Send>), behind a generic call<R>(f) -> Result<R, ChannelDied> and its async twin. Inherent methods become one-liners and the spawn loop becomes a single arm.
findings.next_change: Exposing another inherent OcctKernel method through &dyn GeometryKernel (as task 4744 did for closest_point_on_shape and vertex_point) means editing four or five places in handle.rs plus stubs.rs. The compiler catches a missing spawn arm, but not a missing trait forward (the trait default silently answers), a missing stub, or a doc/variant mismatch.

findings.statement: Selector resolution is implemented twice. resolve_with_attributes (live kernel) and resolve_against_carried_topology (kernel-free) each carry their own copy of the Union/Intersect/Difference composition with first-seen order and HashSet dedup. resolve_leaf_against_carried re-implements the ByNormal predicate of faces_by_normal 'byte-for-byte', so the PRD §7.2 two-way parity that the doc says holds 'by construction' actually depends on two copies staying identical. Inside resolve_leaf, the ByRole, CreatedByFeature and SplitByFeature arms repeat the same collect-filter-sort-map table walk three times. The resolver also closes a module cycle: resolve_leaf calls crate::selector_vocabulary_v2 twelve times, while selector_vocabulary_v2.rs imports seven names back from topology_selectors.
findings.proposal: Factor one generic compose(node, leaf_fn) over SelectorNode, used by both resolvers; extract a shared normal_within(normal, target, tol) predicate. Put the resolver in its own module above topology_selectors and selector_vocabulary_v2 so both become leaves.
findings.next_change: Adding a composite node (e.g. SymmetricDifference) or making another leaf resolvable from carried topology (task 4122 named ByArea and others as honest declines) means editing both resolvers and keeping a third copy of the predicate in step. A divergence shows up only if a parity test happens to cover that leaf. Adding a v2 leaf also means editing the cycle from both ends.

findings.statement: The geometric-relation and motion-joint vocabularies are bare strings matched independently in three crates. is_motion_joint_cell_type hardcodes six joint type names that mirror reify-compiler's pub(crate) joint_signatures::joint_ctor_result_type. Its own doc says that adding a joint kind there without updating this list is 'silent drift, no compile error', and that the unit test pinning the list is 'tautological'. Relation names are matched the same way: RelationInstance.name is a String, and describe_demand routes on 'concentric'/'flush'/'tangent'/… with an `other => other.to_string()` fallback. reify-constraints dispatches residual forms on the same names, and reify-compiler relation_signatures.rs has at least four more match functions over them.
findings.proposal: Introduce RelationKind and JointKind enums in a crate both compiler and eval depend on. The compiler resolves names once; RelationInstance carries the enum, and every match becomes exhaustive.
findings.next_change: Adding a relation (a new mate) or a joint kind (e.g. universal) needs an edit at every match site in compiler, constraints and eval. A missed describe_demand arm silently degrades the conflict diagnostic to the bare name. A missed is_motion_joint_cell_type entry silently never writes the relate-mount origin. Only a per-kind .ri e2e fixture catches either.

findings.statement: The sketch slot-kind rule is stated twice. SketchConstraint::operands and SketchEntity::defining_refs in sketch.rs are declared 'the single statement of which slot takes which kind' and drive validate(). SystemBuilder::emit_sketch_constraint then re-resolves every operand through four nested per-kind lookups (point/curve/arc/line, plus the Fix arm), using string labels ('point', 'circle or arc', 'arc', 'line', 'point or line') that duplicate SketchSlotKind's Display. Both files admit the two 'describe the same rule in two places'. If they ever disagree, release builds log tracing::error and skip that constraint (the debug_assert fires only in debug). That is a partial lowering that still solves, which is exactly the outcome validate() exists to forbid.
findings.proposal: Have validate() return a ValidatedSketch whose constraints carry already-resolved typed operands (an EmittedEntity kind per slot), so the emitter matches on types rather than re-deriving kinds. The drift guards then become unreachable by construction and can be deleted.
findings.next_change: Adding a sketch constraint (e.g. PtOnArc, EqualAngle) or widening a slot (letting tangency accept circles) means editing operands() and emit_sketch_constraint consistently. A mismatch passes CI in release-profile gates and silently drops the constraint from the solve.
