findings.statement: The side-panel's CSS grid track list is built by an inline IIFE in App's JSX that separately restates which children are mounted; it accounts for DesignTree, PropertyEditor, ConstraintPanel, the two splitters, AutoResolvePanel, MechanismPanel and the chat splitter+ChatPanel, but not BucklingPanel or FeaDiagnosticsPanel, which are conditionally mounted in-flow children of the same grid (their roots are display:flex with no position:fixed/absolute, unlike SolverProgressOverlay which is position:fixed). The code's own comment says a track/child mismatch 'shifts every subsequent child up a track and collapses chat into a 4px strip', and the AutoResolvePanel case was already fixed once by sharing the mount predicate (7a4aef93da); the same restatement is still wrong for two panels. The track-count invariant tests (countGridTracks === children.length) cover mechanism, auto-resolve and the debug overlay only.
findings.proposal: Declare the side panel as one ordered list of entries {id, mounted: () => boolean, track: () => string, render} and derive both the rendered children (<For> over mounted entries) and grid-template-rows from that list, so a panel cannot be added to one without the other; alternatively, put all non-resizable optional panels in a single flex column occupying one 'auto' track. Add a countGridTracks case with buckling and FEA diagnostics mounted.
findings.next_change: An agent adding a new side panel (or making an existing overlay in-flow) adds a <Show> child; it must know that a separate string builder 200 lines up must gain a matching track at the same position, which nothing in the type system or the JSX ties together. Today the only catch is the four App.test countGridTracks cases, none of which mounts the new panel, so a wrong version lands green and shows up as a clipped chat pane. Concretely, with chat open and buckling mode-shape frames arriving, tracks=7 but children=8: BucklingPanel takes the 4px splitter track, the chat Splitter takes minmax(160px,1fr), and ChatPanel falls into an implicit row clipped by overflow:hidden.

findings.statement: buildHandlers is a single 1532-line closure returning 58 debug-MCP command handlers, each validating its own params by hand. The file documents 'THE BOUNDARY RULE' in a ~60-line comment that censuses twelve independent copies of the same typeof-string guard (one spelled differently, kept 'as it stood'), backed by TYPE_GUARDED_RESOLVER_TOOLS and a per-copy test row, because 'the guards are INDEPENDENT COPIES, not one shared helper'. Handlers outside that family still read params through `as string` casts the comment itself says a JSON payload can falsify (type_in_editor content, keyboard key, select_entity, toggle_select, open_file path and content). Meanwhile every tool's parameter schema (types, required) is already declared once in Rust as ToolDef.input_schema in gui/src-tauri/src/debug_server.rs, and the Rust registry and the TS handler table are kept in step only by debugParity.test.ts regex-parsing debug_server.rs's source.
findings.proposal: Validate params once at dispatch against a single declared schema per tool: either have the Rust side forward each tool's input_schema and run one validator in initDebugBridge before calling the handler, or declare the schema beside each TS handler and generate/compare the Rust ToolDef from it. Then split buildHandlers into family modules (dom/inspection, pointer, camera, layout/window, lsp probes, fixtures/injection, wait) each exporting `(ctx) => Record<string, CommandHandler>` over a shared resolve module, and retire the copy census comment.
findings.next_change: Adding or changing a debug tool (the most common edit here, per churn) means: add a ToolDef with a JSON schema in debug_server.rs, add a handler inside the 1532-line closure that re-validates the same params by hand, decide whether it joins the BOUNDARY RULE family and if so add it to TYPE_GUARDED_RESOLVER_TOOLS and a test row, and update debugParity allowlists. A handler that forgets its guard (or uses `as string`) answers a malformed request with a true-looking DOM observation; only a per-copy test row would notice, and the comment says each copy 'can be reverted alone with the suite green'.

findings.statement: App (and engineStore.subscribeToEvents) reach the IPC layer by importing ./bridge directly rather than taking it as a dependency, so every App-level or store-level test must replace the whole module with vi.mock('../bridge', factory). Dropped keys in those hand-written factories caused three recorded defects (tasks 6035, 6039, 6045, replayed in bridgeMockContract.test.ts), and the response was a source-text parser over test files (bridgeMockContract.ts) plus a coverage test, rather than an injection seam. App.tsx also imports viewPersistence twice, once as a namespace, with a comment saying the namespace exists 'so vi.spyOn in tests intercepts the call'. The codebase already has the injected pattern for some collaborators (createMechanismStore({getMechanismDescriptors}), createDefPreviewActivation, createEditorSelectionSync) but not for the bridge.
findings.proposal: Give App a bridge port (an object typed as the subset of ./bridge it uses) via a prop or context with the real module as default, and have engineStore.subscribeToEvents accept its subscription functions; tests then build one typed fake from a shared factory, tsc enforces completeness, and the source-parsing guard and the namespace-import-for-spyOn can go.
findings.next_change: Adding a bridge subscription or command that App or engineStore uses requires adding the key to every wholesale bridge factory that renders App or constructs engineStore; the agent must know which ~11 files those are. A missed key surfaces as `undefined is not a function` swallowed by App's try/catch blocks (the failure mode of 6035/6039/6045) and is caught only for factories the source-parser can read.

findings.statement: viewStateStore's visibility queries (getEffectiveVisibility, getAllEffective, getStalePaths, hasOverride) read nodeByPath/parentByPath, plain non-reactive Maps reassigned by rebuildTreeMaps, and three of them short-circuit on an empty map without reading any reactive key. A reactive consumer that reads them before the tree loads therefore subscribes to nothing and never re-runs. Correctness depends on a readiness counter (treeGeneration) owned by App, bumped by App after it calls regenerateAutoViews, and threaded by hand into each consumer: App's effectiveVisibility memo, the fuzzy-rebind effect, and createSelectiveDemandSync, where it is a required parameter documented by a ~72-line docblock. The missing readiness dependency was a shipped bug (esc-6045-1, fixed under #6052 in three commits), and that docblock has itself needed two correction commits.
findings.proposal: Make the tree reactive state of viewStateStore itself (store a tree signal or a store-owned generation read inside every query) so the queries subscribe on their own; drop treeGeneration from App and the createSelectiveDemandSync signature, and delete the readiness prose.
findings.next_change: Any new consumer of effective visibility (e.g. an export filter, a per-pane visibility map, a probe overlay) must know to also track App's treeGeneration signal, which is not reachable from the store and not visible in its type; forgetting it compiles and works in tests that seed the tree first, then silently misses the first post-mount toggle in the real app.

findings.statement: types.ts hand-mirrors the Rust wire types in gui/src-tauri/src/types.rs with no code generation (no ts-rs/specta/typeshare in gui/src-tauri/Cargo.toml), tying the two together with prose ('Mirrors ... in types.rs') and per-field regex-over-Rust-source tests (constraintVerdictTokens.ts over engine.rs, toolDefNames.ts over debug_server.rs). Enum-valued fields cross the boundary as strings: ValueData.determinacy/kind/freshness, ConstraintData.status, DiagnosticInfo.severity, TensegrityWire/SurfaceData.kind, and EvaluationStatus.phase, which Rust stores as String after stringifying an EvalActivity enum of exactly {Evaluating, Idle}. The TS union adds 'resolving', which no producer emits, and the phase's consumers disagree on what 'active' means: engineStore.setEvalStatus treats evaluating|resolving as active, debug wait_for_idle treats only 'evaluating' as active and returns an engine_phase error for any other non-idle phase (its comment names an 'error' phase that does not exist), and StatusBar styles data-phase=resolving.
findings.proposal: Generate the wire interfaces from types.rs (ts-rs or specta), with the closed-set fields as Rust enums serialized to string-literal unions; give phase one exported isActivePhase helper used by engineStore and wait_for_idle; retire the regex-over-Rust parity helpers as fields move under generation.
findings.next_change: Adding a real phase (cancellation for #5215 or a genuine auto-resolve phase) requires editing the Rust string emit, the TS union, engineStore's active set, wait_for_idle's active set and StatusBar, with no compile-time link across the boundary; e.g. emitting 'resolving' today would make every harness wait_for_idle fail fast with engine_phase. Similar edits to freshness/status values are caught only if a regex-over-source test happens to exist for that field.

findings.statement: The set of layout dimensions has no single home: it is enumerated separately in the PanelLayout type, loadPanelLayout's per-key typeof checks, createLayoutStore's initial state, its persistence snapshot, its seven setters, the DEFAULT_* constants, the DebugStores.layout structural type in debug/types.ts (which marks problemsHeight/problemsCollapsed and their setters optional although the real store always has them), the debug resize_panes DIMS table, and the debug reset_app_state body. These copies have already drifted: reset_app_state resets 5 of the 6 numeric dimensions and not problemsCollapsed, while the Rust ToolDef contract for reset_app_state promises it will 'reset layout pane dimensions to their defaults', and no test checks the problems panel after a reset.
findings.proposal: Have layoutStore export one dimension table (key, default, kind) from which PanelLayout, load validation, initial state, persistence and setters derive, plus a reset() method; type DebugStores.layout as LayoutStore, and make resize_panes and reset_app_state iterate the table / call reset().
findings.next_change: Making another panel resizable (the side-panel grid already has optional panels that might gain heights) means touching all nine lists; an agent who misses reset_app_state or DebugStores leaves harness runs order-dependent: a scenario that calls resize_panes {problemsHeight: 400} and then reset_app_state hands the next scenario a 400px expanded problems panel. Nothing catches it today.

findings.statement: initApp manages its 11 event subscriptions through 11 separate `let …Unsub` closure variables and 10 near-identical try/await/if(!alive){u();return}/assign/catch blocks, and tears them down from two hand-maintained lists that already disagree: the defensive teardown at the top of initApp clears 10 and omits debugBridgeUnsub, while onCleanup clears all 11. The same module's peers do this uniformly: engineStore.subscribeToEvents collects unlisteners from one Promise.allSettled array, and bridge.subscribeToClaudeEvents iterates an entry table with rollback.
findings.proposal: Collect handles in one array with a small track(unsub) helper (or iterate a table of [subscribe, handler, onFailure]), tear down from that one array in both places, mirroring subscribeToClaudeEvents.
findings.next_change: Adding a subscription (e.g. eval-generation for the cancel work in #5215, or a new FEA event) means adding a variable and editing three places; the existing omission shows the lists diverge silently. Today the gap is not reachable (handleRetry only runs from the error phase, before the debug bridge initializes), so no test exercises it, and a future re-entrant init path would leak the debug-bridge listener and register a second one.

The function's own docblock records that the rule was dead against every real tree until #5195 added the 'Geometry' token, because the backend Displays both spellings as 'Geometry'. The same node already carries structured backend facts (trait_geometry, default_visible) for the other rules. The purpose-view path (generatePurposeViews, manufacturingReadyVisibilityFor, MATERIAL_TYPE_NAME_RE) is unreachable in production: its only production caller passes an empty purpose list.
findings.proposal: Emit a structured field on EntityTreeNode (e.g. is_geometry_value / a value-kind enum) from the backend and branch on it; delete the purpose-view path or wire activePurposes from the design.
findings.next_change: A Rust-side change to how types Display (a renamed type, a parameterised 'Geometry<3>', a new geometry kind) silently flips default visibility in the outline; the agent changing Display in crates/ has no reason to open a GUI store. Caught only by hand-built type_name fixtures in autoViewGenerator.test.ts and one engine_tests.rs example pin.

findings.statement: SidecarSession.invokeSdk is a 279-line method that builds CLI arguments, lazily writes an MCP config temp file, emits the sandbox notice, spawns the process and wires its error listeners, writes stdin, arms the timeout, captures stderr, and parses the stream-json event stream including four content-block kinds and the result event. The per-line `try { ... } catch { /* Skip unparseable lines */ }` wraps the whole event-handling body, not just JSON.parse, so any exception thrown while mapping an event, including from this.onOutput, is discarded as if the line were malformed.
findings.proposal: Extract a pure buildClaudeArgs(config, sessionId, mcpConfigPath), a spawn helper, and a pure mapStreamEvent(event, turnState) -> {outputs, turnState} reducer; narrow the catch to JSON.parse and log anything else.
findings.next_change: Handling a new stream-json event or content block (e.g. the init/system event, a new block type, a tool-list capture) is an edit inside this method; a TypeError in the new branch is silently swallowed, and the 4000-line session.test.ts, which mocks child_process, notices only if a test asserts on the missing output.

findings.statement: The width of the loop-closure Newton state is a fact computed at four sites, and the snapshot warm-start check disagrees with the other three. The solver's validate_loop_closure_inputs, solve_loop_closure's x0 construction, and snapshot's own post-solve check all use Σ JointKind::flat_len over free_b. The snapshot warm-start check (`if row.len() != free_b.len() { return Some(Value::Undef) }`) uses the free-joint COUNT. snapshot writes `free_values` rows as the full flat x (length Σ flat_len), and sweep::build_snapshot_list threads that row back as the 3-arg warm start. So for any closed-chain mechanism whose free_b holds a planar (flat_len 3), cylindrical (2) or spherical (4) joint, every sweep step after the first returns Value::Undef. extract_loop_closure_chains does put unbound multi-DOF joints into free_b, and joint_range_midpoint returns Some for them, so the cold first step succeeds. The adjacent comment ('the solver's own validate_loop_closure_inputs re-enforces it') claims agreement with a rule that is different.
findings.proposal: Delete the snapshot-side length guard, or compute it with the same helper the solver uses (expose the solver's free_joint_shapes width as one pub(crate) fn). Add a sweep test over a closed chain with a free planar joint that asserts every step is non-Undef.
findings.next_change: An agent fixing a 'sweep of a planar four-bar goes Undef after step 1' report has to know that free_values rows are flat-storage vectors (Σ flat_len, Sphere=4), which is defined in loop_closure_value.rs and loop_closure_solver.rs, not in snapshot.rs. The plausible wrong fix is to shrink the emitted row to free_b.len(). Nothing catches either version today: no snapshot or sweep test drives a multi-DOF closed chain through the warm-start path.

findings.statement: A joint's kind is a string inside a Value::Map, and every consumer re-parses it with its own match. Per-kind behaviour (constructor, transform, analytic Jacobian, motion subspace, DOF count, storage width, value wrapping, bound-value parsing, midpoint, driving-ness, force naming, compiler result type) is spread across string-match tables in 8 files and 2 crates. Two typed forms exist, loop_closure_value::JointKind and JointValue, but they are built from the string at each use site (JointKind::from_str has 6 production call sites) instead of once at construction. Agreement between the tables is enforced by test loops over the string constant JOINT_KINDS, not by exhaustiveness. Some sites have no guard at all: snapshot::wrap_jointvalue_for_joint and sweep::driving_joint_kind end in a `_ => None` catch-all, and joint_jacobian_value ends in `_ => Value::Undef`. JOINT_KINDS' own doc says the per-kind arms in transform_at and joint_jacobian_value 'must be kept in sync with this constant' by hand.
findings.proposal: Parse once: a typed `Joint` enum (one variant per kind, carrying unit axes and ranges) built by the constructors and recovered from the Map by one `Joint::from_value`. Per-kind behaviour goes in exhaustive methods in one module (transform, jacobian_columns, motion_subspace, dof, flat_len, wrap/unwrap JointValue, midpoint, is_driving). The Map stays the serialised Value form, and every site above calls the typed methods.
findings.next_change: Adding a joint kind (helical, universal), or giving an existing kind a new capability (e.g. cylindrical driving in sweep). The agent has to find all ~20 tables by grep, including two in reify-compiler, and learn which are exhaustive and which silently return None/Undef. A missed catch-all site shows up as a silent Value::Undef in snapshot/sweep. The JOINT_KINDS loops catch only the sites someone wrote a loop for.

findings.statement: The policy that resolves a joint's motion value (direct binding → coupling follows its parent → fixed sentinel → range midpoint) and wraps it as a transform_at argument is implemented twice. snapshot.rs has value_for + wrap_midpoint_for_joint + wrap_jointvalue_for_joint for the FK walk. loop_closure.rs has resolve_joint_value + direct_binding_value + value_for_joint for the solver inputs. wrap_jointvalue_for_joint is a line-for-line copy of loop_closure::value_for_joint, which is already pub(crate). The copies have diverged on multi-DOF. snapshot's midpoint fallback unwraps only JointValue::Scalar, so an unbound planar/spherical/cylindrical joint in an OPEN chain makes the whole snapshot Undef. The loop_closure copy resolves the same joint's midpoint for closed chains. The test snapshot_with_unbound_planar_returns_undef pins the Undef. Its doc justifies it with 'joint_range_midpoint returns None for planar … deferred to #2670', but loop_closure.rs's joint_range_midpoint_planar_returns_planar_midpoint asserts Some(Planar([0.5,0.5,π/2])), and task #2670 is status done.
findings.proposal: Make loop_closure's typed resolve_joint_value + value_for_joint the one resolver. snapshot's joint_local_transform should call `value_for_joint(joint, &resolve_joint_value(joint, bindings)?)` and delete value_for and both wrap_* functions. Rewrite the pinned test to assert the midpoint pose.
findings.next_change: Making open-chain snapshots honour multi-DOF midpoints, or changing the coupling rule (e.g. couplings with offsets). The agent edits one copy and has to discover the other in a different module. The test above goes red on the correct fix and reads as if it were protecting a contract. Nothing ties the two resolution orders together.

findings.statement: The diagnostics wrapper's policy is overridden by its only production caller, and its typed output is thrown away and rebuilt from strings. snapshot calls solve_loop_closure_with_diagnostics, scans report.diagnostics for DiagnosticCode::KinematicOverconstrained, and when found re-runs plain solve_loop_closure. Its comment calls the wrapper's '<6 free DOF' short-circuit 'a false positive for sub-6 effective-DOF loops'. KinematicUnderconstrained is discarded. Singularity is turned into an `is_singular: Bool(true)` key on the Snapshot Map. reify-eval's engine_eval::value_contains_singular_snapshot finds that key with a recursive string-key tree walk and mints a second KinematicSingularity diagnostic with its own message text. The solver also returns a flat Vec<f64>. To unflatten it, snapshot re-derives each free joint's JointKind from chain_b's kind strings, a third copy of the solver's private free_joint_shapes, and the third site that checks expected_width.
findings.proposal: Move the residual-subspace DOF policy into the solver, where snapshot needs no override. Have the solve return typed per-free-joint JointValues plus diagnostics. Carry diagnostics out of snapshot through the existing per-builtin `diagnose` hook (snapshot::diagnose already exists for center_of_mass) instead of a magic key and an engine-side scan.
findings.next_change: Surfacing over/under-constraint to users (the briefing's known gap), or fixing the false-positive DOF balance. The agent must learn that the policy lives in the wrapper, the override in snapshot, the user-facing emission in reify-eval, and that a Value-map key is the carrier between them. Changing the wrapper's rule silently changes which solver snapshot runs. No test pins the override as a contract.

findings.statement: The `input_shape` builtin has two TOTS-family implementations with different meanings. input_shape::eval_input_shape (the value-eval path, wired for `input_shape` and `input_shape_apply`) builds a canonical single-DOF stand-in model (canonical_tots_model, start 0 / end 1 / T 3 s, max_force hard-coded 1000.0), runs the full SQP (solve_tots, RNEA and modal simulation every iteration), and keeps only the outcome: Undef if infeasible, otherwise the INPUT profile echoed back. trampoline::input_shape_value (the engine ComputeNode path via reify-eval trajectory_ops) solves on a model built from the profile and returns a re-timed profile. Shaper-field defaults are duplicated, and a comment says they 'mirror input_shape::run_tots'. The `force_limit` field is read in one path and ignored in the other. read_scalar_si and field_f64 are each defined in both files. Family membership is decided by matching the StructureInstance type_name string. The two sites are kept in step by a 280-line #[cfg(test)] module (shaper_family_guard) that line-scans trajectory.ri with a hand-written partial grammar (prefix stripping, angle-bracket depth, `+` bound lists) and admits it misses multi-line headers.
findings.proposal: Keep one implementation. Have eval_input_shape delegate to trampoline::input_shape_value, or return Undef and leave the result to the ComputeNode. Parse the shaper once into a typed enum (Impulse(ZV|ZVD|EI|Cascaded) | Tots{params}) whose constructor is the only name match. A compiler-side registry of Shaper refiners can then replace the text scanner.
findings.next_change: Adding a shaper (e.g. a revolute-specific impulse shaper) or a new TOTS field (jerk limit). The agent must edit both arms, both default tables, and SHIPPED_SHAPER_STRUCTURES. It must also know which of the two arms the user's cell actually ends up with. A default changed in one arm only is caught by nothing. A shaper declared on two lines is invisible to the guard.

findings.statement: Loop-closure records are parsed in three places that do not share the precondition the docs say they share. mechanism_loop_closure_chains (used only by reify-constraints, via a re-export) classifies WellFormed vs Cycle. Its doc says Cycle chains must NOT be fed to solve_loop_closure. snapshot's solve path uses loop_closure::extract_loop_closure_chains instead, which does not classify, and feeds every record to the solver (snapshot's own doc calls the split 'advisory here'). strip_world_sentinel exists twice: loop_closure_solver.rs (pub(crate), used by mechanism_loop_closure_chains and snapshot::parent_conflict_closing_body_ids) and loop_closure.rs (private, used by extract_loop_closure_chains). The loop_closure.rs copy's doc says it 'mirrors reify_constraints::loop_closure::strip_world_sentinel', a module that no longer exists (reify-constraints/src has no loop_closure file). parent_conflict_closing_body_ids says 'sharing the PRECONDITION … is what makes the two call sites agree', but the solver path it must agree with uses the other copy.
findings.proposal: Keep one record parser, returning a typed record (chains, closing_joint, body_id, classification). Both extract_loop_closure_chains and parent_conflict_closing_body_ids derive from it. Delete the loop_closure.rs strip_world_sentinel copy, and have snapshot skip or diagnose Cycle records explicitly.
findings.next_change: Tightening the cycle/ancestor-case handling or the sentinel precondition (e.g. rejecting Cycle records in snapshot). An agent who edits loop_closure_solver's copy, as the SPOT docs direct, changes the classifier and the FK rigid-tie selection but not the chains snapshot actually solves. The predicate-sharing tests do not cover the extract path.

findings.next_change: Surfacing 'your trajectory limits are infeasible' to authors. findings.statement: Stdlib modules call their siblings by user-facing builtin name through the crate-root dispatcher (crate::eval_builtin), which walks the registry and the family dispatcher ladder. In joints.rs, transform_at's coupling arm recurses via eval_builtin("transform_at"), and the planar arm composes via eval_builtin("transform_compose"). The same function's origin step instead calls the typed crate::geometry::compose_transforms. screw/gear/rack_and_pinion call eval_builtin("couple"). loop_closure_solver::solve_loop_closure calls eval_builtin("joint_jacobian") once per free joint and discards the result; its only effect is a tracing::debug event that tests capture. Each such call is an untyped, rename-fragile edge: a failure comes back as Value::Undef, not a compile error.
findings.proposal: Expose typed pub(crate) Rust functions (transform_at(&Joint, &JointValue), compose, couple) that the builtin arms and the internal callers both use. Turn the KCC-γ availability probe into a direct tracing call, or drop it.
findings.next_change: Renaming or re-registering a builtin (the registry migration in lib.rs's eval_builtin is live), or changing transform_at's arity. Internal callers break as silent Undef at runtime. The agent must grep string literals across modules to find them, and the caller's file does not show the dependency.

findings.statement: The per-joint-kind codec between JointValue and the dimensioned Value that transform_at consumes has no single home. loop_closure::value_for_joint (pub(crate)) and snapshot::wrap_jointvalue_for_joint (private) have identical bodies; the snapshot copy's doc even says it 'mirrors loop_closure::value_for_joint'. The inverse direction (loop_closure::jointvalue_from_bound_value) and a partial third encoder (snapshot::wrap_midpoint_for_joint) also match on raw kind strings. Only joint_range_midpoint and is_zero_dof_joint dispatch through the typed JointKind via joint_kind(), whose own doc concedes it is not the SPOT for the value encodings. The binding-resolution ladder (direct binding, then coupling-tracks-parent, then fixed sentinel, then range midpoint) is likewise implemented twice: loop_closure::resolve_joint_value and snapshot::value_for. The copies have drifted. resolve_joint_value returns Planar/Sphere/Cyl midpoints for unbound multi-DOF joints. snapshot::value_for keeps only JointValue::Scalar midpoints (`_ => None`), so by code read the open-chain FK path yields None (and so Undef) for an unbound planar, spherical or cylindrical joint. Its comment still claims 'joint_range_midpoint returns None for planar' pending #2670, and #2670 is done. Adding a joint kind is a compile error only in joint_range_midpoint; the other four string matches fall to `_ => None` silently.
findings.proposal: Give JointKind (in loop_closure_value.rs, where JointValue already lives) the codec as exhaustive methods: encode(&JointValue, parent kind) -> Option<Value> and decode(&Value) -> Option<JointValue>. Make one pub(crate) resolver for the binding ladder. Have snapshot's open-chain and closed-chain post-process paths call that resolver and encoder, then delete wrap_jointvalue_for_joint, wrap_midpoint_for_joint and the duplicated ladder in value_for.
findings.next_change: Add an eighth joint kind (e.g. a screw/helical joint), or close #7497 (a coupling in chain_b must track its parent inside each Newton step). An agent must find all five string-matching sites across two files, know that snapshot.rs carries private copies rather than calling loop_closure, and keep the encode and decode directions symmetric. The only guard is the JOINT_KINDS partition test in loop_closure's test module, which exercises loop_closure's copies and not snapshot's. A missed snapshot arm surfaces as an Undef snapshot for that kind, with no compile error and no named test.

findings.statement: append_body knows which closing-edge class it recorded: parent-conflict, or cycle/self-loop. It knows which body is the closing one, and which error it raised. make_loop_closure_record and make_body_record then erase that into string-keyed Value::Maps. Every consumer re-derives the class from structure. loop_closure_solver::mechanism_loop_closure_chains and snapshot::parent_conflict_closing_body_ids classify Cycle vs WellFormed by whether chain_b contains the closing joint anywhere (closing_side_contains_closing_joint). The doc comments on that predicate run about 40 lines explaining why a tail test is wrong. dynamics::eval::closed_chain_inverse_dynamics assumes 'Mechanism builder appends closing-edge bodies at the end, so the first n_tree entries are the spanning-tree bodies', taking tree_bodies = bodies[..n_total - n_lc]. append_body enforces no such order: it pushes every body in call order. So by code read, an open body() after a closing one is dropped from the tree and the closing body is counted as a tree body. reify-eval engine_eval::detect_mechanism_errors hardcodes the 'duplicate_solid' discriminator, so 'world_parented_closure' has no diagnostic (#7354, pending, covers only that error half). The record is parsed independently in two places: loop_closure::extract_loop_closure_chains and loop_closure_solver::mechanism_loop_closure_chains, each with its own strip_world_sentinel.
findings.proposal: Make the edge class, the closing-body id and the error kind typed at construction. The cheap step is to stamp a 'class' discriminator and keep the existing body_id on each loop_closure record, have dynamics select tree bodies by excluding those body_ids rather than by position, and route detect_mechanism_errors through a discriminator-to-DiagnosticCode table (the shape #7354 proposes). The deeper step is a typed MechanismRecord / LoopClosure struct carried in OpaqueState or a StructureInstance, parsed once at the stdlib boundary, with extract_loop_closure_chains and mechanism_loop_closure_chains merged into its one reader.
findings.next_change: Add a third closing-edge class (e.g. a grounding closure, which mechanism.rs says needs a solver redesign) or a third mechanism error. The agent must find every consumer that infers class or ordering from list contents: snapshot FK, solver classification, closed-chain dynamics' n_tree slice, modal_ops, engine_eval. Nothing in the type system ties them to the producer. Only scenario tests catch a miss, and no test builds an open body after a closing one for inverse dynamics.

findings.statement: worst_case_residual_fraction is pub and #[allow(dead_code)], and has zero production callers. Its G-allow comment and doc claim it is a 'permanent internal helper of the wired trajectory evaluation pipeline (simulate_trajectory_value / solve_tots, both wired via trampoline.rs → trajectory_ops.rs:371/429)'. Neither trampoline in this file calls it, reify-eval has no trampoline.rs, and nothing under crates/reify-stdlib/src/trajectory/ outside impulse_shaper.rs calls residual_vibration, so TOTS does not score shapers through it. The module docstring repeats the claim ('Both reuse [`worst_case_residual_fraction`]'). reify-audit's new_orphans_2026_06_02_g_allow.rs then pins the orphan as allowed, 'owned by' #3869 and #3870, both done. The file layout also puts the #[cfg(test)] module between this helper and a second `use` block that opens the real trampoline code, so the file reads as two files spliced together.
findings.proposal: Either wire it, so TOTS or simulate_trajectory actually reports worst-case band residual, or delete it with its tests and the audit pin. Either way, rewrite the module docstring to describe the two trampolines this file actually holds, and move the test module to the end of the file.
findings.next_change: An agent changing TOTS robustness scoring, or the shaper insensitivity-band metric, will be pointed by this module's docs to worst_case_residual_fraction and edit it. The edit changes nothing user-visible, and its unit tests still pass. Before doing that it must establish, from outside the file, that tots.rs and the trampolines never call it. Nothing catches the wasted or misdirected change; the audit pin actively ratifies the orphan.

findings.statement: Production prose in loop_closure.rs and mechanism.rs is about half the lines, and much of it narrates history or answers reviewers rather than stating contracts, which is the drift class this repo keeps paying for. In loop_closure.rs the module docstring contradicts the function docs. It says FD chain Jacobians are correct only for 'prismatic, revolute, coupling, fixed', with planar/spherical/cylindrical 'deferred to ... #2670', while chain_jacobian_fd's doc says it covers 'all seven JOINT_KINDS post KCC-γ widening', and #2670 is done. It calls the snapshot evaluator 'future task 2585' and points five times at a nonexistent reify_constraints::loop_closure. Function docs narrate signature changes ('widened from (joint, f64) ...', 'Task 7186 changed where ... Before 7186 it was appended ...'). LoopClosureSolverInputs carries a defence of tuple-over-struct. In mechanism.rs, append_body's comments include a rejected-alternatives argument with a measurement ('measured at 1.3 m on the 5-arg form') and four pointers into an untracked plan.json. The fix history shows the cost: the task 7186 burst on these two files needed repeated comment-correction commits.
findings.proposal: Rewrite both module docstrings as current contracts: supported kinds, twist convention, and a pointer to docs/prds/v0_2/kinematic-constraints.md for rationale. Move the residual-conjugation and rigid-tie arguments into that PRD or docs/, with a one-line pointer from append_body. Drop KCC-γ and 7186 narration and the tuple-vs-struct defence, since they belong in commit messages.
findings.next_change: Any change to the chain machinery (#7497, an analytic Jacobian composition) starts by reading a module docstring that names the wrong supported kinds, a crate path that does not exist and a done task as pending. The agent must reconcile prose against code before trusting either. Nothing gates prose truth: the PTODO ratchet does not see prose-form citations like '(taskmaster #2670 ...)'.

findings.statement: extract_loop_closure_chains returns LoopClosureSolverInputs, a positional 5-tuple (chain_a, vals_a, chain_b, vals_b_initial, free_b). Two field pairs are parallel vectors whose equal-length invariant is not carried by the type. It is re-checked ad hoc in chain_transform, chain_jacobian_fd and loop_residual_jacobian_by_joint, and each collapses a violation to a bare None. The whole public surface of the module is Option-returning, with no reason carried. The production code has 34 `return None`, 36 `?` propagations and 7 `_ => None` arms across 8 pub/pub(crate) functions, so snapshot maps any of them to Value::Undef with no named cause. Its own comment calls this a way to 'surface the structural bug'. Meanwhile loop_closure_solver re-validates the same inputs and does produce reason strings.
findings.proposal: Replace the tuple with a named struct whose chains are Vec<(Value, JointValue)>, or an owning type built once with its invariant checked at construction. Return Result with a small error enum naming the failed field or joint. Have snapshot surface that error as a diagnostic rather than a bare Undef.
findings.next_change: #7497 needs the coupling relation (parent index plus ratio/offset) carried into the solver. The natural move is a sixth tuple field, which touches all 10 destructuring sites and makes the positional meaning harder to read. Debugging a closed-chain Undef also needs a reason, which today means bisecting 77 None sites by hand.

findings.statement: Engine::execute_realization_ops is one 2,317-line associated fn (1,095 code lines, 1,212 comment lines) nested up to 16 levels deep. It contains the whole per-realization pipeline inline. Inside the op loop, the Ok(geom_op) match arm runs about 1,200 lines (7734-8936) and holds: selector pre-hydration, dispatch plus BRep fallback, pragma warning, the multi-stage conversion recipe (the Some(plan) arm with conversions, about 630 lines, 7959-8589, containing a labelled 'convert loop, intermediate-cache inserts and attribute forwarding closures), and execute_with_history with attribute population (about 200 lines). After the loop, the success branch is about 750 lines and adds swept-kind recording, a selector tie-scan, the morph decision, an inline VolumeMesh terminal conversion (about 250 lines) and an inline Voxel terminal conversion, then the cache insert. Each terminal repr is an inline `if demanded_repr == ReprKind::X` block rather than a stage. It has grown about 29% since the 2026-07-05 survey measured ~1,794 lines.
findings.proposal: Split along the stages already present: (a) a per-op dispatch function returning a typed OpOutcome {handle, repr, attribute_history, intermediate_inserts} that the loop folds; (b) one function per terminal conversion keyed by demanded_repr (VolumeMesh, Voxel), each returning the new terminal handle and repr; (c) a commit/rollback function that owns intermediate_cache_inserts. Put these in a free-function executor module. That needs only Engine::DEFAULT_KERNEL_NAME and DEFAULT_TESSELLATION_TOLERANCE moved below Engine (see h14 partition).
findings.next_change: Plausible next change: add a third terminal repr conversion (e.g. an Sdf terminal next to the VolumeMesh and Voxel blocks), or a per-op hook (a new per-op diagnostic or a new conversion-stage kind). To do it, the agent has to load and understand about 2,300 lines at 16-deep nesting. It must also work out which locals are live across the loop (realization_step_ids/reprs, solid_attribute_handles, intermediate_cache_inserts, last_produced_repr, morph_source_stash, topology_drop_tally) and which post-loop branch owns rollback of intermediate-cache inserts. A wrong version is caught only by whatever DispatchTestState run/run_demand scenario in the 10,849-line engine_build/tests.rs happens to cover that repr. Nothing types the per-op outcome or the rollback obligation.

findings.statement: Four entry points each hand-copy the per-template realization walk around execute_realization_ops: build_snapshot, build_with_geometry_output, tessellate_from_values and distance_between_placed. Each repeats module_named_steps seeding, step construction, demand lookups, assembling a RealizationOpsInput with up to 11 chained with_* calls, and the post-call write-back. Each makes its own inline choice per axis. Cross-let seeding: build only. Schedule-ordered BuildStep walk: build and tessellate only, built from a 30-line block duplicated verbatim in both. demanded_repr: compute_demanded_reprs in build, build_snapshot and distance; voxel_pipeline_demand_overrides in tessellate. demanded_boundary: false on tessellate. prefer_kernel: None on distance. morph_io: disabled on tessellate and distance. module_binds_selector: build paths only. realized_reprs: build only. produced_repr/produced_kernel/input_cone_hash write-back: build and build_snapshot only. mark_realization_failed: build and build_snapshot only. reset_per_build_state: absent from distance, so its dispatches pile onto the previous build's tallies (documented in engine_admin.rs). distance_between_placed carries the contract only as a comment: 'any changes to the realization execution or terminal_handles bookkeeping in build() must be mirrored here'.
findings.proposal: Model each surface as a value, e.g. a SurfacePolicy built from BuildSurface (seeding set, schedule source, demand source, morph enablement, write-back sink). Have one per-template walk take the policy and a write-back sink trait, so each axis is a single decision in one table, not inline at four call sites. Engine-scoped postures (mesh_contract_mode, long_chain_threshold) would then be read once by the walk instead of being threaded per call.
findings.next_change: Plausible next change: add an engine-scoped posture or a per-realization write-back, such as the next with_* knob, or writing produced_repr on the tessellate path. The agent has to find all four drivers and decide each axis for each surface. It has to know that distance_between_placed skips reset_per_build_state, and that the cross-let seed is unnecessary off-build only because check_constraints_post_geometry runs only in build. Nothing catches a missed surface. The compiler accepts the with_* defaults, which are fail-open for module_binds_selector and realized_reprs, and the parity contract is a comment (see finding 3 for one that has already fallen through).

findings.statement: tessellate_from_values collects produced_repr_out and then throws it away, so tessellate_realizations and tessellate_snapshot never update eval_state.snapshot.graph.realizations[id].produced_repr. The inline comment says this was benign only while every tessellate demand was BRep. It says the symmetric write 'MUST close before ζ ships', tracked by #3437. #3437 is done, yet the discard is still in place. Meanwhile the tessellate path now demands non-BRep reprs: voxel_pipeline_demand_overrides (task 5033 Gap D) sets Voxel/Mesh demands for isosurface-pipeline realizations. realization_content.rs projects readable content by matching on node_data.produced_repr, and BRep is identity-only with no content. A tessellate-only session (GUI tessellate_snapshot) for a voxel-terminal realization therefore leaves the node at its construction-time BRep default. The same path also drops kernel_error, so no Freshness::Failed is recorded. Not reproduced at runtime, so this is PLAUSIBLE rather than CONFIRMED.
findings.proposal: Return Vec<(RealizationNodeId, ReprKind, Option<ErrorRef>)> from tessellate_from_values and apply it in tessellate_realizations/tessellate_snapshot through the same write-back helper the build surfaces use. This falls out of finding 2's single write-back sink. Add a test that pins produced_repr after tessellate_snapshot on a voxel-terminal fixture.
findings.next_change: Plausible next change: a GUI/MCP read of realization content after a slider edit, which drives tessellate_snapshot and not build, on an isosurface model. Or any new consumer of produced_repr. To get this right, the agent has to know that only build surfaces write the graph node, and that the tessellate path's demand differs from the build path's. The only record of that is an inline comment citing a closed task. Nothing catches it: the PTODO ratchet does not see a prose 'MUST close before' citation, and no test pins produced_repr after a tessellate-only call (the forward guard named in the comment pins build_snapshot only).

findings.statement: DiagnosticCode has 214 variants carried by 4,449 doc-comment lines (median 18 per variant, max 77). That makes diagnostics.rs 8,021 lines at 73.5% prose, and 90.6% of its 5,160 production lines are prose. Much of the doc restates facts that live elsewhere and drift. There are 206 'Origin:' emitter pointers; 26 of them are file:line coordinates, and both line coordinates I sampled are stale: expr.rs:670-681 now holds the CmpOperandKind constructor, not unbound-identifier, and guards.rs:155 is a parameter list while the UnresolvedType emitter is at :176. One pointer names the retired crate crates/reify-types/src/value.rs::SampledField. There are 166 'PRD-prose mnemonic' lines, and 9 'Minting rationale' paragraphs that repeat why adding a variant is non-breaking. Of the inline tests, 136 of 151 are per-variant exists/attach/serde-PascalCase checks of derived behaviour, with no table-driven all-variants test.
findings.proposal: Make the doc one line per variant: meaning and severity. Emitter location is derivable by `git grep DiagnosticCode::<X>`, so drop Origin/line pointers. Move PRD mnemonics to the PRDs, or to a strum-derived table if tooling needs them. Replace the per-variant serde tests with one EnumIter/strum-driven round-trip test (ty.rs already derives EnumIter for TypeDiscriminants). Moving DiagnosticCode to its own file is symptom-free; see h14.
findings.next_change: Plausible next change: add a diagnostic code. That happens in 20 of 56 recent commits, which makes this file a hotfile. By convention the agent appends 20-80 lines of doc, including a line-coordinate Origin pointer that starts drifting immediately, plus two per-variant derive tests. Separately, an agent tracing a code to its emitter follows Origin to the wrong line. The only catch is git grep DiagnosticCode::X, which the pointer was meant to replace. Nothing gates pointer correctness.

findings.statement: reify_core::Type (41 variants) has no shared child traversal. So 'does any nested type satisfy P' is re-implemented as separate exhaustive matches that list the same inner-Type-bearing constructor set and differ only in the leaf predicate: type_mentions_conflicted_param (type_compat.rs) vs type_carries_type_param and type_carries_dim_param (reify-core overload.rs). Five more walkers repeat the same constructor classification: unify, substitute_type_params, normalize_type_guarded, walk_type_for_applied, Type's Display. Their doc comments say they are kept 'in lock-step' with each other. Exhaustive matching makes the compiler flag a missing arm, but not a misclassified one: a new inner-bearing variant listed as a leaf in one walker compiles fine.
findings.proposal: Add a `Type::children(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item=&Type>` (and `Type::any_descendant(pred)`) in reify-core, as the single exhaustive classification. Express type_carries_type_param, type_carries_dim_param and type_mentions_conflicted_param as one-line predicates over it. type_carries_trait_object's deliberately narrower walk stays explicit.
findings.next_change: Plausible next change: add a Type variant (six were added in June). The agent must classify it correctly in 8 walkers across 3 crates. The compiler only guarantees that each walker mentions it. Getting the inner/leaf classification wrong in one walker, for example forgetting to recurse into a new wrapper in type_mentions_conflicted_param, would bring back the duplicate EnumTypeArgConflict cascade that the predicate exists to suppress, and only a targeted test would notice.

findings.statement: type_compat.rs opens with `use super::*;` and imports only EnumDef and two overload predicates explicitly. Type, BinOp, UnOp, CompiledFunction, CompiledExpr, Diagnostic, DiagnosticCode, DiagnosticLabel, SourceSpan, HashMap and HashSet all reach it through the reify-compiler crate root. That root itself glob-re-exports 28 sibling modules (`pub(crate) use <module>::*;`), including `pub(crate) use type_compat::*`. So the crate is one flat namespace: reading this file alone you cannot tell which module or crate a name comes from, and every sibling sees every pub(crate) item of every other.
findings.proposal: Replace `use super::*` with explicit imports, starting with the files under change. Retire the lib.rs `pub(crate) use X::*` globs a module at a time, so dependencies are named and grep-able. Track this as a crate-wide stream; see seams.
findings.next_change: Plausible next change: move type_compat's binop-typing half into its own module, or rename one of its pub(crate) predicates. The agent cannot learn from the file which names it depends on, nor from a grep of `type_compat::` who depends on it, because callers reach its items through the root glob without naming the module. A rename breaks unknown call sites. The compiler catches it, but after the agent has already committed to the edit shape, and a shadowing name collision between glob-exported siblings fails silently in favour of whichever glob wins.

findings.statement: AST operators reach the compiler as strings (reify_ast ExprKind::BinOp/UnOp `op: String`). type_compat.rs then parses them ad hoc in several places that must agree with each other: resolve_binop and resolve_unop map strings to BinOp/UnOp, is_comparison_op keeps its own string set ("<","<=",...) that must match resolve_binop's comparison arms, and is_syntactic_zero_literal tests `op == "-"`. Outside this file, type_resolution.rs const-folding matches op.as_str() on "+","-","*","/" (line 449) and on unary "-" (line 488) without going through resolve_binop, and expr.rs:1858 tests `unary_op.as_str() == "-"`.
findings.proposal: Parse operators into BinOp/UnOp at the syntax boundary (ts_parser) so ExprKind carries the enum. is_comparison_op then becomes a method on BinOp, and the string parsers are deleted.
findings.next_change: Plausible next change: add an operator, e.g. a new comparison or logical spelling. The agent has to update the tree-sitter grammar, resolve_binop, is_comparison_op if it chains, and the const-folder. A missed string set compiles and silently misclassifies the operator, for example chained-comparison flattening skips it. Only an end-to-end .ri test catches that.

findings.statement: kleene.rs is the single source for the AND/OR/IMPLIES/NOT truth tables, but not for the left-operand absorption rule that drives short-circuit. That rule (False absorbs AND, True absorbs OR, False vacuously satisfies IMPLIES) is written out separately in reify-expr lib.rs eval_and/eval_or/eval_implies and in dual_eval.rs (the `absorbed` match, 'matching `eval_and`/`eval_or`/`eval_implies` exactly'), and both must agree with the kleene tables.
findings.proposal: Add `kleene::left_absorbs(op, lk: KBool) -> Option<KBool>` (with a small Kleene-op enum or taking BinOp) and call it from both eval paths.
findings.next_change: Plausible next change: add a connective (e.g. xor, which has no absorbing element) or change Undef semantics. The agent has to edit kleene.rs and both short-circuit copies. A mismatch makes the dual (derivative) evaluator record a different branch than the primal one, and only dual_eval branch-signature tests would notice.

findings.statement: Which calls eval_expr intercepts before reify_stdlib::eval_builtin or eval_user_function_call is defined only as inline string-guarded match arms: 23 named FunctionCall arms plus 4 UserFunctionCall families (solve_load_cases/5|6, option_recovery::is_combinator, map_or/3, map_err/2). dual_eval.rs must give 'the same answer in the same place, on the same operand shapes' (its own module doc), so it restates that table by hand: is_intercepted_user_fn repeats the 4 UserFunctionCall gates byte-for-byte, field_reduction_kind/reduction_kind_of/is_kink_builtin repeat the 8 field-reduction arms, and eval_binop's strict-Undef precheck is re-added at two sites. The module doc says a missed mirror fails silently with a WRONG PRIMAL. The guarding test (the_dual_intercept_gate_covers_exactly_the_families_eval_expr_intercepts) lists the families by hand, so it cannot see a fifth family added to eval_expr. The prose that holds the mirror together cites lib.rs by line number, and every cited line is stale. The table is also invisible to the compiler: a user `pub fn map_or(a,b,c)` compiles to UserFunctionCall and is silently replaced at eval, and reserved_name_lint covers type names only.
findings.proposal: Make the interception decision a typed classifier exported once from reify-expr, e.g. `fn classify_call(name, qualified, args) -> Option<Intercept>` for FunctionCall and `fn classify_user_call(name, arity) -> Option<UserIntercept>`, with eval_expr matching on the enum. dual_eval then calls the same classifier, and the compiler's reserved-name lint can query it. A new variant becomes a compile error in every exhaustive consumer, and the line-number prose can be deleted.
findings.next_change: An agent adds a new ctx-needing builtin or combinator (the pattern used by flat_map, generate, map_or and map_err) as one more name-guarded arm in eval_expr. To do it correctly it must know that dual_eval.rs exists, find the matching mirror function using line pointers that are already wrong, and add the same gate there. Nothing catches the omission: the membership test enumerates names by hand, and the primal-invariant tests cover only the existing families. Solvers that use eval_dual then get a different primal than eval_expr for the same model.

findings.statement: compile_expr types every geometry-constructor call (is_geometry_function: box, cylinder, union, sweep, ...) as Type::dimensionless_scalar(), a placeholder that misstates the value's kind. Every consumer that needs the truth has to undo it, either by re-checking the callee name or by overriding the type. conformance/mod.rs (3 sites), geometry.rs (2) and geometry_traits_inference.rs (2, is_geometry_operand) call is_geometry_function on the FunctionCall name. entity.rs sets cell_type explicitly to Type::Geometry and List<Geometry> in two Let-arm branches because 'the general expression compiler types geometry-function calls as dimensionless scalars'. A list literal of geometry calls is typed List<Real>, which a geometry_traits_inference test pins as 'the shape real compilation produces'. The conformance doc points at `expr.rs:782` for the placeholder; the arm is actually at line 3627.

If some consumer depends on the scalar placeholder for content-hash or diagnostic reasons, give it its own explicit marker instead of borrowing a value type.

findings.statement: compile_entity (3,800 lines) works out each let's kind (geometry let, selector let, geometry-list let, rejected list let) as HashSet<&str> locals that live across three passes and a deferred sub-pass. It does not classify each member once. is_geometry_let is called again with known_geometry_lets at 5 sites in compile_entity, plus 1 in the guarded-member helper and 2 in build_structure_def_skeleton. Pass 1 fills the set incrementally (doc: 'order-sensitive (incremental accumulation)'), but pass 2 (line 2929) and pass 3 (lines 4516, 4660) query the completed set. A forward alias (`let shifted = base` declared before `let base = box(..)`) is therefore non-geometry in pass 1's scope registration and geometry in pass 2/3. The pinned test cyclic_ident_alias_does_not_crash covers only the cyclic case. build_structure_def_skeleton re-implements the incremental classification so ctor `lets` stay consistent. Its pointers to the authoritative path (entity.rs:623, 853-856, 822-831, ~631) are stale, and the function doc still describes 'Two-pass compilation'.
findings.proposal: Classify each member once, in pass 1, into a typed per-member `LetKind` (Geometry | Selector | GeometryList(shape) | Rejected | Value). Every later pass and build_structure_def_skeleton reads that classification instead of re-running is_geometry_let against a set, so passes cannot disagree and the skeleton reuses the authoritative answer.
findings.next_change: An agent adds a new let shape (a new geometry-producing form, or a new list kind like #5385). It has to update the pass-1 accumulator, the pass-2 and pass-3 re-checks and the skeleton mirror, and it has to keep their order-sensitivity in agreement. That requires reading a 3,800-line function plus a 460-line mirror whose cross-references are stale. A missed site or a pass disagreement shows up only as a spurious Undef ctor field or a mistyped cell in an e2e test, if one exists for that shape.

findings.statement: The stdlib function solve_load_cases has four implementations spread across four crates: a placeholder .ri body (fea_multi_case.ri, two overloads), the @optimized trampoline reify-eval/compute_targets/multi_case.rs, a name-intercept fallback in reify-expr (eval_solve_load_cases, resolve_load_case_options, invoke_solve_elastic_static) and a permanent Undef stub in reify-stdlib fea.rs. reify-expr is described as a 'pure recursive evaluator', yet it reads LoadCase fields by string ('name', 'loads', 'supports', 'options', 'cases'). It repeats the empty-cases and duplicate-name diagnostics that multi_case.rs also emits, and multi_case.rs says it 'mirrors resolve_load_case_options in crates/reify-expr/src/lib.rs'. invoke_solve_elastic_static finds 'solve_elastic_static' by name and arity only. It evaluates the contract body, bypassing @optimized dispatch, and on ANY Undef it returns a field-less stub ElasticResult. Its own comment labels this a KNOWN LIMITATION that masks genuine solve failures. The intercept gates on arity 5|6 only, so the 3|4-arity body:Solid overload is never intercepted.
findings.proposal: Give the per-case semantics one home, in reify-eval next to the trampoline, and have reify-expr route nested calls through the existing compute_dispatch hook instead of re-implementing the driver. Then delete the stub-on-any-Undef fallback.
findings.next_change: An agent changes LoadCase (adds a field, renames 'supports', or changes option inheritance) or adds a solve_load_cases overload. It must find and change the reify-expr fallback and the reify-eval trampoline in step. Nothing ties them together: the .ri field names are bare strings in both, and the fallback's stub ElasticResult hides a failed per-case solve as a non-Undef value, so a divergence surfaces only where a nested call reaches the fallback.

findings.statement: Value::Field stores its payload in a slot named `lambda: Arc<Value>`, and what the slot holds depends on `source`. For Restricted and Composed it is a positional 2-element List. For SafetyFactor it is List[field, yield]. For AsPrintedZones it is a 7-element List whose third item is itself a positional 7-number List [walls, top_bottom_layers, layer_height, line_width, bx, by, bz]. The only contract is a doc table on reify_ir::Value::Field. sample_field_at and sample_as_printed_zones decode the payload by index (`items.len() == 7`, p[0]..p[6]) and return Undef on any shape mismatch. Two producers, as_printed_material.rs and as_printed_material_r0.rs, each hand-pack the same 7+7 layout. The doc table has already drifted from the code: it says Imported stores Value::Undef, but sample_field_at samples Imported fields as Value::SampledField.
findings.proposal: Replace the positional payloads with typed variants, e.g. `enum FieldPayload { Lambda(..), Sampled(SampledField), Composed{outer, inner}, Restricted{inner, region}, AsPrintedZones(ZonePayload) }`, built and decoded through one constructor, so the layout lives in the type.
findings.next_change: An agent adds a zone parameter (e.g. infill angle) or a new derived field source. It must edit both producers and the index arithmetic in reify-expr, keeping three files in agreement through a doc table. A misordered element silently produces the wrong zone or material, or Undef. Nothing fails at compile time, and only an end-to-end material test catches it.

findings.statement: expr.rs and entity.rs both open with `use super::*;`, which pulls in reify-compiler lib.rs's 30 `pub(crate) use <module>::*` glob re-exports. Every unqualified identifier in these files can therefore come from any sibling module. expr.rs uses unqualified names from 17 other modules this way (units 27 names, type_compat 19, types 14, orientation_signatures 5, math_signatures 5, ...), and entity.rs uses them from 14. The pattern is crate-wide: 27 reify-compiler modules glob-import their parent, the layering heuristic 13 names as a reach-back. It also hides a misleading name: the result-type ladder's family predicates (is_geometry_query, is_dynamics_query, is_field_op, is_fea_envelope_query, ...) live in units.rs, which reaches expr.rs through the glob.
findings.proposal: Replace the lib.rs globs with explicit `use crate::module::{..}` lists in each consumer, starting with expr.rs and entity.rs. Move the builtin-family predicates out of units.rs into a module named for what it holds.
findings.next_change: An agent adding a ladder arm or a lowering helper in expr.rs must locate unqualified callees (check_arg_count_exact, kinematic_query_result_type, resolve_function_overload, ...) across about 30 files with no import line pointing there. Moving or renaming a helper breaks call sites the agent cannot see from the file, and the misleading units.rs name sends readers to the wrong file. The compiler catches only outright name errors, not a wrong same-named helper reached through the glob.

findings.statement: The value layer's rule that arithmetic failure yields Undef, never a panic or a non-finite value, is enforced arm by arm, with no shared mechanism for Int. neg_scalar uses checked_neg and maps overflow to Undef, but eval_add, eval_sub and eval_mul use bare `a + b`, `a - b` and `a * b`. eval_pow uses `base.pow(exp as u32)`. eval_div computes `a % b == 0` and eval_mod computes `a % b` with only a zero-divisor guard. The workspace profile disables overflow checks only for dependencies, so these panic in dev and test builds and wrap silently in release. `i64::MIN % -1` panics in every build mode, so eval_div and eval_mod can panic in release on an Int pair a user can form (e.g. (-9223372036854775807 - 1) % -1).
findings.proposal: Route every Int arm through one helper, `int_op(a, b, i64::checked_*) -> Value` returning Undef on None. It covers add, sub, mul, div, rem and pow alike.
findings.next_change: An agent adds an Int operator, such as integer floor-division, or a new Int arm. With no shared checked helper, it copies the nearest unchecked arm. No test covers Int overflow at any arm.

findings.statement: GeometryKernel is a 27-method trait. Only 4 methods are required (execute, query, export, tessellate); the other 23 are defaulted capability methods that return 'does not support' / 'does not accept' errors. A delegating wrapper therefore loses a capability silently whenever someone adds a method and does not also add a forwarder; the compiler sees nothing wrong. The repo states the invariant ('SingleKernelHolder must delegate EVERY GeometryKernel method', reify-geometry/src/lib.rs) and claims a guard (parity test delegates_all_capability_methods_to_inner_kernel). At this tree SingleKernelHolder forwards 18 of 27 methods, and the parity test lists exactly those 18. The nine methods added since are not delegated and not tested: closest_point_on_shape, vertex_point, register_mesh_handle, volume_mesh, mesh_surface_to_volume, mesh_surface_to_volume_attributed, store_volume_mesh, realize_mesh_from_voxel, surface_options_content_hash. Through the holder, an inner OcctKernelHandle that overrides closest_point_on_shape/vertex_point answers with the trait's 'not supported' error. The holder is used in 55 files, mostly reify-eval integration tests. A second, unchecked encoding of capability exists in CapabilityDescriptor.supports: nothing ties a declared (Convert{from: Mesh}, X) pair to an ingest_mesh override.
findings.proposal: Make delegation total by construction. Either (a) group the capability methods into sub-traits (MeshIngest, VolumeMeshing, PointProjection, ...) exposed through one accessor per capability on GeometryKernel (`fn mesh_ingest(&mut self) -> Option<&mut dyn MeshIngest>`), so a wrapper forwards a handful of accessors and the descriptor's supports pairs can be checked against which accessors return Some; or (b) remove the defaults from the wrapper's path by generating the holder's impl from one macro list that the parity test also iterates. Either way, the parity test should enumerate the trait's methods, not a copied list.
findings.next_change: An agent adds a 28th capability to the trait as a defaulted method, as the trait doc's 'intentionally additive' pattern instructs (e.g. a mesh-native query or a new conversion). To do it correctly it must know, from outside geometry.rs, that SingleKernelHolder, and any other wrapper such as an actor handle, needs a forwarder; that the holder's parity test is a hand-written list it must extend; and that CapabilityDescriptor entries must agree with the override. Nothing catches the wrong version: the default compiles, the parity test stays green, and an integration test through the holder sees 'not supported' while production with the bare kernel works, or the other way round. This has already gone wrong 9 times in a row for the holder.

findings.statement: The mesh contract (INV-GEO-1) has one checking body behind four public entry points (validate, into_validated, check_mesh_contract, check_mesh_contract_welded) and two proof newtypes (ValidatedMesh, WeldRemap), but no consumer requires the proof. All 6 Mesh-consuming GeometryKernel methods take a raw &Mesh, and ValidatedMesh appears in zero signatures outside geometry.rs. Enforcement therefore depends on each wiring site remembering to call a validator. Today three sites do: the engine_build conversion handoff (tessellate source only), the Manifold ingest, and the gmsh preflight. OpenVDB's ingest_mesh_at_resolution re-implements a partial IndexValid length check by hand. Both production callers of `validate` discard the minted witness. Because validate clones the whole mesh to mint the witness, both pay a full Mesh clone for nothing. One of them sits on the BRep->Mesh conversion hot path, which validate's own doc says to avoid. into_validated and check_mesh_contract have zero production callers. The checking body itself is one 343-line function (check_contract) that runs five obligation passes in sequence.
findings.proposal: Make the witness load-bearing. Have the Mesh-consuming trait methods (or a validating front door at the dispatcher) take &ValidatedMesh, so a kernel cannot be handed an unchecked mesh. Collapse the four entry points to the borrowing check plus the by-value mint. Split check_contract into one function per obligation so a new obligation is a new function, not an edit inside a 343-line body.
findings.next_change: An agent wires a new Mesh producer or consumer: e.g. validating MarchingCubes output, adding mesh ingest to a new kernel, or routing OpenVDB ingest through the contract. It has to choose among four entry points whose docs disagree ('prefer check_mesh_contract on hot paths' while the hot path uses validate). findings.statement: GeometryOp handles 'where a numeric quantity is decoded and unit-checked' two ways. 27 variants carry their numbers as untyped `Value` (47 Value fields): Box, Cylinder, Fillet, Extrude, Shell, the profiles and others. The kernel extracts f64 from these and runs a warn-only LENGTH tripwire. 10 variants carry pre-extracted `f64` / `[f64; 3]`: Translate, Rotate, Scale, RotateAround, ScaleNonUniform, Revolve, LineSegment, Arc, Helix, Surface. For those, only the eval-layer gate applies and the kernel tripwire cannot see them. The tripwire is duplicated per kernel. reify-ir's kernel_validation.rs defines `define_kernel_length_extract!` and documents that 'before this existed the two bodies were copy-pasted', yet the macro has zero invocations. reify-kernel-occt/src/lib.rs::extract_length_f64 and reify-kernel-fidget/src/kernel.rs::extract_length_f64 are still hand-copied bodies that differ only in the tracing target. The macro arrived in a 'chore: save WIP before requeue rebase' commit (702c4605e6).
findings.proposal: Pick one decode point for quantity fields. Either carry a typed length/angle newtype in GeometryOp, built only through the eval-layer gate, so kernels receive SI f64 they cannot misread, or keep Value everywhere and route all kernels through the one macro. In the short term, invoke define_kernel_length_extract! in both kernels and delete the copies.
findings.next_change: An agent adds a new op with length parameters (a slot, a counterbore, a new pattern). It must pick Value or f64 for each field with no rule in the type. Picking Value means adding extract_length_f64 calls in every kernel's execute arm, through a hand-copied helper. Picking f64 means remembering to call required_length_value in reify-eval geometry_ops.rs before construction. Either wrong choice compiles: the tripwire is warn-only by ruling, and an f64 field bypasses it entirely. A third kernel adding the op copies the extractor a third time, because the shared macro looks unused.

findings.statement: GeometryKernel::query returns an untyped `Value` for all 35 GeometryQuery variants. Each reply's shape (Value::Real / Bool / List of Int / String) is specified only in variant doc prose, 34 such statements, and each consumer re-decodes it. FaceSurfaceKind and EdgeCurveKind show the cost most clearly. reify-ir already defines both typed enums, yet the OCCT kernel returns them as `Value::String` straight from the C++ FFI (occt lib.rs:4160). reify-eval then re-parses the string through try_from_str at three production sites: selector_vocabulary_v2.rs (errors on unknown names), feature_datum.rs:410 (silently ignores parse failures), and geometry_ops.rs (user-argument parsing). Each nine-name vocabulary is written out in four places: the occt_wrapper.cpp switch, try_from_str, the hard-coded 'expected one of Plane/Cylinder/…' literal in geometry_ops.rs, and the test-support mock.
findings.proposal: Parse at the boundary. Add typed reply variants (e.g. Value::SurfaceKind(FaceSurfaceKind), or a typed `QueryReply` enum keyed by query) and decode the FFI string once inside the OCCT kernel. Derive the diagnostic name list from the enum (strum EnumIter) instead of a literal.
findings.next_change: An agent adds a surface kind (e.g. SurfaceOfRevolution, or a kind from a newer OCCT GeomAbs) or a second kernel that answers FaceSurfaceKind (e.g. Manifold planar-face detection). It must update the C++ switch, try_from_str, the eval warning literal and the mock, and it must know the reply is a string. A misspelling compiles. selector_vocabulary_v2 then errors at runtime, while feature_datum silently treats the edge as non-Line. Nothing at the type level connects the producer to the enum.

findings.statement: StructureInstanceData keeps engine metadata inside its public user-field map under reserved string keys: MATERIALIZED_ANNOTATIONS_KEY = "@@materialized_annotations" (a nested Value::Map keyed by Value::String) and SOURCE_SPAN_KEY = "@@source_span" (a SourceSpan encoded as Value::List[Int, Int] and decoded back with `as u32` casts). The rule that these entries are not fields is enforced by a private filter, user_fields(), which compares keys against both constants. It is called at 9 sites in value.rs (content hash, PartialEq, Ord, Display). But `fields` is `pub`, and production code outside value.rs iterates it directly with no filter, e.g. reify-eval tolerance_combine.rs:533 and engine_build.rs:13170. The exclusion invariant therefore holds only for code that knows about the filter.
findings.proposal: Move the overlays out of `fields` into typed fields on StructureInstanceData (e.g. `annotations: BTreeMap<String, BTreeMap<String, Value>>`, `source_span: Option<SourceSpan>`), left out of Eq/Ord/hash by construction. Then `fields` holds only user members and user_fields() disappears.
findings.next_change: An agent attaches a third per-instance overlay (e.g. provenance or a material binding) by following the documented 'mirrors the @@materialized_annotations precedent'. It must add the key to user_fields and also know that every outside iterator of the pub `fields` map will now see the overlay as a user field. That affects diagnostics that list field names, any 'scan fields for a GeometryHandle' heuristic, and serialization to the GUI. Nothing fails until a consumer misreads the overlay as a member.

findings.statement: 'Should this trait default be advertised/injected?' is encoded as four parallel HashSet<String> skip sets on PreRegisterOutput: pass1_skipped, pass1_param_skipped, pass2_skipped and pass2_compile_errors. check_trait_conformance passes them as four separate arguments into two phases, check_phase_build_available_defaults_map and check_phase_inject_defaults. Each phase re-implements the same ladder of guards, including the cell_type.is_some()/is_none() conjunctions that make the Let guards mutually exclusive. Each set and guard pair was added by its own fix task (1914, 1951, 1952, 2208), and the guards cite those tasks inline: the 'same bug fixed once per path' shape. The set-to-guard table exists only as doc prose on PreRegisterOutput.
findings.proposal: Have the pre-register phase compute one disposition per default, `enum DefaultDisposition { Inject, SkippedSlotTaken, CompileError, … }` keyed by (name, kind), and have both phases consult a single `disposition()` accessor. A new skip reason is then a new variant, matched exhaustively in one place.
findings.next_change: An agent fixes the next phantom-default case, e.g. the documented forward-reference limitation of unannotated lets, or a new DefaultKind. The established pattern says to add a fifth set, thread it through check_trait_conformance into both phases, and mirror the guard in each with the right cell_type conjunction. To do that it must read both phase bodies and the PreRegisterOutput table. A guard added to one phase but not the other advertises a requirement as satisfied while no cell is injected (the 'phantom' lie). It is caught only by phase-level unit tests that hand-build a MergeContext.

findings.statement: The conformance test module (6,076 lines, 69% of mod.rs) mostly drives internal seams rather than the compiler's public entry. Of its 79 tests, 20 hand-build a MergeContext and call individual pub(super) check_phase_* functions. 18 call the pub(crate) check_fn_arg_conformance directly. 1 goes through compile_source. Each check_phase_* has exactly one production caller (check_trait_conformance), so pub(super) visibility exists only for these tests. The module doc that justifies the arrangement is stale: it says 'All four tests in this module…' while there are 79. It concedes that two tests hand-build a RequirementKind::Let that 'no parser path produces'. It sends the reader to 'the escalate_info record for task 2033' for the rationale, a pointer the Comments stance says does not count.
findings.proposal: Express the phase-level cases as .ri fixtures through the compile entry, or through one narrow pub(crate) seam such as check_trait_conformance. Delete the tests that pin parser-unreachable states, or make those states unrepresentable. Replace the module doc with a pointer to a tracked doc, or drop it.
findings.next_change: An agent restructures the trait-conformance pipeline, e.g. merging the four skip sets (finding .6) or reordering phases to fix the forward-reference limitation. Behaviour seen through compile_source stays the same, but about 20 tests that construct MergeContext by hand and call phases by name break. The agent then has to rewrite them against the new decomposition. It cannot tell which tests pin behaviour and which pin structure, because the module's own rationale is stale and lives in an escalation record it cannot read.

findings.statement: Comments in geometry.rs's production region (59% comment lines) record task-progress facts that later commits have made false, and the worst of them invert the point of truth. (1) GEOMETRY_OP_DESCRIPTORS' doc says it covers 'all 49 GeometryOp variants' (there are 55 rows and 55 variants). It also says its operation/parent_role columns are an 'unverified copy until L2 rewires geometry_op_to_operation and parent_handles_for_op … cross-check against the source functions when modifying either'. L2 has landed (7e0f2e0e5b, 4cdda71204): both functions now read this table. (2) ParentRole's doc still says 'see parent_handles_for_op for the authoritative source'. (3) FeatureId::content_hash_bytes is `#[allow(dead_code)]` with a comment that its only caller is the golden test; value.rs:2074 calls it in production. (4) TopologyAttributeTable::lookup_result_face says its production caller (#4263) 'has not landed yet'; reify-kernel-manifold kernel.rs:1211 calls it. (5) A `G-allow` marker on capability_kind cites task #3623 as done. Fix history on the file confirms the cost: 19 of 87 non-merge commits since 2026-07-06 are prose maintenance.
findings.proposal: Delete the drift and progress narration: the table is authoritative, ParentRole is defined by the table, remove the stale dead_code allow and the not-landed notes. Keep task-progress facts (what has or hasn't landed, counts) out of code comments; they belong in the commit or task record.

findings.statement: walk_param_against_arg_type is a second home for the argument-to-parameter compatibility rules that type_compat.rs::type_compatible owns. Of its 12 match arms, 4 defer to type_compatible (via reject_if_incompatible), while the Vector, Point, Matrix/Tensor, Field and TraitObject arms implement their own family and arity rules. Some of those deliberately differ from type_compatible: the Vector arm accepts any Tensor{rank:1} regardless of n, while type_compatible's Rule 1a/1b requires n equality. The arms explain the divergence in comments that cite type_compat.rs by line number ('type_compat.rs:83-108'). The function spans 444 lines, of which 316 are comments (71%), around 128 lines of code. conformance/mod.rs's production region is 60% comments, and 23 of its 67 non-merge commits since 2026-07-06 maintain that prose: 'retire the point3-erasure premise', 'correct two false prose claims', 'stop narrating the comments' own edit history'.
findings.proposal: Move the shape-based acceptance rules next to type_compatible as one named relation (e.g. `conformance_accepts(param, arg) -> Acceptance`) with the deliberate differences written as code, not comments. The walker then only recurses through wrappers and emits diagnostics, and the rationale moves to the PRD or language spec with a one-line pointer.
findings.next_change: An agent adds a numeric Type family (e.g. a Quaternion or Rotation type) or a new coercion rule in type_compat.rs (e.g. Tensor<1,N> -> Point<N>). It has to find and edit the walker's matching arm too, and work out from about 300 lines of interleaved prose which divergences are deliberate. A rule added in one home but not the other gives different accept/reject results at fn-call sites versus struct-ctor/default sites. That is caught only if a pinned .ri twin exists for that exact shape. The prose then needs another 'retire the premise' commit.
