findings.statement: Which constraint a diagnostic is about crosses the engine/front-end boundary only inside message prose, so each consumer parses it or rebuilds it. To drop the checker's own violation lines, compute_diagnostics_with_state rebuilds the strings `constraint {id} violated` and `constraint {label} violated` and filters check_result.diagnostics by exact message equality. The checker already tags those lines with DiagnosticCode::ConstraintViolated (reify-constraints lib.rs). Two blocks later the same function filters EvalCachedGuardedGroupsFallback by code, with a comment that a copy edit to engine wording 'must never silently re-open the leak' by message matching. The CLI parses the same grammar in reverse: main.rs::indeterminacy_subject_in strips INDETERMINACY_PREFIX and INFIX to recover the subject of a ConstraintIndeterminate line. The engine rewrites ids to labels inside message text and matches claims with `starts_with` (engine_constraints.rs). The host function is one 486-line body with about eight sequential stages: parse, compile, guard, warm or cold eval, check, string-filtered merge, span-aware violations, FEA hint and freshness.
findings.proposal: Carry the constraint subject (ConstraintNodeId plus optional label) as a structured field on reify_core::Diagnostic, or key the LSP filter on (code == ConstraintViolated, subject). Have the CLI read the field instead of parsing text. Then split compute_diagnostics_with_state into per-stage functions that each return diagnostics.
findings.next_change: Plausible change: reword the checker's violation message (for example adding the offending values), give violations a structured subject, or add a third label format. The agent must know that the LSP and the CLI each re-derive the message grammar and that the engine rewrites ids to labels inside text. Doing that means reading this 486-line function, main.rs's indeterminacy grammar and engine_constraints.rs. A wrong version double-emits violations in the editor. The forall test catches that only for labeled constraints, because it counts messages containing `forall@v[i]`. Unlabeled duplicates go unflagged.

findings.statement: The question 'which declaration kinds own a member list, and what is it' is answered by separate wildcard-terminated matches, each listing Structure, Occurrence, Trait and Purpose and mapping Purpose to `p.members` only. The sites are analysis::find_parsed_member_span_and_doc, analysis::enclosing_decl_name_at, two inline matches in goto_def::compute_goto_definition_with_parsed, and references::entity_members, a private helper the other files do not use. None of them descends into PurposeDef.structures. Value-member resolution therefore cannot see the members of a `structure def` nested in a purpose: goto-def, hover's find_member_decl, and find-references, rename and highlight (collect_references_at uses entity_members(enclosing)) all look only at the purpose's own members. The document outline (symbol_children) does show those members, and the name-level oracles (purpose_nested_decl_names) do resolve the nested structure itself. The crate's own docs call wildcard-terminated per-kind matches the mechanism of 'silent omission as the parser grew', and made the name-level oracles wildcard-free for that reason. The member-level ones were left as they were.
findings.proposal: Give one function the job, beside decl_name_and_span: `member_scopes(decl) -> impl Iterator<Item=(&str, &[MemberDecl])>`, wildcard-free over Declaration and yielding purpose-nested structures as scopes of their own. Route the five lookups and the outline through it. Better still, put it on reify_ast::Declaration, since reify-eval's source_location re-matches the same kinds.
findings.next_change: Plausible change: make members of purpose-nested structures navigable, or add a member-bearing declaration kind. The agent must find all 5-6 local matches across three files, because nothing links them and the `_` arms make an omission compile cleanly. What catches it today: only a per-surface test written after the fact, as with each #6972 workstream.

findings.statement: cmd_check (544 lines) chooses its engine setup twice, inline, and the two branches disagree. Without --purpose it computes five capability flags (module_has_geometric_conforms, _representation_within, _dfm_rule, _thickness_dfm_rule, _geometry) and from them picks with_registered_kernel versus Engine::new, set_capture_repr_tol, realize_for_check, tessellate_realizations and ensure_openvdb_kernel. With --purpose it routes on module_has_geometry alone and calls none of set_capture_repr_tol, tessellate_realizations or ensure_openvdb_kernel. A RepresentationWithin or thickness-DFM module checked under --purpose therefore misses the side effects that the no-purpose branch's own comment calls necessary to avoid a silent Indeterminate. cmd_build, cmd_report, cmd_eval and cmd_explain each make their own engine-configuration choice. Each subcommand also hand-rolls its argument loop.
findings.proposal: Derive one `CheckEnginePlan` value from the compiled module (which kernel, capture flags, realize, tessellate, openvdb), with a single function that builds the configured engine from it, and use it in both cmd_check branches and the other subcommands. Then split cmd_check into argument parsing, plan, evaluation and verdict reporting.
findings.next_change: Plausible change: add a constraint kind that needs a kernel-side pre-pass (another DFM rule, or a new tolerance assertion). The agent adds a module_has_X predicate and threads it into the no-purpose flag condition, and has to know that the --purpose branch, cmd_build and cmd_eval choose separately. Each fix so far landed per branch. A wrong version is caught only if the CLI test for that feature happens to run it under --purpose.

findings.statement: compute_diagnostics is a public second diagnostics pipeline with no non-test caller, and it diverges from the one the server runs. Unlike compute_diagnostics_with_state, it does not return early on parse errors, so it compiles the partial AST. It does not filter the checker's own violation lines, emits no span-aware violation errors, no fea-not-evaluated hint and no computation-failed or computation-pending diagnostics, and builds a fresh engine on every call. Its doc says it 'shares' the trampoline-free posture, and eval_guard's module doc lists it among 'all three LSP production entry points'. Tests still go through it heavily, so they assert behaviour of a pipeline no editor runs. The posture lock even has to build a separate probe engine to stand in for its internal one.
findings.proposal: Make compute_diagnostics a one-line wrapper, `compute_diagnostics_with_state(&mut EvalState::new(), source, uri).diagnostics`, or delete it and port its 18 test callers. Then there is one pipeline, and the probe-engine workaround in the posture lock goes away.
findings.next_change: Plausible change: an agent fixing an editor diagnostic writes or extends a test through compute_diagnostics, the simplest public entry. The test can pass while the server, which calls compute_diagnostics_with_state through evaluate_and_forward_logs, behaves differently. Doing it right requires knowing that the server never calls this function, and its doc and name do not say so.

findings.statement: No single definition of 'the value cells of a template' exists, and two LSP consumers get it wrong. Three loops in analysis.rs and eval_guard::stage_one_scanned_cells all chain template.value_cells with guarded_groups[*].members and else_members. eval_guard's doc spells out why: 'value_cells is a strict subset of what reaches the graph', and scanning the subset 'made the absence proof unsound'. compute_diagnostics_with_state iterates `template.value_cells` alone in two places. One is the freshness loop, so no computation-failed or computation-pending diagnostic is ever considered for a member inside a `where`/`else` branch. The other is the FEA hint's value_cell_exprs map, so a constraint that reaches an @optimized solver through a guarded let gets no fea-not-evaluated hint. reify-compiler has no accessor, so the chain is re-spelled across the workspace.
findings.proposal: Add `TopologyTemplate::all_value_cells()` (value_cells plus guarded members and else_members) in reify-compiler, and route these sites and the 16 workspace chains through it. Keep a bare value_cells read only where excluding guarded members is deliberate, with a comment saying so.
findings.next_change: Plausible change: add a fourth per-cell diagnostic class, or change how guarded groups are stored, for example by nesting else-branches. The agent must know that guarded members never appear in value_cells, a fact stated only in eval_guard's prose and in the compiler. The two diagnostics.rs loops show the wrong version compiles and passes, because no freshness or FEA-hint test uses a `where` member.

findings.statement: is_reserved_keyword's doc says it decides whether a name is 'a reserved Reify keyword (and therefore not a valid rename target)'. It actually tests membership of completion.rs's TOP_LEVEL_KEYWORDS, BODY_KEYWORDS and EXPR_KEYWORDS, the 26 words the editor offers as completions, which are pub(crate) only so references.rs can borrow them. The language spec's reserved-word table (§2.10, mirrored by reify-audit's RI_KEYWORDS with joint added) has 47 words. The 21 missing from the rename gate are as, chain, def, exists, field, forall, implies, in, joint, map, match, meta, module, none, out, pub, self, set, some, undef and unit. compute_rename and compute_rename_cross_file therefore accept renaming a binding to `match`, `forall` or `unit`. That breaks the gate's stated purpose, keeping the result re-parsing cleanly (Invariant 5). The rename test samples only let, param, structure and if, all from the completion lists.
findings.proposal: Have the grammar's owner (reify-syntax) export one reserved-keyword list, derived from or tested against grammar.js and the spec table. Make the rename gate and reify-audit read it. Keep completion's lists as UX tables over it.
findings.next_change: Plausible change: add a grammar keyword, or trim the completion lists for UX. Either one silently changes what rename refuses, because the coupling is unnamed. Getting it right requires knowing about the spec table, about reify-audit's separate hand copy, and that completion's lists are a UX subset. Nothing catches the drift.

Only the four listed handlers are pinned: lib.rs's test enumerates exactly those requests. AnalysisContext's Send-safety note cites 'server.rs:268-284' for the hover handler. That handler is at line 565, and line 268 falls inside evaluate_and_forward_logs' doc.

Extend blocking_work_requests to hover and completion so the placement test covers them.

findings.statement: Each MCP write tool's contract is fused inside an anonymous closure passed to ToolRegistry::register. That contract is the JSON schema, the hand-parsed params (`params["x"].as_str().ok_or_else(..)`) and the json! result envelope. No typed request or response value exists to reuse: types.rs's UpdateResult/SetParamResult do not describe the wire envelope, and write.rs discards UpdateResult. The GUI's live MCP surface is the reify-debug HTTP server, because the sidecar allowlists mcp__reify-debug__*. That server therefore re-implements the five same-named tools (reify_update_source, reify_set_parameter, reify_open_file, reify_save_file, reify_export) with its own ToolDefs, param parsers and envelope fns. The contracts have since diverged on substance. reify-mcp's reify_set_parameter says the value is a bare number installed as the SI magnitude and that no unit suffix is parsed (task 6184, 2026-08-24). The debug server's tool of the same name says the unit suffix is REQUIRED and a bare number is refused (task 5757, the same day). The GUI's own reify-mcp path, TauriToolContext::set_parameter, goes through commit_parameter to apply_param_to_source_str, which refuses bare numbers on dimensioned cells. So reify-mcp's own description is false on the GUI host. That path is the `mcp_tool_call` Tauri command, and no frontend code calls it. Parity between the surfaces is pinned only by a GUI test that hand-transcribes key sets (`reify_write_tool_envelopes_match_the_reify_mcp_shapes`), so a reify-mcp envelope or semantics change cannot red it.
findings.proposal: Give each MCP tool a typed request/response pair plus one schema owned by reify-mcp, for example `struct SetParameterRequest`/`SetParameterResponse` with serde and a schema derived from it. Expose them for both hosts to dispatch through. Settle reify_set_parameter's value grammar once in that type. Delete or wire the dead mcp_tool_call path so only live surfaces carry the names.
findings.next_change: Plausible change: alter or add an AI write tool (e.g. a unit-aware reify_set_parameter, or a new reify_* write tool). The agent must know that three implementations exist: reify-mcp closures served by the CLI and by the unused GUI mcp_tool_call, and the debug_server copy the sidecar actually reaches. It must also know they already disagree on value grammar, and it would need to read docs/debug-mcp-contract.md to learn this. Nothing catches a wrong version. The parity test compares hand-copied key lists, not reify-mcp's output, and no test compares schema descriptions or input grammar across surfaces.

findings.statement: InProcessLsp::handle_request routes on raw method-name strings in a 14-arm match (lizard CCN 39, 135 lines). Each arm repeats a parse_params/await/map_err/to_value body. The same set of method names is spelled independently in error_prefix (13 consts), gui lsp_bridge.rs::lane_for_method (8 concurrency-safe names, with unlisted names defaulting to the serial lane), gui lsp_lane_routing_tests.rs (three hand-copied const arrays of 6, 8 and 14), blocking_work.rs test_support (4) and gui/src/editor/lspClient.ts (14 calls). The fact that a method is read-only and so concurrency-safe is a server-side property (it takes state.read()), but it is declared in the GUI crate. The routing test's own docstring concedes that 'An arm ADDED there is not caught until it is transcribed here.' The handle_request doc contract already drifted: its list of Ok(Value) requests omits textDocument/references, which the match handles. It also carries a 'Breaking change' paragraph, which is commit-message prose.
findings.proposal: Define a `LspMethod` enum in reify-lsp with FromStr/as_str, an `ALL` table and a `fn is_read_only_query(self)` owned next to the handlers. handle_request then matches on the enum. lane_for_method calls the predicate, and the routing tests iterate LspMethod::ALL instead of hand copies.
findings.next_change: Plausible change: expose a new LSP capability to the GUI, such as signatureHelp, formatting or semanticTokens. The agent must add a match arm and an error_prefix const in reify-lsp, classify the method in the GUI crate's lane_for_method (or silently accept the serial lane), transcribe it into three test arrays, and add a TS call. It must read gui/src-tauri to know the lane table exists. Only the hand-transcribed test catches a rename. An addition, or a mis-classified concurrency class, is caught by nothing.

findings.statement: compute_hover_in_context is one 212-line function (lizard CCN 36, 10 `return Some` exits). It inlines a hover renderer for every symbol class: members, match-arm clusters, structures/occurrences, five Declaration arms, relation builtins and keywords. The Declaration loop ends in `_ => {}`. Of the 11 named Declaration kinds that the crate's own NAMED_DECL_SNIPPETS table enumerates, hover renders 7 (Structure, Occurrence, Enum, Function, Trait, Unit, TypeAlias). Hovering the declared name of a `field def`, `purpose`, `constraint def` or `joint` silently returns None. analysis, goto_def and references each loop over NAMED_DECL_SNIPPETS so a new kind is covered automatically, but hover is not a consumer and no hover test covers those four kinds. The fix history shows the cost: TypeAlias and Unit variants existed by 2026-05-27, and their hover arms arrived as separate RED/GREEN tasks on 2026-08-20 (#6341) and 2026-09-18 (#6972). There have been 22 commits to hover.rs since 2026-07-06.
findings.proposal: Split per-symbol-class renderers into small functions and dispatch declaration-name hover through an exhaustive (wildcard-free) match on Declaration, as decl_name_and_span already does. Add hover as a consumer of NAMED_DECL_SNIPPETS so a missing kind reds.
findings.next_change: Plausible change: a new Declaration kind, or hover for purposes and joints. The agent must find the right spot among nine fall-through stages, pick the first-match ordering correctly (member lookup and keyword lookup can shadow a declaration name), and know that NAMED_DECL_SNIPPETS exists in a cfg(test) module declared from analysis.rs. Nothing reds when a new named kind gets no hover, because the wildcard compiles and the per-kind loops do not include hover.

findings.statement: The MCP wire types carry enum-valued facts as free `String`s: ParameterInfo.kind and .determinacy, ConstraintInfo.status, EvalStatusInfo.phase, and DiagnosticInfo.severity (from reify-core). reify-mcp defines no vocabulary for them, so each ReifyToolContext host invents its own. For kind, the CLI emits "Auto(free)" for a free auto cell while the GUI's cell_kind_gui_str emits "Auto" for both. For status, the CLI always emits "unknown" while the GUI emits satisfied/violated/indeterminate via satisfaction_token. Yet reify_get_constraints advertises filtering by 'satisfied'/'violated' with an exact `!=` compare, so on the CLI host that filter matches nothing. The severity filter, by contrast, is case-insensitive. ValueCellKind has no canonical keyword method. It is rendered to strings by four separate functions in three vocabularies: hover.rs "param/let/auto(free)/auto", CLI mcp_context "Param/Let/Auto(free)/Auto", and GUI engine.rs "Param/Let/Auto" and "param/let/auto".
findings.proposal: Make these fields serde enums in reify-mcp, or reuse reify-core's enums with a fixed serde rename, and give ValueCellKind one `keyword()` rendering that hover, both MCP hosts and the GUI derive from. The filter then compares typed values.
findings.next_change: Plausible change: add a tool filter (e.g. by kind or determinacy), add a new ValueCellKind or Satisfaction variant, or have an AI client branch on `kind == "Auto(free)"`. The agent must read both host implementations and the GUI engine to learn each vocabulary. A wrong spelling compiles and passes, since no type or test ties the values to the enums.

findings.statement: The language-reference topic registry is enumerated three times in this file: 19 `const X: &str = include_str!("chunks/x.md")` items, the 19-entry TOPICS slice, and a 19-arm get_chunk match (lizard CCN 20). A test also pins the bare count 19. Their mutual consistency is enforced from a different crate. reify-compiler's harness_doc_chunks/fence_gate.rs reads language_chunks.rs as TEXT, locates the TOPICS literal by the exact anchor string `pub const TOPICS: &[&str] = &[`, and substring-scans for `include_str!("chunks/<stem>.md")`. That is an ad-hoc parser of another crate's source, which reds if the file is reformatted or the registry is restructured. The 2026-10-07 split of measurement/topology out of geometry (#7344) had to touch all three lists, the count test and the gate, and a follow-up amend added the 'no get_chunk arm' panic message.

Derive TOPICS/available_topics and get_chunk from it, drop the count test, and have fence_gate call `reify_mcp::tools::language_chunks::available_topics()` (as a dev-dependency) instead of parsing the source file.
findings.next_change: Plausible change: add or split a topic (the documented remedy when a chunk exceeds MAX_CHUNK_BYTES). The agent must edit three lists and the 19-count test. It must also know that the fence gate in another crate parses this file's source text, so it cannot restructure the registry into a table without breaking that gate. findings.statement: No shipped binary ever loads a reify.toml. Manifest::load_from_path and Manifest::from_toml_str have zero callers outside reify-config and test code. The only production call of Engine::with_registered_kernels_and_manifest (engine_admin.rs with_registered_kernels) passes None. So the whole parsed schema is inert in production: kernel pins, [auto_type_params], [warm_state] and [[node_overrides]]. The crate's own rustdoc misdescribes this in both directions. It says 'no other workspace crate consumes it yet', but reify-cli, reify-compiler and reify-eval all depend on it. It also says of warm_state_budget_bytes that 'The engine consumer calls this ... env > manifest > default', a ladder whose manifest rung is never fed. Only node_overrides is documented as inert (docs/notes/reify-toml-schema.md). The defaults docs ('callers MUST consume it via Manifest::auto_type_params') are likewise unmet: the compiler uses AutoTypeParamsConfig::default() directly.
findings.proposal: Either wire one production loader (CLI/GUI resolve the project reify.toml and pass it to with_registered_kernels_and_manifest), or state the inert status once on Manifest and point the per-section docs at it. Correct the 'no other crate consumes it' and 'engine consumer calls this' sentences either way.
findings.next_change: Plausible change: add a reify.toml knob, or rely on an existing one (e.g. a kernel pin or warm_state budget). The agent follows the crate rustdoc, adds parse, validation and tests, and believes the knob is live. It must read engine_admin.rs and the CLI and GUI entry points to discover nothing loads the file. findings.statement: JsonRpcRequest.id is a non-optional serde_json::Value without #[serde(default)], so a JSON-RPC notification (a message with no id) fails deserialization. McpDispatcher::dispatch then answers it with a -32700 'Parse error' response carrying id null. An MCP client sends `notifications/initialized` right after initialize, and JSON-RPC requires no reply to a notification. The stdio server's handshake therefore always emits one spurious error line. No test covers an id-less message (jsonrpc_tests covers null-id and array-id only). The GUI debug server's separate JSON-RPC types model `id: Option<Value>` and handle notifications/initialized, so the workspace carries two JSON-RPC envelope implementations with different notification semantics. Within jsonrpc.rs, the response envelope is built inline 8 times, and line 106 uses the literal -32603 instead of the INTERNAL_ERROR const it defines.
findings.proposal: Model `id: Option<Value>`, treat None as a notification that produces no output line, add a test, and build responses through one ok/err constructor as the debug server already does.
findings.next_change: Plausible change: support MCP notifications or a new method (e.g. ping or resources/list) in the CLI's `reify mcp` server. The agent must restructure the request type to distinguish request from notification and suppress the reply. With no notification test and no shared envelope helper, a wrong version that replies to notifications passes.

findings.statement: The doc lowering has no single answer to 'render this expression as text' and uses six ad-hoc strategies. Constraints and constraint defs slice the source by span. A param default splits the declaration text at the first '='. Sub-component args render as the literal `name = ...`. Realization ops render as `format!("{op:?}")` truncated to 80 chars. A purpose objective renders as the placeholder `<minimize>`/`<maximize>`, chosen from the first term only. An annotation Expr renders as `<expr>`. build_stdlib_doc_model passes an empty source string, so for the whole stdlib every param default with a value renders `<default>` and every constraint expr_repr is empty. The rustdoc also misstates the output: it promises 'Structures (in declaration order)' then 'Occurrences' as separate groups, but one loop over compiled.templates interleaves them in source order. ModuleDoc.cross_refs is always Default here, even though reify-doc's docs say ModuleCrossRefs is 'populated by the lowering slice'.
findings.proposal: Introduce one expression-rendering seam, such as an AST/IR pretty-printer reachable from the compiled side or a carried source span on CompiledExpr. Route all six fields through it, so stdlib and user modules render the same way, and correct the ordering and cross_refs docs.
findings.next_change: Plausible change: make `reify doc` show real sub-component arguments, purpose objectives or stdlib defaults. The agent must pick among six existing strategies, learn that CompiledExpr carries neither span nor Display, and discover that the stdlib path has no source. Only build_doc_model_tests, which check a few fixture strings, catch a wrong version.

Each invariant's status is a hand-kept cell in two registries, docs/invariants.md and docs/legibility/design-invariants.md. Nothing links a row to the code that enforces it, and both registries have drifted in both directions. Eight of the 13 rows in docs/invariants.md marked `proposed` already have their named mechanism in the tree:
- INV-EVAL-1: cell_commit.rs commit_cell_result and CacheLeg.
- INV-EVAL-2: cell_eval_ctx.rs.
- INV-EVAL-3: detectors.rs DetectorRegistry and NodeCache.diagnostics.
- INV-EVAL-4: cache_divergence.rs and harness_cache/snapshot_cache_divergence_gate.rs.
- INV-EVAL-5: invariants.rs check_no_stale_undef.
- INV-FEA-2: the catch_unwind at engine_compute.rs:276.
- INV-FEA-3: tests/infra/test_nan_safe_ordering_guard_wired.sh.
- INV-GUI-1: the gui_state! macro, which by its own doc makes an unclassified field fail to compile, i.e. type-enforced.

Rows marked enforced misdescribe their mechanism:
- INV-GEO-4 says the stub arm is instantiated and the has_occt real arm is 'not yet wired'. The reverse is true: the real arm has been instantiated at reify-kernel-occt lib.rs:14385 since ca22b761d8 (2026-07-10). The stub arm only compiles where OCCT is absent, which the gate makes fatal.
- INV-COMP-2 reads 'registered in exactly one place … enforced(test)', but the test it relies on (reify-eval registry_drift_tests.rs) opens by stating that a name is registered in '>= 7 places'. It checks cross-crate agreement, and only for the geometry and selector families.

The design-invariants census table has the same problem:
- PPRDSTATUS is listed as 'chartered', yet reify-audit's bin dispatches it.
- PCITE and PDCHECK ship in the bin with no census row, although the doc requires 'a census row in the same change'.
- INV-PD-1 and INV-PD-2 name `reify-audit --pattern PDROP` / `PVAC` as their enforcement in the present tense; neither pattern exists.

INV-META-1 ('flip status in the same change') is itself `proposed` and has no checker. The last registry edit, 32f1c3e160 'put INV-GUI-2's registry status back in agreement with reality', was a manual repair of exactly this drift.
findings.proposal: Give each row a machine-checkable enforcement pointer (a symbol path or test path) and add one reify-audit pattern or infra test, the INV-META-1 checker, that fails when an `enforced` row's pointer does not resolve, or when a `proposed` row's pointer already does. The census table and the bin's pattern list should derive from one detector registry.
findings.next_change: An agent that lands an enforcement mechanism (for example the PVAC detector or INV-FEA-1's new_production) also has to remember to edit a table row in a .md file it may not have opened. The next reader then trusts the stale status: a `proposed` row invites duplicate work, and an `enforced` row with an inverted description sends a reviewer to the wrong arm. To get it right the agent must know both registries and the INV-META-1 rule. Today nothing catches a wrong or missing flip. Reviewers find it by hand, as 32f1c3e160 did.

findings.statement: reify-compiler restates the expression-nesting bound as three independent literals: recursion_guard::MAX_COMPILE_RECURSION_DEPTH = 256, dot_chain_lint::MAX_EXPR_DEPTH = 256, and shadow_lint::MAX_EXPR_DEPTH = 256. shadow_lint's doc says only that it 'Mirrors the convention in dot_chain_lint.rs'. The three copies apply opposite policies when the bound is exceeded. The guard's doc promises to 'cleanly reject anything beyond with a diagnostic' (ExpressionNestingTooDeep). Both lints instead `debug_assert!(false, …)` and then truncate silently. The lints run first: compile_with_prelude_context_checked_with_config calls them at lib.rs:535-536, before any compile recursion. So in a debug build, which is what the test suite and agents run, the guard's diagnostic path can never be reached through the public pipeline; the process panics in the lint instead. The only over-cap test (geometry.rs deeply_nested_boolean_geometry_does_not_overflow_2mb_stack, 1500 levels) calls compile_geometry_call_no_constraints directly and so skips the lints. The public-API test nests only 64 levels.
findings.proposal: Make MAX_COMPILE_RECURSION_DEPTH the single bound, and have both lints import it. Over the cap, the lints should stop walking without asserting and leave the reporting to the guard's ExpressionNestingTooDeep diagnostic. Add one test that compiles a 300-deep source through the public entry and asserts the diagnostic.
findings.next_change: Raising the compile cap, for example to take a deeper real design, means changing one const. The two lints keep 256, so any input between 257 and the new cap still panics in debug. Equally, a new AST walker added to compile_builder will most likely copy the lint convention rather than the guard. The agent would need to know that lints run before compile and that the guard's diagnostic is the intended user-facing outcome. Nothing would catch a wrong version: no test drives the public pipeline past 256.

findings.statement:
Solver option defaults are declared in the stdlib .ri structure defs and then restated in Rust at up to three further homes, which already disagree.

ElasticOptions declares 17 params. Five have no reader anywhere in production code: mesh_size, max_iter, cg_tolerance, force_tet and target_quantity_of_interest. In particular `param max_iter : Int = 1000` is never consulted; elastic_static.rs uses `SOLVER_MAX_ITER = 2000`.

ModalOptions declares tol = 1e-9 and max_iters = 200. modal_ops::extract_eigen_knobs restates those as Rust fallbacks. run_mechanism_modal then discards them (modal_ops.rs:2422, `let (requested_n_modes, _, _, _) = extract_eigen_knobs(options)`) and builds `EigenSolverOptions { n_modes, ..Default::default() }` (modal_ops.rs:2284). That Default lives in reify-solver-elastic eigensolve.rs and is tol 1e-8, max_iters 1000.

BucklingOptions (10 / 1e-8 / 1000) is restated in extract_buckling_options and again in buckling_kernel's own default (lines 71-72). shell_threshold = 0.2 is restated as a Rust local at elastic_static.rs:5551.

This is the INV-PD-1 (declared-param-reaches-kernel) surface. Its owning PRD, trampoline-param-drop-closure.md (rows A6/A7/A9), records several of these sites, and its PDROP detector is still chartered.
findings.proposal: Decode each options structure once, into a typed struct whose defaults come from the compiled structure_def's default_expr values, which are already in the IR. The trampolines should read that struct, not raw field strings with literal fallbacks. Declared params with no reader become the declared-ignored set that INV-PD-1 requires.
findings.next_change: An agent that changes a default by editing the .ri (the user-visible declaration) has the change silently not apply on at least one path: mechanism_modal and elastic_static, today. An agent that edits the Rust fallback forks the value from the .ri doc the user reads. To get it right the agent must know all three homes for each knob. Nothing catches a wrong version: PDROP is chartered and not built, and the existing tests pin the Rust fallbacks (extract_eigen_knobs_reads_fields_and_falls_back asserts (10, 1e-9, 200, 0.0)).

findings.statement:
A compute target's identity and its result schema are spelled independently on each side of the .ri/Rust boundary.

Identity: the stdlib .ri carries 16 distinct `@optimized("…")` target strings, and register_compute_fns registers 18 string literals. No check relates the two sets. Two Rust targets have no .ri entry:
- solver::tensegrity_load. Its trampoline doc says it receives inputs 'matching the future tensegrity_load signature', a signature that was never declared, so the target is registered but unreachable from .ri.
- fdm::as_printed_material_r0, which is reached only through a Rust rung-to-string map in as_printed_material.rs:500.

reify-lsp keeps a third hand copy, ALL_PRODUCTION_COMPUTE_TARGETS, in diagnostics.rs tests. Its doc admits that an addition upstream 'is NOT caught' because reify-eval exposes no enumerator over compute_registry.fns.

Result schema: 7 StructureInstance type_names minted by trampolines have no stdlib `structure def` at all: ShellExtractionResult, MidSurfaceMesh, SegmentationResult, MidSurfaceAttributes and RegionInfo (shell-extract), TensegrityLoadResult, and CarriedTopology. Their field sets exist only in the Rust minters and in the per-decoder string literals, so INV-PD-2's field census, which is keyed on the .ri declaration, cannot see them.
findings.proposal: Expose a public `Engine::registered_compute_targets()` (or a static target table). Add a compile-side or test-side check that every stdlib `@optimized` string is registered and every registered target has a .ri caller or an explicit engine-inserted allowlist. Declare the shell-extract, tensegrity_load and carried-topology result structures in stdlib .ri so that INV-PD-2 covers them.
findings.next_change: Adding or renaming a target means three string edits (the .ri annotation, the registration, the LSP list). A typo in the .ri annotation compiles and only fails at dispatch, and the LSP list never notices an addition. Adding a field to a Rust-only result type changes the user-visible shape with no declaration and no PVAC coverage. To get it right the agent must know about the LSP list and the reify-audit census. Of the three copies, only the LSP list's rename/removal half is checked.

findings.statement:
reify-core defines the wire type DiagnosticInfo with `code: Option<String>` but no constructor from Diagnostic. Each surface writes its own projection, and they disagree on the one field that INV-SF-6 (diagnostics-carry-codes) exists to protect:
- gui/src-tauri engine.rs::diagnostics_to_info writes `code: None`. It is called from 3 sites and feeds the GUI problems panel.
- reify-cli mcp_context.rs:292 writes `code: None`. It feeds AI/MCP clients.
- reify-lsp convert.rs::convert_diagnostic serialises the DiagnosticCode through serde.

The only values that ever reach DiagnosticInfo.code are ad-hoc GUI strings that are not DiagnosticCode names: "hot-reload-error" (2 sites) and "unresolved-source" (1 site). gui/src/types.ts documents `code === "unresolved-source"` as a contract. As a result, a GUI or MCP consumer that needs to tell diagnostic kinds apart has to match message text, which is the pattern behind per-area findings cg-ck.1 and tooling.2.
findings.proposal: Add `DiagnosticInfo::from_diagnostic(&Diagnostic, file_path, &LineIndex)` in reify-core that serialises DiagnosticCode the way convert.rs does, and route the GUI and CLI projections through it. Model the GUI-only states (hot-reload error, unresolved source) as DiagnosticCode variants instead of free strings.
findings.next_change: A GUI or MCP feature that keys on diagnostic kind (filter by ConstraintViolated, suppress a fallback warning) finds `code` always null and falls back to substring matching on the message. An agent fixing one projection leaves the other two as they are. Doing it right requires knowing that three projections exist in three crates. Nothing catches the dropped code: no test asserts that a coded Diagnostic arrives coded at the GUI or MCP boundary.

findings.statement:
What a support kind clamps is decided in five places, with no shared decode:
- stdlib .ri structure defs FixedSupport and PinnedSupport (fea_multi_case.ri:359/384).
- reify-stdlib supports.rs, whose module doc is the stated contract: 'PinnedSupport on a shell entity … constrains translational DOFs only, leaving rotational DOFs free'.
- reify-solver-elastic shell_boundary::SupportKind {Fixed, Pinned} with build_support_bcs, which implements that contract.
- reify-eval modal_ops' own enum DeclaredSupport {Fixed, Pinned}, decoded by `support.type_name == "PinnedSupport"` with every other type falling through to Fixed, plus its face_realization beam-pin policy.
- elastic_static::loads_supports_to_bc_node_sets, which returns a bare node set and clamps every DOF whatever the kind.

The typed solver-side home is not reached for the case it exists for. The only production call of build_support_bcs, in solver shell_solve.rs, passes SupportKind::Fixed on auto-chosen root nodes. reify-eval compute_targets/shell_solve.rs has no reference to supports at all. A user PinnedSupport on a shell-routed body therefore never reaches the Pinned arm.
findings.proposal: Decode a Support StructureInstance once, in reify-eval, into reify_solver_elastic::SupportKind (extended as kinds are added). Make modal_ops' face_realization and elastic_static's BC build consume that value, and thread user supports into the shell route instead of the coordinate root clamp.
findings.next_change: Adding RollerSupport to the elastic or modal paths, or honouring PinnedSupport on shells, means editing modal_ops' string match, elastic_static's node-set decode and the shell route separately. Nothing ties those three to the stdlib contract or to the solver enum, which is why the shell Pinned contract has stayed unimplemented. To get it right the agent must read four crates. Nothing catches a wrong version: there is no test of PinnedSupport through the shell route.

findings.statement: The set of kernel names is defined in reify-core by KernelId::ALL, as_registry_name and from_registry_name, which is the documented single authority (reify-config re-exports it). module_pragmas.rs nevertheless keeps its own literal `KNOWN_V02_KERNELS = ["fidget", "manifold", "occt", "openvdb"]`, so `#kernel(<ident>)` validation does not derive from KernelId. The compiler stores the pragma as a String (module.kernel_pragma), and reify-eval looks it up again by string in Engine.geometry_kernels, a BTreeMap<String, _> keyed partly by the synthetic "__reify_eval_default_kernel". The name-to-KernelId bridges then disagree on unknown names: dispatcher.rs:779 `.expect()`s, while engine_build.rs:104 silently maps any unknown name to KernelId::Occt. A KernelId variant added in reify-core is therefore not accepted by the compiler, and a pragma name the compiler accepts is never checked against the registry names.
findings.proposal: Derive the accepted pragma set from KernelId::ALL, filtered by a KernelId method such as `is_user_selectable()` that states the gmsh exclusion once. Parse the pragma into KernelId at compile time, so CompiledModule carries a typed value rather than a String.
findings.next_change: Registering a new kernel means editing KernelId and its two string maps, and also remembering KNOWN_V02_KERNELS. If that is forgotten, the new kernel works for manifest pins (reify-config uses from_registry_name) but `#kernel(new)` gets an 'unknown kernel' error. findings.statement:
Which geometry kernels an Engine has is decided by link-time side effects, not by the constructor's arguments. Kernel crates `inventory::submit!` a KernelRegistration, and each binary must anchor them with `extern crate X as _;`. Today reify-cli main.rs anchors occt, manifold and openvdb(cfg). gui lib.rs anchors only openvdb(cfg); occt reaches the GUI through an OCCT_AVAILABLE const read, the mechanism the CLI comment calls unreliable. reify-lsp anchors nothing.

with_registered_kernel then instantiates the lexicographically least BRep-capable registration, or failing that the least of any (kernel_registry::pick_lexmin_brep_kernel_in). Build routing also reads the process-global registry directly, through collect_registry() at 5 engine_build entry points and registry() at engine_constraints.rs:1018. That registry can list kernels this Engine never instantiated: the CLI links manifold but instantiates only the pick plus openvdb.

The result is that the production binaries carry different kernel sets: reify {occt, manifold, openvdb}, reify-gui {occt, openvdb} (no manifold dependency), reify-lsp {}. Tests are shaped by it too:
- 17 extern-crate anchors across 10 reify-eval test files;
- a test_registry_override engine field behind test-instrumentation;
- reify-eval/Cargo.toml prose forbidding dev-deps that 'would pull inventory::submit! in and break registry-size or default-kernel assertions'.

Engine assembly is repeated at 19 production sites in 5 crates, and ensure_openvdb_kernel is called separately at 3 of them.
findings.next_change: Have each binary build an explicit kernel set from the kernel crates it depends on (or a KernelSet passed by name) and pass it to the Engine constructor. Route builds through the engine's own kernel table instead of collect_registry(), and delete the inventory anchors and test_registry_override. The agent must read kernel_registry.rs, CapabilityDescriptor routing in engine_build and the tooling front-end findings (cmd_check, CliToolContext). The CLI registry test (main.rs ~4112), GUI kernel_status_tests and the realization e2e suites catch a wrong version.

findings.statement:
reify-ir has a 4-module SCC {geometry, value, expr, boundary_attachment}. It exists because geometry.rs (13,364 lines) holds two strata:
- leaf geometry identifiers that Value embeds: GeometryHandleId, FeatureId, Role, FaceSurfaceKind, EdgeCurveKind, ModEntry;
- the kernel-interface layer that consumes Value: GeometryKernel, GeometryOp, GeometryQuery, ValidatedMesh.

findings.statement:
Four separate mechanisms decide which geometry kernel serves a request, and only one of them reads CapabilityDescriptor.

1. **GeometryOps**: dispatcher::dispatch over CapabilityDescriptor.supports(op, repr). It is called at 3 sites in engine_build.rs (6417, 7823, 7838) and is the only production reader of the descriptor.
2. **Default kernel**: queries, export, tessellate, post-process, DFM and constraint passes index geometry_kernels by Engine.default_kernel_name. That name is 74 references in 7 reify-eval files (engine_build 48, engine_admin 11, geometry_ops 8, engine_constraints 4, engine_eval, realization_content, realize_solid_sdf).
3. **Handle provenance**: lookups go through the kernel recorded on a handle and silently fall back to the default kernel when that name is absent (engine_build 9262; realization_content 355).
4. **Hard-coded KernelIds**: Mesh to VolumeMesh and morph storage use KernelId::Gmsh (engine_build 9301, 9453). Voxel/SDF uses KernelId::OpenVdb (engine_build 9635, realization_content 242, realize_solid_sdf 149).

The map key itself varies by construction path. Engine::new and with_prelude store the single kernel under the synthetic DEFAULT_KERNEL_NAME, while with_registered_kernels uses KernelId::as_registry_name. So realization_content needs a registry-name-then-default fallback chain. A request for a handle produced by a non-default kernel can therefore reach a different kernel without any diagnostic.

The descriptor declares Operations only, so query/export capability (cg-ck seam 1) and the Gmsh/OpenVdb conversions are not expressible in it. Each new conversion or kernel adds another hard-coded arm. Related canonical findings cover the trait surface (reify-ir geometry.rs::GeometryKernel h9) and the hard-coded openvdb arm (realization_content h11); this finding is the selection axis that spans them.
findings.proposal: Make kernel selection one function in dispatcher.rs taking (request kind: Op | Query | Export | Conversion, handle provenance, demanded repr) and returning a KernelId. Key geometry_kernels by KernelId, removing the synthetic DEFAULT_KERNEL_NAME. Extend CapabilityDescriptor to declare queries, exports and conversions, so the Gmsh/OpenVdb arms become descriptor rows.
findings.next_change: An agent adding a kernel, or routing a conversion (e.g. VolumeMesh via a second mesher), must find all four mechanisms. Without that it would edit dispatcher.rs and miss the default-kernel and hard-coded arms in engine_build.rs and realization_content.rs. It needs to know that the map key depends on the constructor. Nothing catches a wrong version: a misrouted query falls back to the default kernel silently, and no test asserts that each lookup's kernel is the one that produced the handle.

findings.statement:
The same engine writes (open/load file, set parameter, update source, save, export, set FEA case) are scheduled and published by two independent mechanisms, chosen by which front door the request came through.

- **Tauri command path**: commands.rs builds EvalRequest values (8 sites, plus main.rs 1 and mcp_context.rs 1), which the EvalQueue orders, coalesces by EditIdentity and publishes as generation-stamped deltas. eval_queue.rs's module doc calls the queue "the ENGINE lane's single front door: every engine-touching request is submitted here".
- **Debug server path**: debug_server.rs runs 13 engine closures through its own run_on_engine, a spawn_on_large_stack plus with_engine_lock. These are 6 writes (open_source_into_engine_and_refresh_baseline, set_fea_case_on_engine, and write_on_engine_and_refresh_baseline for set_parameter, update_source, save_file, export) and 7 reads. None of them is submitted to the queue. The debug server holds `evals: Arc<EvalQueue>` but reads it only for health and wait_for_idle. It advances its own diff baseline via compute_delta and pushes state with query_frontend.

Interleaving with queued command-path edits is therefore excluded only by the 'serial-debug-ops assumption', which debug_server.rs restates 14 times, and not by the queue's ordering. The CLI MCP surface inside the GUI (mcp_tool_call_evaluation) does go through the queue, so the GUI has three front doors with two scheduling rules. The per-handler symptoms are already filed (handle_set_fea_case h10 for baseline ordering, debug_write_tool_routing_tests h10 for INV-GUI-2). This finding is the axis behind them.
findings.proposal: Route debug-server writes through EvalRequest::edit / evaluation, as mcp_tool_call_evaluation already does, so the queue is the single scheduling and publication mechanism. The debug server then awaits the ticket's published state instead of keeping its own baseline.
findings.next_change: An agent adding a debug write tool, or changing the queue's coalescing or publication rule, has to know that the debug server bypasses the queue. eval_queue.rs's doc says the opposite. A write added in the debug-server style escapes edit coalescing and generation stamping, and nothing catches that: the INV-GUI-2 scanner checks emission seams, not queue admission.

findings.statement:
The build-scheduler axis has a single source, BuildScheduler::from_env, read once at Engine construction (engine_admin.rs:279). Its effect is not given one mechanism. demand_scoped_unified_pass encodes LegacyMultiPass as `None` in an Option<UnifiedPassResult>, and that same `None` also means 'no eval_state'. Each build surface then tests the Option inline:

- build_with_geometry_output: 4 sites (4363 realization_read_cells, 4518 BuildStep walk, 4805 post-process gate, 754 cycle detection).
- tessellate_realizations: 2 sites.
- tessellate_snapshot: 2 sites.
- The constraint re-check compares the enum directly (5178).
- build_snapshot: 0 sites. It never consults the schedule.
- distance_between_placed: 0 sites.

The legacy arm was introduced as a 'one-release kill-switch' when the default flipped on 2026-06-23 (2a7c699849, task #4362). It is still live 110 days later with no retirement cite, and its survival is pinned by 26 files outside engine_fixpoint.rs, including the differential harnesses under reify-eval/tests/harness_cache. The canonical build_with_geometry_output h11 counts the per-surface knob axes in general; this finding is the scheduler axis's encoding and lifetime.
findings.proposal: Either retire LegacyMultiPass, as its one-release promise intended, and make the schedule non-optional, or give the scheduler one strategy value that each surface asks for its BuildStep sequence, separate from the 'no eval state' case.
findings.next_change: An agent adding a build surface, or changing what the unified schedule drives, must replicate the `is_some()` gates. It must also know that `None` conflates legacy with no-state. Retiring the kill-switch means touching 8 Option sites and 26 test files. A surface that forgets the gate silently runs legacy order under UnifiedDag, and only the differential corpus might catch it.

findings.statement:
The debug/release profile axis in verify.sh has no profile record. Every per-profile fact is a pair of global variables suffixed _DEBUG/_RELEASE, and an inline `[ "$x" = "release" ]` selects between them. There are 5 such selections in 3 functions: confirm_failed_run 1468, emit_nextest_pass 3312/3357/3433, and add_test_passes 3642. The pairs are _CONFIRM_MANIFEST, _CONFIRM_SIDECAR, REIFY_VERIFY_RETRY_NEXTEST_FILTER_FILE, _RETRY_NEXTEST_*_APPLIED and _VERIFY_TEST_TIMEOUT, together with their REIFY_VERIFY_*_{DEBUG,RELEASE} env overrides.

emit_nextest_pass does not receive the profile at all. It receives the cargo flag string `rel` (" --release" or "") and recovers the profile twice by pattern match: `case "$rel" in *release*)` at 3301 and 3431.

The profile is also not independent of the role axis. When --profile is not given, DF_VERIFY_ROLE picks the profile (887-893), and per-role walls are applied inside the release branch. The canonical add_test_passes h11 counts one duplicated confirm-path selection; this finding is the whole profile axis.
findings.proposal: Pass the profile name explicitly to emit_nextest_pass, and derive the cargo flag, manifest, sidecar, retry filter and wall from one profile table (an associative array keyed by profile) that every consumer reads.
findings.next_change: An agent adding a per-profile setting (a third profile, or a per-profile retry ceiling) adds another variable pair and another `= release` branch at each consumer. It must also know that emit_nextest_pass infers the profile from a flag string. A mismatch is caught only if one of the ~56 --print-plan text tests happens to cover that profile.

findings.statement:
There is no single engine-configuration value. Each knob has its own source, and each front end assembles its own posture.

Inside reify-eval, knobs are read from the process environment at different moments:
- REIFY_BUILD_SCHEDULER, once in the with_prelude constructor (engine_admin 279).
- REIFY_WARM_STATE_BUDGET_BYTES, in the constructor (340), or merged with a manifest [warm_state] value by set_warm_pool_budget_from_manifest (2651).
- REIFY_LONG_CHAIN_THRESHOLD_MS, re-read at each of 4 build entry points (engine_build 3583, 4450, 5788, 6748).
- PATH, re-read per fdm_slice dispatch.

The manifest route (kernel pins, warm_state) is never taken in production (canonical tooling reify-config Manifest h1).

The persistent cache, compute trampolines, repr-tol capture and the openvdb kernel are instead opted into by setter calls at each of 17 front-end construction sites, and the mix differs:
- **CLI main** (9 constructions): sets the persistent cache dir 3 times and repr/openvdb capture at 6 call sites.
- **CLI MCP**: sets the persistent cache but registers no compute fns.
- **LSP** (4 constructions): none of these.
- **GUI** (3 constructions): registers compute fns and ensures openvdb, but never calls set_persistent_cache_dir.

The GUI does run a startup sweep of a cache dir it resolves itself, and its resolver inputs differ from the CLI's. gui engine.rs::bootstrap_persistent_cache_sweep passes user_config: None and project_config: None, while reify-cli cache.rs::resolve_cache_root_layered loads ~/.config/reify/config.toml and the project config. The GUI therefore sweeps a different directory than the CLI writes whenever a config file sets the cache dir. The canonical findings mcp_context ensure_engine h10 and cmd_check h3 are two cells of this matrix.
findings.proposal: Introduce an EngineConfig resolved once (env + manifest + front-end overrides), passed to one constructor, and a small set of named postures (batch-CLI, interactive-GUI, LSP-analysis) that front ends select. That way the persistent cache, compute registration and kernel set become fields rather than setter calls.
findings.next_change: An agent adding an engine knob, or a front end such as a new MCP host, has to choose a sourcing style and copy the posture setters from whichever front end it happens to read. The GUI/CLI cache-dir mismatch shows what happens when they differ. Nothing compares postures across front ends: each front end's tests construct their own engine.

findings.statement:
The solver execution-mode axis has a declared single policy seam, resolve_execution_modes. Per its doc, it is "the single policy seam for PRD task #16 / #18" and covers determinism, thread count and the PARALLEL_DOF_THRESHOLD tiny-problem rule. It returns a pair of byte-for-byte mirror enums, AssemblyMode and SolverMode.

It has exactly one production caller, compute_targets/elastic_static.rs:3144. Every other assemble/solve path hard-codes AssemblyMode::Deterministic / SolverMode::Deterministic inline: buckling_kernel (6), assembly/global (5), boundary/dirichlet (2), membrane_load (2), tensegrity_load (2), shell_solve (2), reify-mesh-morph elasticity (2) and reify-eval modal_ops (1). So the determinism/parallelism axis is a choice for one compute target and a constant for the others. Two enums carry one fact and are kept in lockstep only by returning them as a pair.
findings.proposal: Fold the two enums into one ExecutionMode and make every assemble/solve entry take it, so callers obtain it from resolve_execution_modes, or from a Deterministic constant named as such at the trampoline layer.
findings.next_change: An agent enabling threads for buckling, shell or modal solves (the large-DOF paths) has to thread a mode parameter through each kernel. It would likely copy resolve_execution_modes's threshold logic or skip it. Nothing ties the hard-coded call sites to the policy seam.

findings.verdict_notes: git grep resolve_execution_modes( and the SolverMode/AssemblyMode::(Deterministic|Parallel) hits per file. For each file I split production from test regions with an awk cutoff at the first #[cfg(test)] or mod tests. I read the enum definitions and the resolver doc at solver.rs 77-125. — The core structure holds: there is a single production caller (elastic_static.rs:3144), and the other assemble/solve paths pass Deterministic inline. The enums have identical variants and a doc that says they 'mirror each other byte-for-byte'. The measurement is materially inflated. The 'inline mode constructions' count includes assembly/global.rs, whose hits are the assembler's own match arms and its panic text (only 1 of the 5 production hits is a Parallel match). It also counts dirichlet.rs, whose hits are in its test module (production region starts before line 275, hits at 319 and 346), and warm_state.rs and mass_matrix.rs, which have no production hits. Real production hard-coded Deterministic constructions are about 15 in 6 files: buckling_kernel 6, modal_ops 1, mesh-morph elasticity 2, membrane_load 2, shell_solve 2, tensegrity_load 2. The statement that all 22 lines in 8 files are Deterministic constructions is therefore false. Whether those paths should be parallel is a product question that the finding assumes.

findings.statement:
The pre-done gate's fail-open/fail-closed posture is split across two layers, with two knobs of opposite polarity and different defaults:
- REIFY_AUDIT_FRESHNESS_STRICT in scripts/reify-audit-freshness.sh defaults to fail-open. It runs a stale binary unless set to 1.
- REIFY_AUDIT_PREDONE_WARN_ONLY, read with std::env::var inside the detector by p5_phantom_done::pre_done_refusal_severity, defaults to refuse (High). It downgrades to Low when set to 1.

The detector reads its knob from the ambient environment rather than through AuditContext, so the CLI's --pattern/--pre-done surface cannot see or report it. The deploy script (deploy-reify-audit-predone-hook.sh) documents only the STRICT knob in its probe messages. The repo already has a single posture primitive for the same enforce/bypass question in hooks: hooks/main-gate-lib.sh::gate_switch_on, which reads env, then git config, then a flag file, and serves 4 knobs. Neither pre-done knob uses it.
findings.proposal: Carry a single pre-done posture (strict | fail-open | warn-only) into AuditContext from the bin, and have the freshness wrapper pass it through. Alternatively, source both from one gate_switch_on-style resolver, so the effective posture is printed once per run.
findings.next_change: An operator or agent adjusting the pre-done gate during an incident has to know that two independent knobs exist and that their polarities are opposite. An agent adding a third posture would add a third style. Nothing reports the effective posture of a pre-done run.

Read scripts/reify-audit-freshness.sh around 70-80 and 400-425, the reify-audit.rs --help text at 105-120, .claude/skills/audit/references/cli-invocation.md 395-400, the tests/infra/test_reify_audit_freshness.sh Check 18 comment, and hooks/main-gate-lib.sh 48-102. — The two env knobs exist, with opposite defaults, one read in bash and one in Rust (freshness.sh:402; p5_phantom_done.rs:1104). The framing as one posture split across two layers is not supported, because they gate different axes. STRICT governs binary-freshness (fall open vs refuse), and WARN_ONLY governs one finding's severity. cli-invocation.md:397 states they 'gate DIFFERENT things and are not substitutes'. Three parts of the claim are contradicted. First, the reify-audit --help text lists REIFY_AUDIT_PREDONE_WARN_ONLY, so the CLI does surface it. Second, 'nothing reports the effective posture' is wrong, because the downgraded finding is still emitted and prefixed '[warn-only]'. Third, the env-var delivery path is the documented rationale: the knob is inherited from the fused-memory systemd unit (the Check 18 comment and the function doc), a path gate_switch_on's git-config and flag-file layers do not obviously serve. The deploy script's probe messages not mentioning WARN_ONLY is true but minor.

findings.statement:
Engine::check's verdicts for three constraint families depend on which other public Engine calls ran before it, not on its arguments.

Three check-time passes read Engine side tables that only other public surfaces populate:
- dispatch_constraints reads achieved_repr_tol. That table is written only by tessellate_realizations or tessellate_snapshot, and only after set_capture_repr_tol(true). An empty table turns every RepresentationWithin into Indeterminate.
- measure_dfm_rules and measure_gdt_conformance inject kernel handles from realization_handles. That table is written only by the Build/BuildSnapshot surfaces and cleared only at the next Build entry.

check's rustdoc states the required sequence: callers 'must call set_capture_repr_tol(true) followed by tessellate_realizations(&compiled) before calling check()', and DFM needs a subject 'realized by a prior build() call'. The sequence is spelled at exactly 1 of the 6 non-test check() call sites: reify-cli cmd_check's no-purpose arm (main.rs 907-918). The other five silently get Indeterminate or no DFM/GD&T measurement: the CLI --purpose arm, reify-lsp analysis.rs and diagnostics.rs, GUI EngineSession::check_with_solve_slot, and GUI preview.

In the GUI, check runs before that reload's tessellate_snapshot. It also runs right after reset_geometry_for_reload, which resets the kernels and the realization cache but not realization_handles. So check-time DFM/GD&T can only see handles left by an earlier export build, which now dangle (InvalidReference → Indeterminate, thanks to OCCT's monotonic ids). reset_geometry_for_reload's own contract ('exactly once per whole-file reload … never on a slider edit') is kept only by its single GUI call placement (engine.rs 1556).
findings.proposal: Make the measurement an input. Either have check take (or build itself, behind a flag) a MeasurementContext holding achieved_repr_tol and the realization→handle map produced by an explicit realize/tessellate step, or expose a single check_with_geometry(module, CheckGeometry) entry that runs realize → tessellate → check in one call. Then the CLI, LSP and GUI choose a posture instead of a call order. Clear realization_handles in reset_geometry_for_reload, or make it part of the same per-build reset.
findings.next_change: The plausible next change is one of three: add RepresentationWithin or DFM support to the LSP or GUI, add a new measured constraint family, or move the GUI reset or tessellate relative to check. Doing it correctly requires knowing that check's answers are only as good as the call sequence that preceded it. That sequence lives in a rustdoc paragraph and in cmd_check's inline ordering. Nothing catches a wrong version: an out-of-order caller gets Indeterminate, which is the defined C1 fallback, so no test fails.

findings.statement: Engine::trace_undef_causes joins two inputs that different calls keep current: self.undef_causes(), the origin map, and the current snapshot. The origin map is written only inside a cold eval() (engine_eval.rs:6894, gated on the capture_undef_causes toggle set by the caller beforehand), and engine_edit.rs contains 0 references to last_undef_causes or capture_undef_causes. The snapshot is advanced by eval and by every edit path. After any edit_param, edit_source or edit_check, the walk therefore runs the new snapshot's undef cells against origins classified for the previous cold eval. The GUI hits exactly this path. EngineSession sets set_capture_undef_causes(true) at construction (engine.rs:1192). Each slider tick then runs preview_parameter → edit_check → build_gui_state → build_values, which calls trace_undef_causes for every Undef cell (engine.rs:5247) and renders 'undef because …'. A cell that became Undef because of the edit gets the cause recorded for the pre-edit state, or none.
findings.proposal: Return the undef-origin map on EvalResult (and from edit_param/edit_source, re-classified over the edited cone), or store it inside EvaluationState next to the snapshot it was classified from, so it is replaced atomically with that snapshot. trace_undef_causes then reads one coherent state. The capture toggle becomes a parameter of the eval call instead of a prior setter.
findings.next_change: An agent fixing a wrong GUI 'undef because' hover, or adding undef tracing to the LSP's warm edit_source path, has to discover two things: the cause map is a cold-eval byproduct gated by a constructor-time toggle, and the snapshot it is joined with has a different producer set. The existing tests use the cold path and do not catch it.

findings.statement:
Several per-call outputs of Engine operations are not returned. They are left in long-lived Engine fields, read afterwards through last_* getters, or reconstructed by the consumer.

EvalResult, BuildResult and TessellateResult carry none of the dispatch attribution, the eval set, the demand-prune measurement or the set of realizations dispatched this pass.

The GUI reads them after the call at 6 sites:
- last_dispatch_count_by_realization at commands.rs 400 and 579. The 400 site is named `_post_refresh` with a comment that the suffix is 'load-bearing', because build_gui_state has already re-run tessellate and overwritten the tally.
- last_eval_set at commands.rs 587.
- last_demand_prune_measurement at engine.rs 1382 and 4276.
- last_substantive_value at engine.rs 5225.

last_demand_prune_measurement is written only by edit_param (engine_edit.rs:2989) and cleared nowhere. eval() resets last_eval_set (engine_eval.rs:6929) but not this field. So after a slider edit followed by a whole-file reload, which goes through check → eval on the same long-lived engine, build_gui_state surfaces the previous edit's prune record as current.

Where no getter exists, the GUI rebuilds the fact. surface_geometry_derived_cells derives 'which realizations ran this pass' by string-parsing mesh entity_path keys (parse_realization_key) as a proxy. Its own comment records the case where the proxy replays a stale value as Final, and says closing it 'needs reify-eval to report the dispatched-realization set on TessellateResult directly'.
findings.proposal: Return these as fields on the operation's result: dispatch_by_realization and dispatched_realizations on TessellateResult/BuildResult, and eval_set and demand_prune on the edit and eval results. Retire the last_* getters, or keep them only behind test-instrumentation. The GUI then builds its DTOs from the value its own call returned, and the mesh-key proxy is deleted.
findings.next_change: An agent might add a GUI panel, or a debug RPC that reports per-build dispatch or demand. It might also reorder build_gui_state relative to tessellate, or make the reload path warm. Doing this correctly requires knowing which call last overwrote each last_* field, and that eval clears some of them but not others. The only record of this is comments in the GUI ('_post_refresh is load-bearing', the dispatched_entities LIMIT paragraphs). A misordered read compiles and shows plausible numbers.

findings.statement:
The per-lane mutex protocol has no single owner. The protocol is: the lock file is <lane_dir>.lock, exclusive for a reseed or reclaim, shared for a liveness probe, and a fixed FD.

How each script restates it:
- seed-warm-lane.sh: derives the path at line 930, uses FD 9, and has three wait modes.
- thin-warm-lane.sh: line 384, FD 9, -n.
- warm-lane-gc.sh: lines 594 and 766, FD 8, -n.
- warm-lane-lock-guard.sh: line 197, shared probe by path.
- warm-lane-audit.sh: line 1336, _probe_live by path.
- dark-factory's _seed_warm_lane also opens it.

scripts/lib_lane_x_flock.sh shows the repo already uses a library shape for a different lock, but the lane lock has none.

The production path is a cross-repo temporal handshake. DF takes its own outer flock and then runs seed-warm-lane.sh --assume-lane-lock-held on both pool acquires, according to seed's comment at 919-925. In that mode seed skips its acquire entirely and performs 0 checks that the lock is held. Seed's exclusivity invariant (§9.5 inv.2/inv.11) therefore rests on the caller having performed a prior step that seed cannot observe.

The restatements have already disagreed on the base directory: lock-guard and audit derive <REIFY_WARM_LANE_MOUNT>/<lane>.lock, while seed and thin use the lane path under <mount>/worktrees (existing finding scripts/warm-lane-lock-guard.sh|h1).
findings.proposal: Give the lane lock a sourced library, lib_lane_lock.sh, mirroring lib_lane_x_flock.sh. It should own lane_lock_path(lane_dir), lane_lock_acquire(mode, wait) on one FD, lane_lock_probe and lane_lock_assert_held. lane_lock_assert_held does a non-blocking probe on a fresh FD that must report contended. --assume-lane-lock-held then calls that assertion, so the cross-repo handshake is verified at use.
findings.next_change: Several changes need the protocol: changing the lock location (the mount/worktrees split), adding a new lane consumer such as another reclaim pass, or changing DF's acquire to stop holding the lock across the seed. Each requires finding all six derivations and the DF side. If DF stops holding the lock but keeps passing the flag, seed reseeds unlocked. No test spans the handshake, since tests/infra drives seed with its own holders.

Path derivations are independent at seed:930, thin:384, gc:594/766, lock-guard:197 and audit:1336. Under --assume-lane-lock-held, seed only clears _should_acquire_lane_lock and does no verification that the lock is held. The statement that the lane lock 'has none' (no library) is false. scripts/lib_lane_lock.sh is 'The SINGLE tri-state warm-lane lock probe'. It is sourced by warm-lane-audit.sh and warm-lane-lock-guard.sh, and covered by tests/infra/test_lane_lock_probe.{sh,py}. The lib is explicitly designed to be acquirer-count-agnostic, and the cross-repo handshake (one inode per host, the DF acquirers) is written up in docs/design/merge-verify-lane-dispatch-seam.md. So the probe half of the protocol has a single owner, and a documented seam covers the handshake. What remains is the exclusive-acquire half (seed, thin and gc each with their own FD and path) and the unobserved assume-held flag. The claimed six restatements overcount the probe side.

findings.statement:
The INV-GEO-1 mesh-contract posture (Enforce/Warn) has two homes with different sources, and only one of them is reachable through the Engine.

Engine home: Engine reads MeshContractMode::from_env() at construction (engine_admin.rs:285), exposes pub set_mesh_contract_mode, and threads the value explicitly through RealizationOpsInput to the eval-side conversion handoff (engine_build.rs 3588/4455/5793/6299/12490 → 8461).

Manifold home: the Manifold kernel's ingest ignores all of that. It reads its own process-global `static MODE: OnceLock<MeshContractMode>` from the same env var on first use. The GeometryKernel trait carries no mode parameter.

The two agree only while the env var is the sole input. An Engine configured with set_mesh_contract_mode(Warn), which today only mesh_contract_handoff_diagnostic.rs does, warns at the eval handoff while Manifold ingest still enforces whatever the process env said when the first mesh was ingested.
findings.proposal: Pass the posture to the kernel. Either add it to the ingest call (or to a per-operation options struct the Engine already threads), or have Engine push it at registration through a kernel configuration method. Delete the kernel-local OnceLock so MeshContractMode::from_env has one caller.
findings.next_change: Next changes include a per-session or per-project break-glass (e.g. from reify.toml or a GUI toggle), or a gmsh/OpenVDB ingest that should honour the same posture. Either way, the author would set it on the Engine and find the Manifold path unaffected, because the OnceLock is invisible from Engine and no test drives a Warn engine through Manifold ingest.

But Engine::set_mesh_contract_mode is #[cfg(any(test, feature = "test-instrumentation"))], not a pub production setter. That is why it has 0 production callers. In a production binary both homes derive from the same env var, a deployment-time posture, and the code comment says mid-process re-reading would be meaningless. The two-readers-of-one-env-var duplication is real but low-cost.

findings.statement:
The snapshot-reading entry points check_snapshot, build_snapshot and tessellate_snapshot take a &CompiledModule. They combine its templates with whatever EvaluationState the previous eval, edit_param or edit_source left. Snapshot records no identity for the module it was built from: its fields are id, version, graph, values, topology_fingerprint, provenance and forall_emitted, with no content hash. topology_fingerprint is computed, but none of the three entry points compares it, so the pairing of module and snapshot is purely temporal.

The consumers compensate on their side. reify-lsp keeps its own mirror, EvalState.last_content_hash, beside the engine. Its diagnostics.rs carries a debug-only warning for the case where 'last_content_hash was set without a preceding eval()', and then forces a cold start. The GUI keeps compiled and engine paired inside EngineSession::core to call tessellate_snapshot.
findings.proposal: Record the source module's content_hash in Snapshot or EvaluationState at eval. Have each *_snapshot entry point return an error (or None with a diagnostic) on a mismatch, then delete the LSP mirror.
findings.next_change: A plausible next change is a surface that keeps one engine across several modules, for example multi-document LSP warm reuse or GUI tabs. It would pass module B to a *_snapshot call while the engine holds module A's state. That compiles and returns values for A's cells under B's templates. Today only per-consumer mirrors prevent it.

findings.statement:
compose_morph returns its outcome (Result<VolumeMesh, MorphFailure>) and also records the outcome kind into process-global AtomicU64 COUNTERS: 4 record_* calls (lib.rs 264, 298, 318, 331). Every consumer of morph outcomes reads the globals rather than any per-build value:
- reify-cli prints diagnostics::format_summary(&snapshot()) after builds (main.rs 1622, 1746).
- The GUI debug RPC handle_mesh_morph_stats resets and snapshots them. Its doc concedes that a concurrent recorder can make a post-reset snapshot non-zero.
- reify-eval/tests/morph_arm_e2e.rs asserts on them.

Because the counters are shared across every engine and thread in the process, the tests serialize through 3 independent locks: the mesh-morph crate's TEST_LOCK, morph_arm_e2e's MORPH_DIAG_LOCK, and debug_server's TEST_LOCK. reset_for_test is exported cross-crate behind a 'testing' feature with G-allow justifications.
findings.proposal: Have the Engine's morph producer aggregate the outcome compose_morph already returns into a per-build tally on the build or tessellate result. Keep the process counters only as a telemetry sink, not as the consumer interface. Cross-crate tests then assert on returned values and need no lock.
findings.next_change: Plausible next changes: per-body morph stats in the GUI, a per-build morph summary in BuildResult, or running two engines in one process (the LSP and GUI preview engine). Each needs per-call attribution that the globals cannot give. A new test asserting on the counters must also find and take the right one of the three locks, or it flakes.

findings.statement: EvalContext is an optional-capability builder where every missing capability degrades silently: missing determinacy -> silent Undef, missing diagnostics sink -> warnings dropped; the 'MUST keep .with_determinacy and .with_runtime_diagnostics' invariant was enforced by a doc comment. INV-EVAL-2 proposed a required-args constructor (CellEvalCtx).
findings.checked: Read lib.rs EvalContext/new/simple/_test_at_depth/with_scope (lines 80-292) and eval_pred_for_value_elem. The 7 capability fields are still pub Option<..>; new() and simple() default every one to None; DeterminacyPredicate still returns Undef when determinacy is None, and runtime warnings are still silently dropped when diagnostics is None. Mitigation exists only one layer up: reify-eval/src/cell_eval_ctx.rs (#5039) is a required-args free fn with a fn-pointer type guard and behavioural tests. Adoption is 13 cell_eval_ctx( call sites (engine_edit 8, engine_eval 3, unfold 2) against 68 eval_ctx_with_meta( call sites across 7 files (engine_build 16, engine_eval 22, geometry_ops 12, engine_edit 9, realization_staleness 6, unfold 2, engine_purposes 1). The pre-existing Engine::cell_eval_ctx method still coexists and is cross-checked by a parity test. docs/invariants.md still lists INV-EVAL-2 as 'proposed'. The constructor's type now enforces the invariant at about 16% of construction sites. reify-expr itself has none.
